title: United States: White House hard-pass deactivations for CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters, September 2026
summary: On September 18, 2026, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, announced on Truth Social, a social media platform, and in the Oval Office that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House, the president's office and residence in Washington, D.C. He described the outlets' coverage as "FICTION and LIES." On September 19, 2026, the outlets' reporters were denied entry at the White House gates after their hard passes, the standing credentials that let reporters enter the White House press area without applying each day, were deactivated. The outlets sued on September 21, 2026, and the case is pending as of 2026-09-22.
what_happened:
On September 18, 2026, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, announced on Truth Social and during an appearance in the Oval Office, the president's office in the White House, that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House. He cited accumulated coverage that he called "FICTION and LIES."

The same day, the White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA), the organization of reporters who cover the president of the United States, then led by Jacqui Heinrich, said the Constitution's press protections "do not depend on whether the president likes a news organization's coverage."

On September 19, 2026, the Secret Service, the United States federal agency responsible for protecting the president, turned away CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett at the White House gates. One of the reporters said she was told "they had to take my badge because it was disabled."

On September 20, 2026, the other television networks in the White House press pool, the small rotating group of reporters who cover the president in spaces too small for the full press corps and share what they gather with other outlets, declined to fill CNN's rotating slot in solidarity, according to the Associated Press. News outlets then published explainers on how the White House press pool works.
stated_justification: In his announcement on September 18, 2026, Trump described the outlets' coverage as "FICTION and LIES." The same day he told a Bloomberg reporter, "I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you're terrible." The White House has not identified a specific story that prompted the decision (as of 2026-09-22).
effect_on_reporting: Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico can no longer enter the White House grounds with their hard passes, which were deactivated on September 19, 2026 (as of 2026-09-22). On September 20, 2026, the other networks in the White House press pool declined to fill CNN's rotating slot, so no replacement crew covered it for the shared pool feed that other outlets use.
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: In effect. Challenged in Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03287, in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, the federal trial court in Washington, D.C. (filed 2026-09-21; pending; hearing scheduled for 2026-09-23).
what_we_dont_know: The White House has not said which story or stories prompted the decision (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: White House exclusion of the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One, February 2025
summary: On February 16, 2025, the White House, the office of the president of the United States, began barring journalists from the Associated Press (AP), a United States news agency, from the Oval Office and Air Force One, the aircraft that carries the president. The exclusion followed AP's decision to keep using the name "Gulf of Mexico" after an executive order of the president, Donald Trump, renamed the body of water the "Gulf of America" for United States federal purposes. Trump told reporters, "We're going to keep them out until such time as they agree that it's the Gulf of America," according to NPR. AP sued on February 21, 2025; as of 2026-09-22, a partial stay by a federal appeals court leaves AP excluded from the Oval Office and Air Force One.
what_happened:
On February 16, 2025, the White House began excluding Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, the president's office, and from Air Force One, the president's aircraft. AP's style guide had continued to use the name "Gulf of Mexico" after an executive order, a written directive of the president of the United States, Donald Trump, renamed it the "Gulf of America" for United States federal purposes. AP said it would keep using the historical name while noting the new one.

On February 21, 2025, AP sued White House officials, including Taylor Budowich, the White House deputy chief of staff, in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, the federal trial court in Washington, D.C. (Associated Press v. Budowich, No. 1:25-cv-00532). The complaint alleges "First Amendment retaliation," a claim under the part of the United States Constitution that protects freedom of the press.

On February 25, 2025, a federal judge declined to order AP's access restored immediately while the case proceeded, according to Euronews. The case later produced a preliminary injunction, a partial stay by the D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court for Washington, D.C., and a refusal by the full appeals court to rehear the case (see the case page).
stated_justification: Trump told reporters in February 2025, "We're going to keep them out until such time as they agree that it's the Gulf of America," according to NPR. The White House tied AP's access to its use of the name set by the executive order.
effect_on_reporting: AP reporters and photographers lost access to the Oval Office and Air Force One, small spaces where the news agency had held a regular place in the rotating press pool that covers the president. Trump and his aides barred AP's White House reporters from "dozens of events since February," including events limited to the pool, according to NPR.
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: Partly in effect. Under a partial stay granted 2 to 1 by the D.C. Circuit on 2025-06-06, AP remains excluded from the Oval Office, Air Force One, Mar-a-Lago and the Cabinet Room and keeps access to the East Room. See Associated Press v. Budowich.

title: United States: Department of Defense press credential rules requiring approval before release of information, September 2025
summary: On September 21, 2025, the United States Department of Defense, the federal department that provides the country's military forces, issued new credential rules for reporters at the Pentagon, its headquarters building, under the Secretary of Defense, Pete Hegseth. The rules require that information be approved for public release by an authorizing official "before it is released, even if it is unclassified," and require accredited reporters to pledge not to solicit or publish such information without approval or lose their badges. The Pentagon called the rules "an important step in preventing leaks that damage operational security and national security." A federal judge ruled against the rules in March and April 2026, and the department has appealed (as of 2026-09-22).
what_happened:
On September 21, 2025, the Department of Defense of the United States, under the Secretary of Defense, Pete Hegseth, issued press credential rules that require accredited reporters to sign a pledge not to solicit or publish unclassified but sensitive information without authorization from an appropriate Pentagon official. The rules also restrict reporters' movement inside the Pentagon, the department's headquarters, without an escort.

Hegseth said, "The press is no longer allowed to roam the halls of a secure facility. Wear a badge and follow the rules," and added, "or go home."

Military Times and Defense News, two publications that cover the United States armed forces, said the policy "threatens to punish reporters who ask legitimate questions in the course of their daily work." Most reporters with Pentagon credentials declined to sign and turned in their badges in October 2025 (see the October 2025 entry).
stated_justification: The Department of Defense said the rules were "an important step in preventing leaks that damage operational security and national security."
effect_on_reporting: Reporters who declined to sign the pledge lost their Pentagon credentials and building access. Reporters who sign may not solicit or publish sensitive unclassified information unless a Pentagon official has approved its release.
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: Partly in effect. On March 20, 2026, United States District Judge Paul Friedman ruled that the rules' credential-revocation provisions violated constitutional protections and ordered credentials restored for seven New York Times journalists. The department issued revised restrictions on March 23, 2026, which the Pentagon Press Association called "a clear violation of the letter and spirit" of the ruling. On April 9, 2026, Friedman wrote that the department "simply cannot reinstate an unlawful policy under the guise of taking 'new' action," and the department appealed. Most major outlets work without Pentagon building credentials.
what_we_dont_know: The Department of Defense has not published a list of what counts as "sensitive but unclassified" information under the rules (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: News organizations turn in their Pentagon press credentials, October 2025
summary: Beginning on October 15, 2025, reporters from at least 30 news organizations vacated the press workspace at the Pentagon, the headquarters of the United States Department of Defense, rather than sign the department's new credential pledge, with a deadline of October 17 to remove their belongings. They included ABC News, NBC News, CBS News, Fox News, CNN, the Associated Press, Reuters, Bloomberg News, The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, NPR and Politico. One America News Network said it would sign. As of 2026-09-22, most of these outlets cover the Pentagon from outside the building.
what_happened:
Beginning on October 15, 2025, reporters from at least 30 news organizations began vacating the press room at the Pentagon, the headquarters of the United States Department of Defense, removing equipment and furniture rather than sign the credential pledge the department issued on September 21, 2025. The deadline to remove belongings was October 17, 2025.

The outlets that declined included ABC News, NBC News, CBS News, Fox News, CNN, the Associated Press, Reuters, Bloomberg News, The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, NPR and Politico. One America News Network was reported as the only major outlet to accept the terms.

Military Times and Defense News, two publications that cover the United States armed forces and were among the outlets that declined, said the policy "threatens to punish reporters who ask legitimate questions in the course of their daily work."
stated_justification: The Department of Defense gave no separate reason for requiring the pledge as a condition of the badge. It described the underlying rules as "an important step in preventing leaks that damage operational security and national security."
effect_on_reporting: Reporters from most major news organizations lost routine access to the Pentagon building and its press workspace, and cover the department from outside it (as of 2026-09-22).
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: Partly in effect. The New York Times sued the Department of Defense on December 4, 2025. On March 20, 2026, United States District Judge Paul Friedman ruled that the credential-revocation provisions violated constitutional protections and ordered credentials restored for seven Times journalists. After the department issued revised restrictions, Friedman wrote on April 9, 2026 that it "simply cannot reinstate an unlawful policy under the guise of taking 'new' action," and the department appealed. Most other outlets cover the Pentagon from outside the building.

outcome_note: Credentials were ordered restored for seven New York Times journalists on 2026-03-20; the ruling against the revised policy on 2026-04-09 is on appeal. Most other outlets remain outside the building.

title: United States: White House takes over selection of the presidential press pool, February 2025
summary: On February 25, 2025, the White House announced that it would decide which journalists join the press pool, the small rotating group of reporters who cover the president of the United States in spaces such as the Oval Office and Air Force One and share what they gather with other outlets. The White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA), the organization of reporters who cover the president, said that for more than a century "working journalists" and "not government officials" had "determined pool rotation procedures." As of 2026-09-22, the White House selects the pool, according to the Associated Press.
what_happened:
On February 25, 2025, the White House announced that it would select the journalists who join the limited-space press pool that covers the president of the United States in the Oval Office, on Air Force One and at other small venues. The White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA), the organization of reporters who cover the president, and its member outlets had managed the rotation for more than a century.

The WHCA president, Eugene Daniels, said the association had not been consulted and that the change "suggests the government will choose the journalists who cover the president." The WHCA said it would continue to press for comprehensive access and full transparency.

The announcement came nine days after the White House began excluding the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One (see the February 2025 entry).
stated_justification: The White House asserted its authority over access to spaces such as the Oval Office and Air Force One. It has not given a further reason for taking over pool selection (as of 2026-09-22).
effect_on_reporting: The White House, rather than the working press corps, decides which outlets rotate into the pool that covers the president in small venues, and the pool has included outlets that were not part of the previous rotation (as of 2026-09-22).
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: In effect. The White House "now picks and chooses which members of the media make up the pool," according to the Associated Press.

title: United States: Federal Communications Commission chairman's remarks and the suspension of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, September 2025
summary: On September 17, 2025, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the United States regulator of broadcasting, Brendan Carr, said broadcasters could "do this the easy way or the hard way" over remarks by the television host Jimmy Kimmel, and warned of "additional work for the FCC ahead." Within hours, the station owners Nexstar and Sinclair said they would pull Jimmy Kimmel Live! from their stations, and ABC, the network that airs it, did the same, according to NPR. ABC announced that the show would return on September 23, 2025, according to Al Jazeera.
what_happened:
On September 17, 2025, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the United States regulator that licenses radio and television stations, Brendan Carr, spoke publicly about broadcasters that carried Jimmy Kimmel Live! Kimmel had spoken on air about speculation by some of Donald Trump's supporters over the motives of the person who killed Charlie Kirk, according to NPR.

Carr said, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to change conduct to take action on Kimmel or, you know, there's going to be additional work for the FCC ahead." NPR reported that the show was pulled "hours after the U.S. government threatened to cancel broadcasting licenses."

Nexstar and Sinclair, companies that own many local television stations affiliated with ABC, announced they would pull the show indefinitely. ABC, the network that airs it, then did the same, according to NPR.
stated_justification: Carr said, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to change conduct to take action on Kimmel or, you know, there's going to be additional work for the FCC ahead."
effect_on_reporting: Jimmy Kimmel Live! went off the air on ABC and on stations owned by Nexstar and Sinclair from September 17, 2025, until ABC returned it to its schedule after "a weeklong impasse," according to Al Jazeera.
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: Ended. ABC announced that Jimmy Kimmel Live! would return on September 23, 2025, according to Al Jazeera.
what_we_dont_know: The FCC, ABC, Nexstar and Sinclair have not made public any private communications between them about the suspension (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: Paramount settlement of Donald Trump's lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview, July 2025
summary: On July 1, 2025, Paramount, the parent company of the United States broadcaster CBS News, announced that it would settle for US$16 million a lawsuit brought by Donald Trump, the president of the United States, over how the CBS program 60 Minutes edited a 2024 interview with Kamala Harris, then vice-president. The money goes to Trump's future presidential library and the plaintiffs' fees and costs, and 60 Minutes will release transcripts of future interviews with presidential candidates, "subject to redactions as required for legal or national security concerns." Paramount "has maintained that the lawsuit was completely without merit," according to CBS News.
what_happened:
Donald Trump sued CBS News' parent company, Paramount, over 60 Minutes' editing of a 2024 interview with Kamala Harris, then vice-president of the United States. The lawsuit alleged that the network aired two differently edited excerpts of the same answer, on Face the Nation and on 60 Minutes, in a deceptive way. Ronny Jackson was a co-plaintiff.

On July 1, 2025, Paramount announced a US$16 million settlement, reached with a mediator. The money goes to Trump's future presidential library and the plaintiffs' fees and costs rather than to Trump or Jackson personally. Paramount said the lawsuit was without merit and that the editing followed standard practice.

Under the settlement, 60 Minutes will release transcripts of interviews with presidential candidates, subject to redactions for legal or national security reasons.
stated_justification: Trump's lawsuit alleged that CBS aired two differently edited excerpts of the same answer from the Harris interview in a deceptive way. Paramount "has maintained that the lawsuit was completely without merit," according to CBS News.
effect_on_reporting: Under the settlement announced on July 1, 2025, 60 Minutes will release transcripts of its interviews with presidential candidates, "subject to redactions as required for legal or national security concerns."
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: Settled. The lawsuit ended with the settlement announced on July 1, 2025.
what_we_dont_know: Paramount has not said whether its pending merger with Skydance Media, which awaited approval from United States regulators, bore on its decision to settle (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: Executive Order 14290 directing an end to federal funding for NPR and PBS, May 2025
summary: On May 1, 2025, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, signed Executive Order 14290, "Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Biased Media." It directs the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB), a private non-profit corporation created by the United States Congress in 1967 to distribute federal money to public radio and television, and federal agencies to stop funding NPR and PBS, the country's non-profit public radio and television networks. The order says public funding for news is "not only outdated and unnecessary but corrosive to the appearance of journalistic independence." NPR and PBS said the president cannot cut funding that Congress has appropriated to CPB.
what_happened:
On May 1, 2025, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, signed Executive Order 14290, titled "Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Biased Media." An executive order is a written directive through which the president manages the federal government. The order directs the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB) and federal agencies to end direct and indirect funding of NPR and PBS. It says the two networks violate the requirement of balanced coverage in the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, the United States law that created CPB.

NPR and PBS said CPB is a private, congressionally chartered non-profit and that decisions on federal funding rest with Congress, the national legislature, not with the president. Both said they would contest the order rather than comply voluntarily.

Later in 2025, Congress took separate action on public broadcasting funds, including moves to take back money it had already appropriated to CPB.
stated_justification: The order says public funding for news programming is "not only outdated and unnecessary but corrosive to the appearance of journalistic independence." The accompanying White House fact sheet said, "Neither entity presents a fair, accurate or unbiased portrayal of current events to tax-paying citizens."
effect_on_reporting: The order directs CPB and federal agencies to stop funding NPR and PBS, whose member stations include smaller rural and tribal stations that rely most heavily on CPB grants for their operating budgets.
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: In effect. NPR and PBS say the order is not self-executing and have contested it; disputes over CPB funding continued through 2025 through separate action by Congress.
what_we_dont_know: The sources cited do not state the order's effect in dollars on individual member stations or the outcome of NPR's and PBS's legal response (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: U.S. Agency for Global Media action to shut down Voice of America operations, March 2025
summary: Beginning on March 15, 2025, the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), the United States federal agency that oversees the government's international broadcasters, placed most of its staff on paid administrative leave and moved to shut down the operations of Voice of America (VOA), the United States government's international broadcaster. Kari Lake, a senior advisor at USAGM, carried out the action under an executive order of the president of the United States, Donald Trump, to reduce the federal bureaucracy. VOA journalists sued on March 21, 2025, and on March 28, 2025, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order, a short-term order made before a full hearing, that barred the agency from reducing its workforce.
what_happened:
In March 2025, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, signed an executive order directing federal agencies to reduce their workforce. Kari Lake, installed as a senior advisor at the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), the federal agency that oversees Voice of America (VOA), moved to shut down VOA's operations. The agency cancelled leases and placed nearly all VOA staff on administrative leave beginning on March 15, 2025.

On March 21, 2025, VOA and USAGM journalists, represented in part by the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), a union of United States federal employees, sued the Trump administration and Lake. They argued that the shutdown violated the law that establishes VOA's editorial independence.

On March 28, 2025, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the agency to restore operations, in Widakuswara v. Lake. Further staff cuts and litigation continued into 2026, including a March 2026 order returning about 1,000 VOA staff to work.

title: United States: Department of Justice rescission of rules limiting subpoenas of journalists, April 2025
summary: On April 25, 2025, the Attorney General of the United States, Pam Bondi, head of the Department of Justice, the federal department that prosecutes federal crimes, rescinded rules adopted in 2021 and 2022 under her predecessor, Merrick Garland, that barred prosecutors from seeking reporters' records or testimony to identify the sources of leaks. Bondi's memo said leaks of sensitive information to the media undermine the department's ability "to uphold the rule of law, protect civil rights, and keep America safe." The department returned to a test that weighs law enforcement interests against press freedom, according to the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, a United States non-profit that provides legal help to journalists.
what_happened:
On April 25, 2025, the Attorney General of the United States, Pam Bondi, issued a memo rescinding Department of Justice rules, adopted in a 2021 memo and a 2022 rewrite of the department's media guidelines under Attorney General Merrick Garland, that set a firm rule against subpoenaing journalists' records or compelling their testimony to identify the sources of unauthorized leaks. A subpoena is a legal order that compels a person to testify or hand over records.

The rescission returned the department to a pre-2022 balancing test that weighs law enforcement interests against press freedom. The earlier rules had been adopted after it became known that the Department of Justice, during Trump's first term as president and later under President Joe Biden, had secretly obtained reporters' phone and email records.

The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, a United States non-profit that provides legal help to journalists, said leak investigations "chill newsgathering and reporting in the public interest."

title: United States: White House suspension of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's hard pass, November 2018
summary: On November 7, 2018, the White House suspended the hard pass of CNN's White House correspondent, Jim Acosta, after what Gulf News called a "heated confrontation" between Acosta and the president of the United States, Donald Trump, at a news conference after the country's midterm elections. A hard pass is the standing credential that lets a reporter enter the White House press area without applying each day. On November 16, 2018, a federal judge granted CNN a temporary restraining order requiring the pass to be reinstated, and the White House restored it on November 19, 2018, after which CNN dropped its lawsuit.
what_happened:
On November 7, 2018, after an exchange between CNN correspondent Jim Acosta and the president of the United States, Donald Trump, at a news conference following the midterm elections, the White House revoked Acosta's hard pass, the credential that gave him routine access to the White House grounds.

CNN sued. On November 16, 2018, Judge Timothy J. Kelly of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, the federal trial court in Washington, D.C., granted a temporary restraining order, a short-term order made before a full hearing, requiring that the pass be reinstated. He applied the due process framework of Sherrill v. Knight, a 1977 appeals court decision that a White House press pass may not be denied without notice, a chance to respond and written reasons.

The White House restored Acosta's pass on November 19, 2018, and CNN dropped its suit. The White House then issued written rules for reporters' conduct when asking questions at news conferences.

title: United States (Louisiana): 25-foot buffer zone law around police officers, May 2024
summary: On May 28, 2024, the governor of Louisiana, a state in the southern United States, Jeff Landry, signed a law that makes it a crime to stay within 25 feet (about 7.6 metres) of a working law enforcement officer after the officer has told a person to step back. The law applies to everyone, including journalists. Supporters described it as protecting officers' safety while they work. On January 31, 2025, a federal judge blocked its enforcement while a challenge to it is decided.
what_happened:
On May 28, 2024, the governor of Louisiana, Jeff Landry, signed a law creating a 25-foot (7.6-metre) zone around working law enforcement officers. Once an officer gives a verbal warning, anyone who stays within that distance commits a crime and can face jail.

Nieman Lab, a publication about journalism, reported in August 2024 that the law limits the ability of journalists and bystanders to film police activity, including alleged misconduct, because 25 feet is farther than the distance from which most phone and body-worn video of police encounters is recorded. The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, a United States non-profit that provides legal help to journalists, added Louisiana guidance to its guide to recording laws.

Journalists and civil rights observers challenged the law in federal court.
stated_justification: Supporters described the law as protecting officers' safety while they perform their duties. Landry said on signing it, "This is part of our continued pledge to address public safety."
effect_on_reporting: Journalists and others filming police in Louisiana had to stay at least 25 feet (7.6 metres) away once warned, or face jail, until a federal judge blocked enforcement on January 31, 2025.

title: United States (Louisiana): Federal court order blocking enforcement of the police buffer zone law, January 2025
summary: On January 31, 2025, Judge John W. deGravelles of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana, a federal trial court, blocked enforcement of the state's 25-foot (7.6-metre) police buffer zone law with a preliminary injunction, an order that keeps the situation as it is while a case is decided. He wrote that "the distance required is likely to impede Plaintiffs' non-obstructive newsgathering" and that "the Act has a chilling effect on Plaintiffs' First Amendment rights." The plaintiffs included journalists and civil rights observers. Louisiana was reported to be appealing the order.
what_happened:
On January 31, 2025, Judge John W. deGravelles of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana blocked enforcement of the state's 25-foot police buffer zone law. He ruled that the plaintiffs, including journalists and civil rights observers, were likely to succeed on their claim that the distance requirement would impede newsgathering that does not obstruct police, in breach of the First Amendment, the part of the United States Constitution that protects freedom of speech and of the press.

The challenge argued that the law made routine filming of police from a normal observing distance a crime and gave officers broad discretion to order bystanders back whether or not they were interfering. Louisiana defended the law as an officer-safety measure and was reported to be appealing the injunction to the Fifth Circuit, the federal appeals court based in New Orleans.

title: United States (Florida): Halo Law buffer zone around first responders, January 2025
summary: On January 1, 2025, the "Halo Law" took effect in Florida, a state in the south-eastern United States. It creates a 25-foot (7.6-metre) buffer zone around first responders, such as police officers, firefighters and paramedics, while they are performing their duties, and anyone who enters the zone "to 'harass, impede or threaten' first responders after receiving a warning" faces up to 60 days in prison and a fine of US$500. The law applies to journalists as well as the public. The governor of Florida, Ron DeSantis, signed it in 2024.
what_happened:
Florida's "Halo Law," signed by the governor of Florida, Ron DeSantis, in 2024, took effect on January 1, 2025. Like Louisiana's buffer zone law of the same year, it sets a minimum distance that the public, including journalists, must keep from first responders performing official duties once warned to step back, and treats a violation as a crime.

The law firm Phelps Dunbar grouped Florida's law with Louisiana's as two state laws raising First Amendment concerns for reporters covering police. It noted that both leave anyone recording police to judge a safe distance on the spot or risk arrest.

Unlike Louisiana's law, Florida's had not been blocked by a court as of the sources cited.

title: United States: Nixon White House "enemies list" naming journalists, September 1971
summary: On September 9, 1971, the office of Charles Colson, special counsel to the president of the United States, Richard Nixon, sent White House Counsel John Dean, the president's lawyer on official matters, a memorandum naming 20 people as an initial "enemies list." The list named political opponents, including journalists, for possible action through federal agencies, such as tax audits by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the United States federal tax agency. The IRS commissioner, Donald C. Alexander, refused to launch audits of the people on the list. The lists became public during the Watergate investigations into Nixon's White House.
what_happened:

On August 16, 1971, Dean had written a memo about "how we can use the available federal machinery to screw our political enemies," including through tax audits, denial of federal grants and contracts, and litigation.

Journalists were among the people named on the versions of the list, including the CBS News correspondent Daniel Schorr. The IRS commissioner, Donald C. Alexander, refused to launch audits of the people on the list. The lists became public during the Watergate investigations.

title: United States: Espionage Act prosecutions of sources for leaks to the press, 2009 to 2013
summary: A report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York that documents cases of journalists imprisoned or killed worldwide, published on October 10, 2013, found that since 2009 the United States Department of Justice had brought felony charges against six government employees and two contractors, including Edward Snowden, accused of leaking classified information to the press. The charges were brought under the Espionage Act, a 1917 United States law against disclosing defence information, during the presidency of Barack Obama. The Project On Government Oversight, a United States non-profit that investigates the federal government, said the department under Obama and Attorney General Eric Holder "has used it more than all prior administrations combined."
what_happened:
On October 10, 2013, the Committee to Protect Journalists published a special report documenting that, since 2009, the Department of Justice of the United States, under the president, Barack Obama, had brought felony charges under the Espionage Act against six government employees and two contractors, including Edward Snowden, for leaking classified information to journalists. Across all earlier United States administrations there had been three such prosecutions.

The report said the prosecutions, together with the collection of reporters' phone and email records in leak investigations, left sources reluctant to speak to journalists about diplomacy, national security and intelligence. One source told the report's author, "I worry now about calling somebody because the contact can be found out through a check of phone records or e-mails."

The Freedom of the Press Foundation, a United States non-profit that builds secure communication tools for journalists, later said the pattern set a precedent that later administrations, including Donald Trump's first, could extend.
stated_justification: The prosecutions were brought case by case on national security grounds, not under one stated policy. Matthew Miller, then spokesman for Attorney General Eric Holder, told the report's author, "It was never a conscious decision to bring more of these cases than we ever had. It was a combination of things."
effect_on_reporting: Journalists and their sources in national security reporting said they avoided contact by phone or email for fear of being identified through records requests, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: Ended. The prosecutions are cited by press freedom organizations, including the Freedom of the Press Foundation, as a precedent for later administrations' use of the Espionage Act against sources.

title: Hungary: National Sovereignty Protection Act and Sovereignty Protection Office, December 2023
summary: On December 20, 2023, the president of Hungary, Katalin Novák, promulgated the National Sovereignty Protection Act, passed by the National Assembly, Hungary's parliament, during the government of the prime minister, Viktor Orbán. The law created a Sovereignty Protection Office empowered to investigate organizations, including news outlets, that it determined might be influenced by foreign actors or threaten national sovereignty. A week earlier, ten Hungarian media outlets had said the law "is capable of severely restricting the freedom of the press." After a change of government in 2026, the National Assembly abolished the office on June 30, 2026.
what_happened:
On December 20, 2023, the president of Hungary, Katalin Novák, promulgated the National Sovereignty Protection Act, which the National Assembly, Hungary's parliament, had passed. The law created a Sovereignty Protection Office with power to investigate organizations, including news outlets, that it determined might be influenced by foreign actors or threaten national sovereignty.

In a joint evaluation a week before promulgation, ten Hungarian media outlets said the law "is capable of severely restricting the freedom of the press, potentially making it difficult or even impossible for independent newsrooms, journalists and media companies to operate," according to Reporters Without Borders (RSF), an international organization based in Paris.

After a change of government in 2026, the National Assembly abolished the Sovereignty Protection Office on June 30, 2026. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York, wrote in July 2026 that the office "had been used to harass and delegitimize independent media by labeling them threats to national sovereignty," and described Hungary's initial media reforms as promising but not yet backed by lasting safeguards.
stated_justification: The law's sponsors presented it as protecting Hungary's national sovereignty against foreign influence over civil society and the media. Novák said the office would comply with Hungary's Basic Law, its constitution, and have no impact on press freedom, according to RSF.
effect_on_reporting: Hungarian news outlets that receive foreign funding could be investigated by the Sovereignty Protection Office from December 2023 until its abolition on June 30, 2026. CPJ wrote in July 2026 that the office "had been used to harass and delegitimize independent media by labeling them threats to national sovereignty."
status: Status as of 2026-09-22: Rescinded. The National Assembly abolished the Sovereignty Protection Office on June 30, 2026. CPJ wrote that lasting safeguards for media independence are still needed.

title: India: one-year prison sentence for the journalist Ravi Nair in a criminal defamation case, February 2026
summary: On February 10, 2026, a court in India sentenced the investigative journalist Ravi Nair to one year in prison and a fine of 5,000 rupees (about US$55) for criminal defamation, an offence under which a statement that damages someone's reputation can lead to a fine or prison sentence. title: Israel: ban on independent entry of foreign journalists into the Gaza Strip, 2023 to 2026
summary: Since the war in Gaza began in October 2023, the government of Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering the Gaza Strip, the Palestinian territory on the Mediterranean coast between Israel and Egypt, independently; foreign correspondents have entered only on trips escorted by the Israeli military. On January 7, 2026, Al Jazeera reported that the Foreign Press Association, which represents journalists from international news organizations, had condemned the government's decision to keep the ban. The government had told Israel's Supreme Court that the ban should be maintained due to "security reasons," according to Al Jazeera. On February 25, 2026, the Committee to Protect Journalists reported that the ban was still in place.
what_happened:
Since the war in Gaza began in October 2023, the government of Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering the Gaza Strip independently. Foreign correspondents have been able to enter only on trips escorted by the Israeli military, which limits their ability to check conditions on the ground for themselves.

On January 7, 2026, Al Jazeera reported a statement by the Foreign Press Association (FPA), which represents journalists from international news organizations working in Israel and Gaza. The FPA said, "Instead of presenting a plan for allowing journalists into Gaza independently and letting us work alongside our brave Palestinian colleagues, the government has decided once again to lock us out."

On February 25, 2026, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York that documents cases of journalists imprisoned or killed worldwide, published a special report recording 129 media workers killed in 2025 and holding Israel responsible for about two of every three of those deaths. CPJ separately documented what it called a pattern of harm to Palestinian journalists and media workers, and in 2026 published a review of the method it uses to count them.
stated_justification: Israeli authorities have cited military security concerns for restricting the movement of foreign journalists in Gaza. In January 2026, the government told Israel's Supreme Court that the ban should be maintained due to "security reasons" and that its position was "based on the position of the defence establishment," according to Al Jazeera.

title: Russia: law on asset freezes and service denials for exiled "foreign agents", August 2026
summary: On August 4, 2026, the president of Russia, Vladimir Putin, signed a law, adopted unanimously by the Russian parliament on July 24, 2026, that allows the authorities to freeze bank accounts, block property and vehicle sales and deny consular services such as passport renewal to Russians in exile who have been designated "foreign agents" or who cooperate with organizations Russia has labelled "undesirable." A "foreign agent" is a Russian legal designation that places a person or organization on a government register and subjects them to added restrictions. Of those designated, "the vast majority are journalists," according to Reporters Without Borders (RSF). The law entered into force the same day.
what_happened:
On August 4, 2026, the president of Russia, Vladimir Putin, signed into law legislation passed by the State Duma, the lower house of Russia's parliament, on July 24, 2026. It applies to Russians living in exile who have been designated "foreign agents" or accused of cooperating with organizations Russia has designated "undesirable," a group that Reporters Without Borders (RSF), an international organization based in Paris, says is made up mostly of journalists.

The law allows the authorities to freeze bank accounts and suspend online banking, ban sales of real estate and vehicles, revoke driving licences, redirect income to state-controlled accounts for seizure, block access to Russia's public services portal and deny consular services, including passport renewal.

RSF said the law adds "yet another layer to an already extensive legal arsenal aimed at crushing independent journalism." RSF and Freedom House, a United States-based organization that rates political rights and civil liberties by country, both described it as part of a series of Russian legal measures since 2012 that use the "foreign agent" and "undesirable organization" designations to isolate and financially pressure independent and exiled journalists rather than prosecute them for specific reporting.

Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China with its own courts and legal system.

title: United States postmaster bars the magazine The Masses from the mail under the Espionage Act
summary: Weeks after the United States entered the First World War, the New York postmaster used the new Espionage Act, a law against interfering with military recruitment, to bar the socialist magazine The Masses from the mail. A judge's order protecting the magazine was reversed on appeal.
what_happened: Congress passed the Espionage Act in June 1917, a law that made it a crime to interfere with military recruitment or operations during the First World War. New York's postmaster, Thomas Patten, used the act to declare the August 1917 issue of The Masses, an anti-war socialist magazine, unmailable because of its cartoons and articles opposing the war and the draft. The magazine asked the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, the federal trial court covering Manhattan, to block the ban. Judge Learned Hand agreed, ruling that the magazine's writers had criticized the war without directly urging readers to break the law. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, the appeals court above Hand's, reversed him months later, and the mail ban stood. The Post Office went on to deny mailing privileges to dozens more anti-war and socialist publications under the same law.
stated_justification: Postmaster Patten found the magazine's cartoons and articles likely, in the language of the Espionage Act, to cause insubordination in the armed forces and to obstruct recruiting.
effect_on_reporting: The Masses lost the low second-class postal rate that let it reach subscribers across the country and stopped publishing within months; dozens of other anti-war and socialist papers lost mailing privileges the same way.
issue_of_the_day: The United States had entered the First World War three months earlier and introduced a military draft. The Masses had run cartoons and articles opposing the war and conscription, which the Post Office treated as material likely to obstruct recruiting.
outcome_note: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed Judge Hand's order later in 1917, and the Post Office's mail ban on The Masses stood.

title: United States Postmaster General Burleson strips the Milwaukee Leader of its mailing rate
summary: Postmaster General Albert Burleson used the wartime Espionage Act to strip the Milwaukee Leader, a socialist daily, of its low-cost second-class mailing rate, cutting off its main channel to readers. The Supreme Court upheld the revocation in 1921, over two dissents warning it amounted to press controls.
what_happened: During the First World War, Postmaster General Albert Burleson's Post Office found the Milwaukee Leader, a socialist daily edited under publisher Victor Berger's direction, in violation of the Espionage Act for articles opposing the war, and revoked its second-class mailing permit, the low postal rate newspapers depended on to reach subscribers nationwide. The paper's publishing company asked the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, to order the Post Office to restore the rate, arguing the denial violated the Constitution's protections for speech and due process. In United States ex rel. Milwaukee Social Democratic Publishing Co. v. Burleson, decided March 7, 1921, the Court upheld Burleson's action by a 7 to 2 vote. Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes and Louis Brandeis dissented, warning that letting a postmaster judge a paper's loyalty amounted to a form of press controls over the mail.
stated_justification: The Post Office found the Leader's wartime articles violated the Espionage Act, and the majority opinion held that the Constitution was not a shield for those who used its privileges to work against the government.
effect_on_reporting: The Leader lost the inexpensive second-class postal rate other newspapers used to reach subscribers across the country, forcing it onto costlier first-class postage and cutting its circulation.
issue_of_the_day: The Leader had published articles criticizing United States participation in the First World War and the draft, which the Post Office treated as violations of the Espionage Act's ban on obstructing military recruitment.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court upheld the revocation of the Leader's mailing rate 7 to 2 in United States ex rel. Milwaukee Social Democratic Publishing Co. v. Burleson.

title: United States Supreme Court strikes down a Minnesota law used to shut a newspaper
summary: A Hennepin County attorney used Minnesota's 1925 Public Nuisance Law to shut down The Saturday Press, a Minneapolis paper accusing officials of corruption. In 1931 the Supreme Court of the United States struck the law down, ruling that stopping a paper before publication was itself a form of press controls.
what_happened: Minnesota's 1925 Public Nuisance Law let a judge permanently shut any newspaper or periodical found to be malicious, scandalous or defamatory. In 1927 the Hennepin County Attorney, Floyd Olson, used the law to close The Saturday Press, a Minneapolis weekly run by Jay Near that had accused local officials and gangsters of corruption. Near appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, arguing the law violated the free-press guarantee that the First Amendment applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause. On June 1, 1931, the Court ruled 5 to 4 in Near v. Minnesota that the law amounted to a prior restraint the Constitution did not allow, meaning government could not stop publication in advance, even of material later found libelous; a publisher could still be sued afterward, but the paper itself could not be shut down first. The decision became the foundation of later United States rulings against government orders blocking publication before it happens.
stated_justification: Minnesota officials said the Public Nuisance Law applied to papers that habitually published malicious, scandalous or defamatory material, and treated The Saturday Press's allegations against local officials as exactly that kind of publication.
effect_on_reporting: The Saturday Press was shut down under the injunction; after the Supreme Court's ruling, states lost the power to close a newspaper in advance for its content, though publishers remained open to being sued afterward.
issue_of_the_day: The Saturday Press had run articles accusing Minneapolis officials, police and a local gangster of corruption and racketeering, allegations the county attorney treated as scandalous and defamatory under the state's 1925 nuisance law.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court of the United States struck down the Minnesota law 5 to 4 as a restraint on publication in advance that the Constitution did not allow.

title: United States creates an Office of Censorship and a wartime code for the press
summary: Twelve days after the bombing of Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt created the Office of Censorship. Its director, Byron Price, a former Associated Press editor, wrote a Code of Wartime Practices asking newspapers and broadcasters to withhold information such as troop movements, and most of the press followed it voluntarily.
what_happened: Twelve days after Japan's December 7, 1941 bombing of the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor drew the country into the Second World War, President Franklin Roosevelt signed an order on December 19, 1941 creating the Office of Censorship. He named Byron Price, a former executive news editor of the Associated Press wire service, to run it. Price's office wrote a Code of Wartime Practices for American newspapers and, separately, for radio stations, asking editors and broadcasters not to publish or air information of possible use to an enemy, such as troop, ship and plane movements, weather conditions, casualty lists and damage to military targets. The code was voluntary rather than a legal requirement, and American publishers and broadcasters, largely supportive of the war effort, followed it without a formal enforcement mechanism. The office also opened and read international mail, cables and other communications. It was abolished once the war in the Pacific ended.
stated_justification: Roosevelt said Americans hated press controls as much as they hated war but treated it as unavoidable in wartime, arguing that military information of possible use to an enemy had to be kept from publication at its source.
effect_on_reporting: Newspapers and broadcasters voluntarily withheld reporting on troop and ship movements, fortifications, weather, casualty lists and damage to military targets for the war's duration under the Office of Censorship's code.
issue_of_the_day: The United States had just entered the Second World War after the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor, and the government wanted to prevent newspapers and broadcasters from unintentionally publishing information useful to enemy forces.
outcome_note: The Office of Censorship operated on the press's voluntary compliance through the war and was abolished by executive order after Japan's surrender.

title: United States Senate panel subpoenas dozens of New York Times journalists over Communist ties
summary: The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, led by Senator James Eastland, issued 35 subpoenas over past or present Communist Party ties in the press, and 26 of them went to New York Times staff. The newspaper protested but several employees who would not answer were fired or forced to resign.
what_happened: The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, a Senate panel investigating Communist Party influence chaired by Senator James Eastland of Mississippi, issued a wave of subpoenas in November 1955 for closed hearings on Communism in the press, radio and television industries. Of 35 subpoenas issued, 26 went to past or present employees of The New York Times. The newspaper's own editorial page said the investigation appeared aimed squarely at the paper, while also saying it did not believe in permanent guilt and thought employees could make up for past association with the Communist Party through good work. Even so, several Times staff members who indicated they would invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination rather than answer the subcommittee's questions were dismissed or pressured to resign before or after testifying, including one employee let go before the hearings even began. Other newspapers, including the New York Daily News and the Hearst-owned Daily Mirror, fired staff members in the same way.
stated_justification: The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee said it was investigating Communist Party influence within newsrooms, and its subpoenas asked witnesses about past or present party membership.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists at The New York Times and other papers who would not answer the subcommittee's questions about Communist Party ties were fired or pressured into resigning, a pattern that spread to other newsrooms during the hearings.
issue_of_the_day: Senator Eastland's subcommittee was investigating what it described as Communist Party influence in American newsrooms and broadcasting during the Cold War, and treated past party membership among journalists as grounds for scrutiny.
outcome_note: The dismissals and resignations at The New York Times and other papers were not reversed; the paper said at year's end it had made no further dismissals beyond the initial cases.

title: Nixon White House compiles an enemies list naming journalists for official pressure
summary: White House Counsel John Dean wrote a memo on how to use federal agencies against President Nixon's political opponents, and the resulting list of more than 200 names included journalists such as CBS News correspondent Daniel Schorr. It became public during the 1973 Senate Watergate hearings.
what_happened: Staff in President Richard Nixon's White House began compiling a list of political opponents in June 1971. On August 16, 1971, White House Counsel John Dean wrote a memo titled 'Dealing with our Political Enemies,' describing how the administration could use the machinery of the federal government, including the Internal Revenue Service, the United States tax-collection agency, to conduct tax audits and other scrutiny of people and organizations it considered critical. The list grew to more than 200 names by September 1971 and included a media category naming journalists alongside politicians, activists and business figures. CBS News correspondent Daniel Schorr discovered he was number 17 on the list; The Washington Post columnist Mary McGrory was included for what an internal notation called her 'daily hate Nixon articles.' Dean revealed the list during his testimony to the Senate Watergate Committee, the Senate panel investigating the Watergate scandal, on June 27, 1973, making it public for the first time.
stated_justification: Dean's memo described the effort as a way to use the available machinery of the federal government against people the administration regarded as its political enemies, without citing any specific conduct by the journalists named.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists named on the list, including Daniel Schorr and Mary McGrory, learned their reporting or commentary had made them targets for the same federal pressure, including possible tax audits, that the administration considered using against other political opponents.
issue_of_the_day: Nixon's aides were reacting to sustained critical coverage and commentary from named journalists during his first term, including Mary McGrory's columns, which an internal notation described as habitually critical to the president.
outcome_note: The list became public during John Dean's Senate Watergate Committee testimony, discrediting the effort as Nixon's presidency unraveled over the wider Watergate scandal.

title: United States government seeks an injunction to stop The New York Times publishing the Pentagon Papers
summary: After The New York Times began publishing a leaked secret history of the Vietnam War, the Nixon administration obtained a court order stopping further publication, the first such order against a major American newspaper. The Supreme Court lifted it two weeks later, ruling the government had not justified blocking publication in advance.
what_happened: Military analyst Daniel Ellsberg copied a classified Defense Department history of United States involvement in Vietnam, later known as the Pentagon Papers, and gave it to The New York Times, which began publishing excerpts on June 13, 1971. The Department of Justice obtained a temporary restraining order from a federal court on June 15, 1971, the first time the United States government had gone to court to stop a major newspaper from publishing a specific story, arguing publication would harm national security. When The Washington Post also began publishing excerpts, the government sought an injunction against it too. The Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, heard the consolidated case on an emergency basis and ruled 6 to 3 on June 30, 1971, in New York Times Co. v. United States, that the government had not met the heavy burden required to justify stopping publication in advance, and both papers resumed publishing.
stated_justification: Government lawyers argued that publishing the classified history would cause grave and irreparable harm to United States national security and ongoing diplomatic and military efforts in Vietnam.
effect_on_reporting: The New York Times and The Washington Post were barred by court order from publishing further excerpts of the Pentagon Papers for roughly two weeks until the Supreme Court lifted the injunction.
issue_of_the_day: The Pentagon Papers documented decades of internal government decision-making on the Vietnam War that contradicted public statements by several administrations, and the Nixon administration sought to prevent further disclosure of the classified history.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the government's request for an injunction against publication failed to overcome the heavy presumption against prior restraint.

claims.statement: The Supreme Court's per curiam opinion said any system of restraints on publication ordered in advance came to the Court bearing a heavy presumption against being constitutional.
claims.evidence_quote: Any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity.

claims.value: Black concurrence on the press's role
claims.statement: Justice Hugo Black wrote that the press was protected precisely so it could disclose the government's secrets and inform the public.
claims.evidence_quote: The press was protected so that it could bare the secrets of government and inform the people.

claims.statement: The Pentagon Papers were commissioned by Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara and covered the United States role in Indochina from the Second World War until May 1968, before Daniel Ellsberg leaked them in 1971.
claims.evidence_quote: Pentagon Papers, papers that contain a history of the U.S. role in Indochina from World War II until May 1968.

title: United States Supreme Court rules reporters have no privilege to refuse grand jury subpoenas
summary: Louisville Courier-Journal reporter Paul Branzburg was subpoenaed by a Kentucky grand jury, a body that investigates possible crimes, after he wrote about drug users he had observed. The Supreme Court ruled in 1972 that the First Amendment gives reporters no special right to withhold sources or information from a grand jury.
what_happened: Paul Branzburg, a reporter for the Louisville Courier-Journal newspaper in Kentucky, wrote articles describing drug users he had observed making and using hashish, without naming them. A Jefferson County, Kentucky grand jury, a body of citizens that investigates possible crimes and can compel testimony, subpoenaed Branzburg in 1969 to identify the people he had written about; he refused, arguing the First Amendment protected him from having to reveal confidential sources and information gathered for reporting. His case was combined with two others raising the same question and reached the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court. On June 29, 1972, the Court ruled 5 to 4 in Branzburg v. Hayes that reporters have the same obligation as any other citizen to answer relevant questions before a grand jury, rejecting the claim of a constitutional reporter's privilege to withhold sources.
stated_justification: The Kentucky grand jury said it needed Branzburg's testimony to investigate the drug offenses he had personally witnessed while reporting, and the Supreme Court's majority held reporters had the same duty as other citizens to answer such questions.
effect_on_reporting: Reporters in the United States gained no constitutional shield against being compelled to testify before a grand jury or reveal confidential sources, leaving protection for sources to depend on state shield laws or prosecutorial discretion.
issue_of_the_day: Branzburg's articles on drug use and manufacturing drew the attention of Kentucky prosecutors, who wanted him to identify the people he had described witnessing commit the underlying offenses.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court upheld the grand jury's power to compel Branzburg's testimony 5 to 4, finding no First Amendment reporter's privilege.

claims.statement: The Supreme Court held that a reporter cannot claim First Amendment protection for withholding confidentially received information from a grand jury.
claims.evidence_quote: A reporter cannot claim First Amendment protection in withholding confidentially received information from a grand jury.

claims.statement: The Court framed the issue as whether reporters must respond to grand jury subpoenas and answer relevant questions the same way other citizens do.
claims.evidence_quote: The sole issue before us is the obligation of reporters to respond to grand jury subpoenas as other citizens do, and to answer questions relevant to an investigation into the commission of crime.

claims.statement: The Court said the First Amendment does not void every incidental burden on the press that results from enforcing general criminal or civil law.
claims.evidence_quote: It is clear that the First Amendment does not invalidate every incidental burdening of the press that may result from the enforcement of civil or criminal statutes of general applicability.

title: United States military bars journalists from the invasion of Grenada
summary: When United States forces invaded the Caribbean island of Grenada on October 25, 1983, military commanders kept all journalists away from the island for the first two days of fighting, citing operational reasons. Protests from news organizations led the Pentagon to create a rotating press pool for future operations.
what_happened: United States forces invaded the eastern Caribbean island nation of Grenada on October 25, 1983, under the Reagan administration, in an operation named Urgent Fury. Admiral Wesley McDonald, the operation's commander, barred journalists from the island for what he called operational reasons, and the Pentagon arranged no transportation, movement or communications facilities for reporters trying to reach Grenada on their own. Journalists were held on the nearby island of Barbados for roughly 48 hours while the fighting continued. After protests from news organizations and members of Congress, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the senior body of United States military leadership, ordered limited press access restored by October 28. The exclusion prompted a Pentagon-appointed panel, the Sidle Commission, to recommend a rotating pool of reporters for the early stages of future military operations, a system the Pentagon adopted in 1985.
stated_justification: Military commanders said the initial exclusion of journalists protected reporters' safety during active combat, a rationale journalists disputed by noting they had always accepted the risks of covering war as part of their profession.
effect_on_reporting: No independent journalists were present to document the first two days of the invasion, and the press pool of about 15 reporters that eventually reached Grenada on October 27 remained tightly escorted by the military.
issue_of_the_day: Defense officials had for years blamed unrestricted press coverage for damaging public and political support during the Vietnam War, and applied that lesson by excluding reporters from the opening phase of the Grenada operation.
outcome_note: The Pentagon created a standing national media pool in 1985 on the Sidle Commission's recommendation, formally reversing the total exclusion used in Grenada.

claims.statement: When American soldiers landed on Grenada's beaches at 5 a.m. on October 25, 1983, journalists were not present to document the invasion.
claims.evidence_quote: When American soldiers stormed the island's beaches at 5 a.m., journalists weren't there to document the invasion.

claims.statement: Admiral Wesley McDonald barred reporters from the island for what he described as operational reasons.
claims.evidence_quote: Adm. Wesley McDonald banned reporters for 'operational reasons.'

claims.statement: A Pentagon-appointed panel concluded that while open coverage remained preferable, a pool of reporters would be an acceptable way to cover the early stages of a surprise military operation.
claims.evidence_quote: while open coverage of conflict would be the preferred method, a pool of reporters would be acceptable and, at times, desirable in covering early stages of combat or surprise attacks.

title: Haiti's Duvalier government arrests and deports Radio Haiti-Inter staff, driving its director into exile
summary: Under President Jean-Claude Duvalier, Haitian authorities arrested and deported staff of Radio Haiti-Inter, an independent station that had reported critically on the government, forcing its director, journalist Jean Dominique, into exile in 1981. He returned only after Duvalier's government fell in 1986.
what_happened: Jean Dominique had worked at Radio Haiti since the late 1960s and bought the station in 1971, renaming it Radio Haiti-Inter and building it into Haiti's leading independent broadcaster under the government of President-for-life Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier, who had succeeded his father, François Duvalier, in 1971. In 1981, authorities arrested and deported Dominique's wife, journalist Michèle Montas, along with other Radio Haiti-Inter staff, and Dominique himself was forced into exile the same year. The station's independent reporting on government abuses had long drawn official friction. Dominique did not return to Haiti until February 1986, after the fall of Duvalier's government ended nearly three decades of rule by father and son. He would later be forced into exile a second time, in 1991, after a separate military takeover, before returning again in 1994.
stated_justification: Haitian authorities did not publish a specific charge against Radio Haiti-Inter's staff; contemporary accounts describe the arrests and deportations as part of the Duvalier government's broader intolerance of the station's independent reporting.
effect_on_reporting: Radio Haiti-Inter lost its director and other staff to arrest, deportation and exile in 1981, suppressing one of Haiti's few independent broadcast voices until Dominique's return five years later.
issue_of_the_day: Radio Haiti-Inter had built a reputation for independent reporting critical of the Duvalier government at a time when most Haitian media avoided such coverage, drawing sustained official friction toward the station.
outcome_note: Jean Dominique returned to Haiti and to Radio Haiti-Inter in February 1986 after the fall of President-for-life Jean-Claude Duvalier's government.

claims.statement: Jean Dominique was forced into exile in 1981 after his wife, journalist Michèle Montas, and other Radio Haiti-Inter staff were arrested and deported by the government.
claims.evidence_quote: forced into exile in 1981 after his wife, Michèle Montas, and other Haiti Inter staff were arrested and deported by the regime

claims.statement: Dominique was described as a critic of the Duvalier family's rule of Haiti from 1957 to 1986.
claims.evidence_quote: a critic of the Duvalier dictatorship (1957-86)

claims.statement: Dominique returned to Haiti after the fall of President-for-life Jean-Claude Duvalier in February 1986.
claims.evidence_quote: He returned after the fall of President-for-Life Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier in February 1986.

title: Brazil's Vargas government creates a state messaging department with broad press powers
summary: President Getúlio Vargas created the Department of Press and state messaging in 1939 during Brazil's Estado Novo dictatorship, giving the government direct control over what newspapers, radio and film could publish. The department operated as a central instrument of press controls for six years, until the Estado Novo ended in 1945.
what_happened: Getúlio Vargas, president of Brazil, had ruled by decree since closing Congress in 1937 and declaring the Estado Novo, or New State. In 1939 his government created the Departamento de Imprensa e Propaganda, the Department of Press and state messaging, known as the DIP, to control news content and promote the government's political program across newspapers, radio and film. The DIP reviewed material before publication, dictated approved themes and language, and could shut down or discipline outlets that stepped outside its guidelines. It functioned as the government's central instrument of press control for six years, shaping coverage of Vargas's policies and suppressing criticism of his government. The DIP was dissolved in 1945 when the Estado Novo ended and Vargas was removed from power by the military, though its intelligence and information functions were later inherited by successor government bodies.
stated_justification: Vargas's government presented the DIP as the coordinating body for national state messaging under the Estado Novo, tasked with promoting the government's program rather than acknowledging a role in suppressing criticism.
effect_on_reporting: Brazilian newspapers, radio stations and filmmakers operated under the DIP's pre-publication review and approved-content guidelines for six years, with the department able to discipline or close outlets that published material outside its guidelines.
issue_of_the_day: Vargas had ruled by decree since 1937 under the Estado Novo and used the DIP to promote his government's program and nationalist agenda while suppressing coverage critical of his rule.
outcome_note: The DIP was dissolved in 1945 when the military removed Vargas from power and the Estado Novo dictatorship ended.

claims.statement: The Department of Press and Propaganda, the DIP, was created in Vargas's Brazil in 1939 to promote Getúlio Vargas's political propaganda.
claims.evidence_quote: O DIP, Departamento de Imprensa e Propaganda foi criado no Brasil de Vargas em 1939 para promover a propaganda política de Getúlio Vargas.

claims.statement: For six years the DIP served as a powerful instrument of censorship in Brazil.
claims.evidence_quote: Por seis anos, foi um poderoso instrumento de censura no país

claims.statement: Brazil's Estado Novo was a dictatorial period from 1937 to 1945 under President Getúlio Vargas, the period during which the DIP operated.
claims.evidence_quote: dictatorial period (1937–45) in Brazil during the rule of President Getúlio Vargas

title: Chile's military government shuts opposition radio stations and newspapers after the 1973 coup
summary: On the day of the September 11, 1973 military coup that overthrew President Salvador Allende, Chile's armed forces bombed and shut down radio stations that opposed the takeover, arrested journalists and closed newspapers aligned with the ousted government, under the military junta led by Augusto Pinochet.
what_happened: On September 11, 1973, Chile's armed forces, led by General Augusto Pinochet, moved to overthrow the elected government of President Salvador Allende. As the coup unfolded, the military moved against radio stations that continued broadcasting statements opposing the takeover. Radio Magallanes was bombed and hit with gunfire around 10 a.m. and went off the air about 27 minutes later, with four of its journalists arrested in the raid. Radio Candelaria, the last station still opposing the coup, lost its signal shortly before the presidential palace, La Moneda, was bombed at 11:52 a.m. In the following days, the new military government shut down news outlets that had supported Allende's government and barred many journalists identified with them from working in Chile's now military-controlled press, forcing some into what one journalist later called internal exile and driving others abroad.
stated_justification: The military junta that took power on September 11, 1973 treated broadcasters and newspapers that had supported Allende's government as extensions of a political order it had just overthrown, and moved to suppress them as part of securing control.
effect_on_reporting: Radio stations supporting Allende's government went off the air within hours of the coup, journalists were arrested during the takeover, and outlets aligned with the ousted government were shut down and their staff blacklisted from the Chilean press.
issue_of_the_day: Chile's armed forces were in the process of overthrowing President Salvador Allende's elected government on September 11, 1973, and moved to suppress broadcasters and newspapers that continued to support him as the coup unfolded.
outcome_note: Press restrictions continued under military rule until Chile's return to civilian government in March 1990, after Pinochet lost a 1988 plebiscite on his continued rule.

claims.evidence_quote: Less than an hour later, at 10 a.m., Radio Magallanes was bombed and hit with machine-guns.

title: Argentina's military junta threatens journalists with prison for reporting on its opponents
summary: Hours after seizing power on March 24, 1976, Argentina's military junta, led by General Jorge Videla, issued Communiqué No. 19, threatening up to 10 years in prison for reporting favorable to groups it called subversive. Hundreds of journalists were later detained, killed or forced into exile.
what_happened: Argentina's armed forces overthrew President Isabel Perón's government on March 24, 1976 and installed a military junta headed by General Jorge Videla. The same day, the junta issued Communiqué No. 19, threatening imprisonment of up to 10 years for anyone who published or reproduced material from organizations the government had banned, and threatening up to 10 years for reporting that the government said disrupted, harmed or discredited the armed forces. Security forces raided newspapers around the country, arresting and jailing editors and reporters and closing some publications outright. Jacobo Timerman, editor of the newspaper La Opinión, was detained in April 1977 and later held under house arrest. At the English-language Buenos Aires Herald, editor Robert Cox and journalist Andrew Graham-Yooll kept publishing the names of people who had disappeared under the military's rule, until death threats forced both men to leave the country. A subcommittee investigating the period found that roughly 500 journalists had left Argentina for political reasons, while dozens more were reported missing or held in detention centers.
stated_justification: The junta's Communiqué No. 19 framed reporting on groups it had banned, or coverage it considered damaging to the armed forces, as itself a punishable offense carrying years of imprisonment.
effect_on_reporting: Newspapers were raided and some closed, editors and reporters were jailed, and rights investigators later documented dozens of journalists missing or in detention and roughly 500 who left the country for political reasons during the military's rule.
issue_of_the_day: Argentina's military had just overthrown the elected government and moved immediately to prevent reporting sympathetic to leftist groups it had outlawed or reporting it considered damaging to the armed forces' standing.
outcome_note: Argentina returned to civilian, elected government under President Raúl Alfonsín in December 1983, ending the junta's press decrees.

claims.statement: The junta's Communiqué No. 19 provided for imprisonment for an indefinite period for anyone who disseminated or reproduced communiqués or pictures from organizations it had outlawed.
claims.evidence_quote: he, who, by whatever means, disseminates or reproduces communiqués or pictures from...illegal associations...shall be punished, by imprisonment for an indefinite time period

claims.evidence_quote: approximately 500 journalists were forced to leave the country for political reasons
