title: Zimbabwe enacts a law requiring all journalists and media houses to hold government licenses
summary: Zimbabwe's parliament passed the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA), requiring every journalist and media company to obtain a government license renewed every two years, weeks before a closely contested 2002 presidential election.
what_happened: In March 2002, weeks before a presidential election, Zimbabwe's government, led by President Robert Mugabe, enacted the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA). The law required every journalist and media company to be licensed by a government-appointed regulator, the Media and Information Commission, with licenses renewable every two years, and created new offenses for publishing information officials deemed false. Freedom House said the law "requires all journalists and media companies to be licensed, imposes strict content restrictions, and grants broad powers to a government-controlled regulator." Independent outlets and press-freedom groups opposed the law in principle, saying statutory licensing of print media had no place in a democracy; some foreign correspondents were denied accreditation and independent papers, including the Daily News, were later prosecuted for operating without a license. A 2007 amendment eased individual accreditation requirements outside covering Parliament or official events, but Freedom House said the framework remained "extremely restrictive."
stated_justification: The law's licensing and content provisions were presented as regulating professional standards and accountability in the media; the sources reviewed did not record a specific quoted government defense beyond the law's own grant of power to a state-appointed regulator.
effect_on_reporting: Every journalist and media house needed a government-issued, renewable license to operate; independent outlets that published without one, including the Daily News, faced closure, and Freedom House called the framework "extremely restrictive, with onerous licensing requirements."
issue_of_the_day: Zimbabwe's contested March 2002 presidential election, in which President Mugabe faced international criticism over the vote's conduct.
outcome_note: The record reviewed documents a 2007 amendment easing individual accreditation but does not establish to day precision when AIPPA's licensing framework was repealed.

title: Investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya is shot dead in Moscow; a former police officer is later convicted of organizing the killing
summary: Anna Politkovskaya, a Novaya Gazeta journalist known for reporting critical of Russia's conduct of the war in Chechnya, was shot dead in her Moscow apartment building; a Moscow court later convicted a former police officer of organizing surveillance for her killers.
what_happened: Anna Politkovskaya, a reporter for the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was known for reporting on human-rights abuses during Russia's war in Chechnya, a mostly Muslim region in Russia's North Caucasus, and for criticism of President Vladimir Putin's government. On October 7, 2006, Putin's birthday, she was shot dead in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building. Investigators eventually charged several men, including Sergei Khadzhikurbanov, reported as a former police officer, and, later, Dmitry Pavlyuchenkov, a former officer in a Moscow police surveillance unit, who pleaded guilty in 2012 to tracking Politkovskaya's movements and supplying the gun used to kill her. A Moscow court sentenced Pavlyuchenkov to 11 years in exchange for his cooperation; he told the court, "I want to appeal to the family of Anna Stepanovna; I simply want to ask for their human forgiveness." Five men were eventually convicted; who ordered the killing was never conclusively established in court. The Kremlin did not immediately comment on her death.
stated_justification: No government body said it was responsible or offered a public justification; investigators built their case around the men convicted of organizing and carrying out the killing, including a former police surveillance officer, without conclusively naming who ordered it.
effect_on_reporting: The Russian Union of Journalists' Igor Yakovenko called it "clearly a contract killing," and the International Federation of Journalists said it "reflects on the state of lawlessness that is threatening to overwhelm the whole of Russian journalism."
issue_of_the_day: Politkovskaya's investigative reporting on human-rights abuses in Chechnya and her criticism of the Russian government's conduct there.
outcome_note: Courts convicted and sentenced five men, including former police officer Dmitry Pavlyuchenkov, for organizing or carrying out the killing; who ordered it was never conclusively established in court.

title: Iran expels a BBC correspondent and restricts foreign journalists after a disputed 2009 election
summary: After Iran's disputed June 2009 presidential election produced mass protests, the government expelled BBC correspondent Jon Leyne, revoked foreign press credentials, confined most foreign journalists to office-based reporting, and blocked access to numerous websites.
what_happened: Iran's June 12, 2009 presidential election, which officials declared a large win for incumbent Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, prompted mass street protests over allegations of fraud. The government accused foreign media of inciting unrest; the state Fars news agency accused BBC correspondent Jon Leyne of "dispatching fabricated news and reports, ignoring neutrality in news, supporting rioters and trampling the Iranian nation's rights," and authorities ordered him to leave the country. The government revoked accreditation for many foreign journalists, barred them from reporting from the streets, and permitted only phone interviews and official government sources; Al Arabiya's Tehran operation was temporarily suspended. Foreign minister Manouchehr Mottaki called the election "a very transparent competition" and accused Britain of interference without providing evidence. Some journalists, including The New York Times' Roger Cohen, continued reporting despite the restrictions. Authorities also blocked numerous websites and limited mobile-phone text messaging during the unrest that followed.
stated_justification: State media accused BBC correspondent Jon Leyne of "dispatching fabricated news and reports, ignoring neutrality in news, supporting rioters and trampling the Iranian nation's rights"; Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki called the election "a very transparent competition" and blamed unrest on foreign interference.
effect_on_reporting: Foreign correspondents lost accreditation and were confined largely to phone interviews and official sources rather than street reporting; one report said the government revoked all foreign press passes during the unrest, forcing some journalists to work without official credentials.
issue_of_the_day: Iran's disputed June 12, 2009 presidential election and the mass protests that followed allegations the vote was rigged for incumbent Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.
outcome_note: The sources reviewed do not establish when Iran lifted the specific 2009 restrictions on foreign correspondents covering the post-election protests.

title: Hungary's parliament gives a government-appointed media council power to fine outlets for unbalanced coverage
summary: Hungary's parliament, controlled by Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party, passed a media law creating a government-appointed National Media and Infocommunications Authority empowered to fine any outlet, print, broadcast or online, for coverage it deemed unbalanced or offensive to public morality.
what_happened: In December 2010, Hungary's parliament, where Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party held a two-thirds majority, passed a media law creating the National Media and Infocommunications Authority, a regulator whose board is appointed by the parliamentary majority for nine-year terms. The law let the authority impose fines, reported at up to roughly half a million dollars per violation, on any news outlet it judged had produced "unbalanced" coverage or violated vaguely defined standards of "public morality," and required outlets to register with the state. The law took effect January 1, 2011. The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe called the media council's power "unprecedented in European democracies," and former European Union Commissioner Laszlo Kovacs said, "The law provides total control to the government over all the media, both public and private." Orban said the government was "monitoring its practical application" and would address concerns if verified; a Media Council legal official acknowledged the country's earlier "unfettered press freedom" had also produced problems.
stated_justification: Prime Minister Orban said the government was "monitoring its practical application and if any of the political concerns are verified ... we are ready to remedy them," while a Media Council legal official said Hungary's earlier "unfettered press freedom" had "yielded some negative fruit as well."
effect_on_reporting: Every news outlet, print, broadcast or online, became subject to fines of up to roughly half a million dollars for coverage a government-appointed board deemed unbalanced; the OSCE called the board's power "unprecedented in European democracies."
issue_of_the_day: The incoming Fidesz government's broader effort, after its April 2010 election win, to restructure Hungary's state institutions, including media regulation.
outcome_note: The law took effect January 1, 2011, and, after European Union criticism, Hungary amended some provisions in 2011 but kept the media authority's core licensing and fining powers.

title: Ecuador's Organic Communication Law creates a regulator that issues hundreds of sanctions against journalists and outlets
summary: Ecuador's National Assembly passed the Organic Communication Law under President Rafael Correa, creating the Superintendency of Information and Communication (SUPERCOM), a regulator that issued more than 675 sanctions against journalists and media outlets over the following four years.
what_happened: On June 25, 2013, Ecuador's National Assembly, controlled by allies of President Rafael Correa, passed the Organic Communication Law, which created the Superintendency of Information and Communication (SUPERCOM), a regulator empowered to fine, reprimand or order public apologies from journalists and outlets found to have violated the law's content rules, provisions the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights said were used against coverage unfavorable to the government. Within four years, SUPERCOM had opened 1,081 cases and issued 675 sanctions, by its own count, split by the monitoring group Fundamedios into 324 fines, 137 written reprimands and 54 forced public apologies. SUPERCOM itself said the law guaranteed rather than restricted press freedom because "in four years no media outlet has been closed." After Correa left office, President Lenin Moreno proposed eliminating SUPERCOM in 2018; his communications secretary said, "If we're in a constructive process, we should get rid of the Supercom."
stated_justification: SUPERCOM described its own record as evidence the law protected rather than restricted the press, saying "in four years no media outlet has been closed," while United Nations and Inter-American human-rights bodies said the law had been "used as an instrument to unduly interfere in the content of media outlets and punish them, especially when their coverage is unfavorable."
effect_on_reporting: SUPERCOM opened 1,081 cases and issued 675 sanctions against journalists and outlets in four years, including fines, written reprimands and forced public apologies, a pattern Fundamedios and international monitors said pressured critical coverage.
issue_of_the_day: President Correa's long-running public disputes with Ecuadorian media over their coverage of his government, including a separate 2011 libel case against the newspaper El Universo.
outcome_note: President Lenin Moreno's government moved to eliminate SUPERCOM in 2018; Fundamedios director Cesar Ricaurte said the surrounding legal framework nonetheless remained "intact."

title: Egypt arrests and later convicts three Al Jazeera journalists on terrorism-related charges
summary: Months after the military removed President Mohamed Morsi, Egyptian security forces arrested Al Jazeera English journalists Peter Greste, Mohamed Fahmy and Baher Mohamed at a Cairo hotel; courts later convicted them of aiding a banned organization, and international pressure led to pardons.
what_happened: On December 29, 2013, Egyptian security forces arrested Al Jazeera English correspondent Peter Greste, bureau chief Mohamed Fahmy and producer Baher Mohamed at Cairo's Marriott Hotel, months after the military, led by then-Defense Minister Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, removed elected President Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood, which the government later designated a terrorist organization. Prosecutors charged the journalists with aiding the Brotherhood and "spreading false news"; a June 2014 trial convicted them, and an August 2015 retrial, after the first conviction was overturned on appeal, again found them guilty of "aiding a terrorist organisation," partly, the judge said, because they had not registered with the country's journalist "syndicate," sentencing Fahmy and Mohamed to three years. Al Jazeera called the verdict "a deliberate attack on press freedom"; Greste, already deported and tried in absentia, said, "We did nothing wrong. The court presented no evidence." President Sisi pardoned Fahmy and Mohamed on September 23, 2015, as part of a wider amnesty.
stated_justification: Prosecutors charged the journalists with aiding the banned Muslim Brotherhood and "spreading false news"; the August 2015 judge cited, in part, their failure to register with the country's official journalist "syndicate" and unauthorized broadcast equipment.
effect_on_reporting: All three lost their liberty for over a year on charges press-freedom groups said lacked evidence; Al Jazeera said the verdict was "yet another deliberate attack on press freedom," and the United Nations said it was "very disturbed" by the sentences.
issue_of_the_day: The Egyptian military's July 2013 removal of President Mohamed Morsi and the government's subsequent designation of his Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization.
outcome_note: President Sisi pardoned Fahmy and Mohamed on September 23, 2015; Greste had already been deported to Australia in February 2015 under a prisoner-transfer arrangement.

title: Poland's new government gains power to replace public broadcaster leadership, and journalists are dismissed
summary: Weeks after winning power, Poland's Law and Justice (PiS) party passed a law letting the treasury minister directly appoint and dismiss the heads of public radio and television, and dozens of journalists at the public broadcaster were subsequently dismissed or resigned.
what_happened: Poland's Law and Justice (PiS) party won parliamentary and presidential elections in 2015 and, within weeks of taking office, passed a "small" media law, signed by President Andrzej Duda on December 31, 2015, giving the treasury minister power to appoint and dismiss the heads of public radio and television broadcasters directly, without the previously required independent broadcasting council process. Reporters Without Borders said the law "gave the ruling party close control of the public media." Under Prime Minister Beata Szydlo's government, dozens of journalists and executives at the public broadcasters TVP and Polish Radio were dismissed or resigned in the following months, part of what one former colleague called a "political cleansing" that began at the top and moved through the ranks, affecting first "journalists and editors of news and current affairs programmes." RSF said firing "experienced journalists whose professionalism has never been disputed violates a democratic society's rules and threatens press freedom," and that the changes "helped precipitate Poland's rapid fall" in its press-freedom rankings.
stated_justification: The government did not offer an individualized public justification for each dismissal in the sources reviewed; a former colleague of those removed described management as seeking staff viewed as ideologically reliable rather than only professionally qualified.
effect_on_reporting: RSF said the dismissals of experienced, professionally undisputed journalists violated "a democratic society's rules and threatens press freedom" and "badly hurt the quality of public radio programmes," contributing to Poland's fall in press-freedom rankings.
issue_of_the_day: Law and Justice's decisive October 2015 election win and its stated aim of overhauling public institutions it viewed as insufficiently accountable to voters.
outcome_note: The appointment power and pattern of dismissals continued through the remainder of the PiS government's term; ownership of the public broadcasters changed only after a later change of government.

title: Cambodia's government forces the closure of The Cambodia Daily with a disputed multimillion-dollar tax bill
summary: Cambodia's tax authority presented the independent, English-language Cambodia Daily with a $6.3 million bill the paper called arbitrary and undocumented, forcing the 24-year-old newspaper to close rather than pay, amid a wider campaign against independent media before 2018 elections.
what_happened: The Cambodia Daily, an independent English-language newspaper covering Cambodian politics and human rights since 1993, was presented by the tax authority with a $6.3 million bill covering several years of alleged unpaid taxes. The paper said the figure was "arbitrary" and not based on any audit of its books, and Prime Minister Hun Sen, in a speech, called the paper's owners "thieves" and said, of their response, "When they didn't pay and we asked them to leave the country, they said we are a dictatorship." Unable to pay or successfully dispute the bill by the government's deadline, the paper published its final edition on September 4, 2017, headlined "Descent Into Outright Dictatorship," and closed after 24 years. Human Rights Watch's Phil Robertson called the closure "one of the gravest threats to freedom of the press in Cambodia since the 1991 Paris Peace Accords." The closure came amid a wider campaign against independent media and civil-society groups ahead of Cambodia's 2018 elections, which Hun Sen's party went on to win after the main opposition party was dissolved by court order.
stated_justification: The tax department presented the $6.3 million bill as owed back taxes; the newspaper said the figure was "arbitrary" and not based on an audit, and Prime Minister Hun Sen said of the dispute, "When they didn't pay and we asked them to leave the country, they said we are a dictatorship."
effect_on_reporting: An independent newspaper that had covered Cambodian politics and rights issues for 24 years closed rather than pay a bill it could not verify; Human Rights Watch called it "one of the gravest threats to freedom of the press in Cambodia since the 1991 Paris Peace Accords."
issue_of_the_day: Preparations for Cambodia's 2018 general election and a wider government campaign against independent media and civil-society groups seen as sympathetic to the opposition.
outcome_note: The Cambodia Daily did not reopen; its closure coincided with a wider campaign against independent outlets and civil-society groups ahead of Cambodia's 2018 election.

title: Tanzania requires bloggers and online publishers to register and pay an annual government fee
summary: Tanzania's government, under President John Magufuli, issued regulations requiring anyone running a blog or website with user content to register with the telecoms regulator and pay an annual fee reported at roughly $930, with vaguely worded content bans.
what_happened: On March 16, 2018, Tanzania's government issued the Electronic and Postal Communications (Online Content) Regulations, requiring bloggers, online publishers and operators of websites with user-generated content to register with the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA) and pay a licensing fee reported at roughly $930 a year, a large sum in a country where average annual income is a small fraction of that. The regulations banned vaguely defined categories of content, including material causing "annoyance" or leading to "public disorder," and let the TCRA order content removed without judicial process. The advocacy group ARTICLE 19 said the TCRA "is not independent and giving the body the power to determine illegal content and order its removal lacks due process guarantees." Local media reported officials said the fee was meant to curb "moral decadence" online. Six human-rights and media groups challenged the fee in court and won an injunction in April 2018 while the case proceeded.
stated_justification: Officials said the regulations were meant to curb what local reporting described as "moral decadence" online and to make bloggers and online publishers accountable in the way licensed broadcasters already were.
effect_on_reporting: Anyone running a blog or user-content website had to register and pay roughly $930 a year, a large sum locally, or risk prosecution; ARTICLE 19 said the regulator enforcing the rule "is not independent" and lacked "due process guarantees" for content takedowns.
issue_of_the_day: A broader push under President Magufuli's government to regulate online speech and civic activity ahead of Tanzania's 2020 general election cycle.
outcome_note: A court granted media and rights groups an injunction against the fee in April 2018 while their challenge proceeded; the sources reviewed do not establish the challenge's final outcome.

title: Myanmar sentences two Reuters journalists to seven years under the Official Secrets Act for reporting on a massacre
summary: A Myanmar court sentenced Reuters reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo to seven years under the colonial-era Official Secrets Act after police handed them classified documents at a dinner shortly before their arrest, while they were investigating the killing of Rohingya Muslim villagers.
what_happened: Reuters reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo were investigating the killing of ten Rohingya Muslim men and boys by soldiers and villagers in Rakhine State when police, in December 2017, invited them to dinner and handed them rolled-up documents just before officers arrested them for possessing the papers. Prosecutors charged them under Myanmar's Official Secrets Act, a colonial-era law against handling state documents without authorization. On September 3, 2018, a judge convicted and sentenced both men to seven years in prison. Reuters editor-in-chief Stephen Adler called it "a sad day for Myanmar, Reuters journalists Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo, and the press everywhere." Human Rights Watch's Brad Adams said, "7 years for reporting the truth is what we expect from dictatorships," and Britain's ambassador said the case "struck a hammer blow to the rule of law." Aung San Suu Kyi's government, in which she held the position of State Counsellor, a de facto head-of-government role created for her since the constitution barred her from the presidency, did not intervene.
stated_justification: Prosecutors charged the two reporters under the colonial-era Official Secrets Act for possessing documents a police officer had handed them at a dinner shortly before their arrest, a setup the reporters' defense argued at trial.
effect_on_reporting: Two working journalists received seven-year prison sentences for reporting on a documented mass killing; Human Rights Watch's Brad Adams said, "7 years for reporting the truth is what we expect from dictatorships," and the case drew wide international condemnation.
issue_of_the_day: The Reuters investigation into the killing of ten Rohingya Muslim men and boys by Myanmar soldiers and local residents in Inn Din village, Rakhine State, in September 2017.
outcome_note: President Win Myint pardoned and released Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo on May 7, 2019, after 511 days in prison, as part of a mass amnesty.

title: India imposes a communications blackout in Jammu and Kashmir after revoking the region's special status
summary: As it revoked Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional autonomy, India's government cut broadband, mobile internet, text messaging and phone service across the region, leaving local journalists unable to file stories, verify information or communicate with sources for months.
what_happened: On August 5, 2019, India's government, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, revoked Article 370 of the Indian constitution, which had granted the Muslim-majority region of Jammu and Kashmir a degree of autonomy, and split it into two federally administered territories. Ahead of the announcement, authorities cut broadband, mobile internet, text messaging and phone service across the region and detained several local political leaders. The government said the changes would bring stability and end "separatism, terrorism, dynastic politics and corruption." Local journalists could not reach sources, verify information, send photographs or video, or in many cases confirm stories with editors outside the region; some had to travel to a government-run media center to use monitored internet access. Mobile and broadband internet were restored only in stages over the following months and year, and the International Federation of Journalists said journalists in Kashmir faced "declining advertising revenues, job losses, pay cuts" and "self-censorship" on top of the shutdown itself.
stated_justification: The government said the change would bring stability to the region and end "separatism, terrorism, dynastic politics and corruption"; it did not separately justify the communications shutdown beyond citing broader public-order and security concerns.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists could not reach sources, verify facts, send photographs or video, or confirm stories with editors, and the International Federation of Journalists said the disruption was "an egregious violation of citizens' rights to information from a free press."
issue_of_the_day: The Indian government's August 2019 revocation of Article 370, which had granted Jammu and Kashmir a degree of constitutional autonomy since 1949.
outcome_note: High-speed mobile internet remained restricted into 2020; the International Federation of Journalists reported the blackout as still affecting journalists' work a full year after it began.

title: Saudi Arabia's government kills journalist Jamal Khashoggi inside its Istanbul consulate
jurisdiction: Saudi Arabia, national (extraterritorial: consulate in Istanbul, Turkey)
summary: Jamal Khashoggi, a Washington Post columnist and critic of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, was killed by Saudi agents inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul; the CIA concluded the crown prince ordered the killing, which Saudi Arabia denied.
what_happened: Jamal Khashoggi, a Saudi journalist who wrote columns for The Washington Post critical of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, entered the Saudi consulate in Istanbul, Turkey, on October 2, 2018, to obtain paperwork for his upcoming marriage, and did not come out. After more than two weeks of denials, Saudi Arabia acknowledged he had died inside the consulate, saying a team of 15 Saudi nationals sent to persuade him to return to the kingdom had killed him accidentally in a struggle; Turkish officials said the killing was planned and that his body was dismembered and never recovered. The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) concluded, based partly on intercepted communications, that the killing "would not and could not have happened" without the crown prince's approval; a Saudi government spokesperson called the assessment "false." A Saudi court later convicted eight unnamed operatives, sentencing five to death, later commuted after payments to Khashoggi's family, while clearing senior officials of responsibility.
stated_justification: Saudi officials said a 15-member team was sent only to persuade Khashoggi to return to the kingdom and that he died accidentally during a physical struggle; a Saudi spokesperson called the CIA's contrary assessment "false."
effect_on_reporting: A journalist critical of the crown prince was killed inside his own country's consulate; the CIA's assessment that the killing could not have happened without the crown prince's approval drew international scrutiny of Saudi treatment of dissenting journalists abroad.
issue_of_the_day: Jamal Khashoggi's Washington Post columns criticizing Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's consolidation of power and human-rights record.
outcome_note: A Saudi court convicted eight unnamed operatives and sentenced five to death, later commuted; the CIA's assessment that the crown prince ordered the killing did not result in charges against him.

claims.evidence_quote: a team of 15 Saudi nationals were sent to confront Khashoggi at the consulate and that he was accidentally killed in a chokehold by men who were trying to force him to return to the kingdom.

claims.evidence_quote: The claims in this purported assessment is false,

claims.evidence_quote: Turkish officials have said the killing was intentional and have been pressuring Saudi Arabia to extradite those responsible to stand trial.

claims.statement: The CIA concluded the killing could not have happened without the crown prince's approval.
claims.evidence_quote: would not and could not have happened

title: Venezuela expels or denies entry to dozens of foreign journalists covering anti-government protests
summary: During 2016 to 2018 protests against President Nicolas Maduro's government, Venezuelan authorities expelled, deported or denied entry to dozens of foreign correspondents, most citing bureaucratic pretexts such as visa irregularities rather than a stated substantive reason.
what_happened: As protests against President Nicolas Maduro's government intensified from 2016 into 2018, Venezuelan immigration and intelligence agencies expelled, deported or refused entry to dozens of foreign correspondents. On September 1, 2017, during a major opposition demonstration, authorities expelled five Al Jazeera English journalists, including Teresa Bo and John Holman, along with reporters for Le Monde, Colombia's Caracol, NPR and the Miami Herald. Brazilian television reporter Leandro Stoliar, detained for ten hours in 2016 while investigating a corruption case, said, "I felt like a prisoner, like a criminal." Authorities gave varied, often bureaucratic reasons, citing visa irregularities, missing equipment paperwork or unspecified immigration violations, rather than a single stated policy. Reporters Without Borders' Emmanuel Colombie said the pattern of inconsistent reasons "creates [a] climate of uncertainty and constitutes [a] threat to freedom of information." The expulsions continued into 2018 and 2019, affecting journalists from France, Spain, Peru, Argentina and elsewhere.
stated_justification: Authorities cited varied administrative reasons in different cases, including visa irregularities, missing equipment paperwork and unspecified immigration violations, rather than a single stated policy for expelling foreign correspondents.
effect_on_reporting: Dozens of foreign correspondents were expelled, deported or refused entry over roughly two years; RSF's Emmanuel Colombie said the inconsistency of the reasons given "creates [a] climate of uncertainty and constitutes [a] threat to freedom of information."
issue_of_the_day: Sustained anti-government street protests in Venezuela in 2016 and 2017 over the economic crisis and President Maduro's moves to consolidate power.
outcome_note: The pattern of expulsions and entry denials continued into 2018 and 2019 with no announced change in policy in the sources reviewed.

title: Australian Federal Police raid the national broadcaster over reporting on alleged war crimes in Afghanistan
summary: Australian Federal Police spent hours searching the headquarters of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) over its 2017 "Afghan Files" reports on alleged killings by Australian special forces that breached the laws of armed conflict, seizing files under a warrant citing the Crimes Act's ban on publishing classified material.
what_happened: In 2017, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), the national public broadcaster, published the "Afghan Files," reports based on leaked defense documents describing allegations that Australian special forces killed people in breach of the laws of armed conflict. On June 5, 2019, Australian Federal Police (AFP) officers spent about eight hours searching ABC's Sydney headquarters, examining thousands of files and journalist Dan Oakes' emails, under a warrant citing the Crimes Act 1914's ban on "publishing classified material." Officers left with two USB drives of sealed files pending legal review. ABC managing director David Anderson said, "The ABC stands by its journalists, will protect its sources and continue to report without fear or favour on national security and intelligence issues when there is a clear public interest," and news director Gaven Morris said, "journalism is not a crime." The AFP said its actions were "independent and impartial at all times." The raid followed a separate police search, one day earlier, of a News Corp journalist's home over unrelated leaked material.
stated_justification: The AFP said the raid concerned "allegations of publishing classified material, contrary to provisions of the Crimes Act 1914," and separately said its investigative actions had been "independent and impartial at all times."
effect_on_reporting: Police searched the newsroom for eight hours and reviewed a journalist's personal emails and thousands of files before leaving with sealed material; ABC's news director said, "journalism is not a crime," and its editorial director called the reporting "outstanding" and in the public interest.
issue_of_the_day: ABC's 2017 "Afghan Files" reporting on allegations that Australian special forces soldiers killed people in breach of the laws of armed conflict.
outcome_note: The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions decided in October 2020 not to charge journalist Dan Oakes over the Afghan Files reporting.

claims.evidence_quote: in relation to allegations of publishing classified material, contrary to provisions of the Crimes Act 1914

title: United Kingdom detains journalist's partner under terrorism law and oversees destruction of Guardian hard drives holding Snowden files
summary: British authorities detained David Miranda, partner of Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald, for nine hours at Heathrow Airport under anti-terrorism powers, and separately had Guardian staff destroy hard drives holding files leaked by Edward Snowden rather than hand them to a court.
what_happened: In August 2013, as The Guardian was reporting on National Security Agency (NSA) surveillance based on documents leaked by former contractor Edward Snowden, British authorities detained David Miranda, the partner of Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald, for nine hours at London's Heathrow Airport, the maximum allowed without charge under Schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act 2000, a law letting officers stop and question travellers at ports without suspicion of a crime. Officers questioned him and seized electronic devices; the government said police were right to stop people suspected of possessing "highly sensitive stolen information that would help terrorism." Separately, British intelligence officials visited The Guardian's London offices and, editor Alan Rusbridger said, watched as Guardian staff used power drills to destroy hard drives containing Snowden material in the building's basement, after officials told the paper, in Rusbridger's account, "You've had your fun. Now we want the stuff back." Rusbridger said the paper chose destruction over handing material to a court because copies existed elsewhere, including in the United States.
stated_justification: The government said Miranda's detention was justified because he was suspected of carrying "highly sensitive stolen information that would help terrorism," and that authorities had "a duty to protect the public and our national security."
effect_on_reporting: A journalist's partner was held for nine hours and had devices seized without being charged with any offense, and Guardian staff destroyed computer hard drives under official observation rather than hand Snowden material to a court, an episode Greenwald said would only make him "far more aggressive" in reporting.
issue_of_the_day: The Guardian's 2013 reporting, based on files leaked by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden, on mass surveillance by the United States and United Kingdom.
outcome_note: The Court of Appeal ruled in January 2016 that Miranda's detention itself was lawful, but found Schedule 7's stop powers incompatible with press-freedom protections for journalistic material generally.

claims.evidence_quote: Under schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act 2000, UK authorities are allowed to stop, search and detain passengers at rail, air and sea ports without probable cause, for up to nine hours.

title: Serbia's Public Information Act lets courts fine independent newspapers into financial danger
summary: Serbia's parliament passed a Public Information Act allowing courts to levy same-day fines against newspapers for vaguely defined offenses against the state's interests, and independent papers were fined far more often and more heavily than pro-government ones.
what_happened: In October 1998, Serbia's parliament, dominated by allies of Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic, passed the Law on Public Information, requiring media to avoid publishing material judged to violate "the inviolability of human dignity and the right to a private life" and barring "untruths which violate the rights of the individual," with courts empowered to impose large fines within 24 hours of a complaint and little opportunity to appeal before payment came due. By early 2000, independent outlets had received 31 fines averaging 420,000 dinars each, roughly three times the average fine on pro-government papers. Newspapers including Glas javnosti, Danas, Cacanski Glas and the magazine Vranjske were fined repeatedly. Milosevic said enforcement of the law had been "very weak" and that critics were "under foreign control"; the ruling Yugoslav Left party called for "decontamination of the journalistic profession," describing independent media as a "fifth column." The law was suspended after Milosevic lost power in October 2000.
stated_justification: President Milosevic said the law's enforcement had been "very weak" and dismissed critics as being "under foreign control"; the allied Yugoslav Left party called independent outlets a "fifth column" and demanded "decontamination of the journalistic profession."
effect_on_reporting: Independent newspapers received fines nearly three times larger, on average, than pro-government papers, payable within days of a court decision, financial pressure some outlets said threatened their survival.
issue_of_the_day: Independent Serbian media's coverage of NATO's escalating confrontation with Yugoslavia over Kosovo through 1998 and 1999.
outcome_note: The law was suspended after Milosevic lost power in October 2000 elections and a change of government in Serbia.

title: Minnesota State Patrol arrests CNN crew live on air in Minneapolis
summary: Minnesota State Patrol troopers arrested CNN correspondent Omar Jimenez and his crew on live television while they covered protests after the police killing of George Floyd. Officers gave no reason before handcuffing the three men; Governor Tim Walz apologized hours later and called the arrest a failure of the state's own procedures.
issue_of_the_day: Protests in Minneapolis followed the police killing of George Floyd on May 25, 2020. Jimenez's crew was reporting live on the unrest and the state's response near the site of the killing when troopers moved to clear the area at dawn on May 29.
what_happened: Just after 5 a.m. on May 29, 2020, Minnesota State Patrol troopers in riot gear approached a CNN crew, correspondent Omar Jimenez, photojournalist Leonel Mendez and producer Bill Kirkos, reporting live from Minneapolis on protests over George Floyd's killing four days earlier. Jimenez identified himself on camera, showed his credentials and offered to move; troopers handcuffed him anyway, without giving a reason, and the arrest aired live. Mendez and Kirkos were also detained and the crew's equipment was seized. All three were released about ninety minutes later after CNN's president contacted state officials. Governor Tim Walz, Minnesota's head of government, apologized publicly the same day, saying the state bore responsibility for failing to protect journalists covering the unrest. CNN pointed out that a white CNN correspondent working nearby, Josh Campbell, was allowed to stay after identifying himself, a contrast that became part of the story.
stated_justification: Troopers gave no explanation to the crew before or during the arrest. State Patrol did not publish a contemporaneous justification; Governor Walz later called the episode a failure rather than defending it.
effect_on_reporting: CNN's live broadcast was interrupted by the arrest of an identified, credentialed crew, and the incident became one of the most widely seen examples in a wave the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker recorded of officers detaining or using force against journalists covering the 2020 protests nationwide.
status: Closed; the crew was released the same morning and Governor Walz apologized publicly.
what_we_dont_know: Minnesota State Patrol did not publish a named officer or a stated reason for singling out Jimenez's crew for arrest.
outcome_note: The crew was released within about ninety minutes and Governor Walz apologized the same day, calling the arrest his own failure.

claims.statement: CNN correspondent Josh Campbell, reporting nearby, was allowed to stay after identifying himself, while Jimenez was handcuffed.
claims.evidence_quote: I identified myself … they said, 'OK, you're permitted to be in the area.'

claims.statement: Jimenez described the troopers who led him away as not violent, even as he was arrested without explanation.
claims.evidence_quote: As far as the people who were leading me away — there was no animosity there, they weren't violent with me.

claims.statement: Governor Walz took personal responsibility for the arrest the same day.
claims.evidence_quote: This one is on me and I own it...I failed you last night in that.

title: Federal officers restrict press access to Portland protests; judge orders them to stop
summary: After federal officers deployed to Portland used tear gas, pepper spray and rubber bullets on journalists and legal observers covering protests, the American Civil Liberties Union sued, and a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction barring officers from dispersing, arresting or using force against clearly identified press.
issue_of_the_day: The federal government sent Department of Homeland Security officers to Portland in July 2020 to protect a federal courthouse during nightly protests that followed George Floyd's killing; officers' use of force against bystanders, including identified journalists, prompted the lawsuit.
what_happened: Through June and July 2020, journalists and legal observers covering nightly protests in Portland, Oregon said police and later federal officers deployed by the Department of Homeland Security used tear gas, pepper spray, rubber bullets, flash-bang grenades and physical force against them even after they identified themselves as press, and in some cases arrested them or seized their equipment. The American Civil Liberties Union of Oregon sued on their behalf, seeking a court order to stop the practice. On July 16, 2020, U.S. District Judge Michael Simon issued a preliminary injunction barring officers from dispersing, arresting, threatening to arrest or using force against journalists and legal observers who could be identified by press passes, badges or distinctive clothing, and from ordering them to stop recording or seizing their equipment. The order, later extended and applied against federal officers as well, ran through the fall of 2020.
stated_justification: Federal and local officials generally described the use of force as necessary to disperse crowds and protect the courthouse and officers; no agency specifically justified using force against identified journalists.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists reported being unable to safely document the protests and the federal response to them for weeks until the injunction took effect, after which the order gave them a specific, enforceable right to record police activity from a normal distance.
status: The preliminary injunction remained in effect through the fall 2020 protests, covering both Portland police and federal officers.
what_we_dont_know: The full extent of federal officers' compliance with the injunction, and whether any officer was individually disciplined, was not established in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: The court ordered officers to stop dispersing, arresting or using force against identified journalists and legal observers.

claims.evidence_quote: This injunction is a critical protection for journalists and legal observers exercising their fundamental right to record and observe police activities at these important protests.

title: Political appointees alter CDC coronavirus guidance before public release
summary: Reporting in 2020 found that political appointees at the Department of Health and Human Services rewrote or edited the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's public coronavirus guidance and its weekly scientific bulletin before release, bypassing the agency's normal scientific review.
issue_of_the_day: The reporting concerned the CDC's coronavirus testing guidance and its weekly Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report during the summer and fall of 2020, as the Trump administration sought to align public messaging with the president's own statements about the pandemic.
what_happened: Reporting published in September 2020 found that Michael Caputo, an HHS spokesperson, and an adviser he brought in, Paul Alexander, sought to change or delay CDC scientific communications, including the agency's weekly Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, so that public messaging would not conflict with statements President Trump had made about the pandemic. In one instance, HHS staff rewrote CDC coronavirus testing guidance and published it on the CDC's own website without the agency's normal scientific review, a document CDC officials later said did not reflect the views of many scientists inside the agency. Assistant Secretary Brendan Giroir said he coordinated input from task-force scientists but told reporters he did not know why some edits bypassed the standard review process. The episode became the subject of a congressional oversight investigation into political interference at the CDC during the pandemic.
stated_justification: Caputo told colleagues his goal was to "execute the president's agenda and to knock down any messaging, any communications that were seen as conflicting with what President Trump was saying about coronavirus."
effect_on_reporting: Reporters covering the pandemic received CDC guidance and public statements that outside scientists said had been shaped by political appointees rather than by the agency's own scientific review, undercutting the reliability of official public health communications reporters relied on.
status: A congressional select subcommittee investigated the interference; no HHS official was reported to have been disciplined for the specific episode.
what_we_dont_know: The full list of CDC documents altered by HHS political appointees, and which specific public statements resulted, was not fully detailed in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: No agency reversal of the practice was documented in the sources reviewed; a congressional investigation examined the interference without a public admission of wrongdoing.

title: Justice Department bars seizing reporters' phone and email records
summary: After it came to light that the Trump-era Justice Department had secretly obtained the phone and email records of reporters at The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN, Attorney General Merrick Garland issued a policy barring prosecutors from using subpoenas or other compulsory process against journalists in leak investigations.
issue_of_the_day: In mid-2021, The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN separately disclosed that the Justice Department had secretly seized their reporters' phone and email records years earlier while investigating leaks, including of information about contacts between Trump campaign associates and Russia.
what_happened: In 2021, the Justice Department notified The New York Times, The Washington Post and CNN that it had secretly obtained phone records, and in the Times' case attempted to obtain email records, from reporters during leak investigations that began under the first Trump administration, in one case accompanied by a nondisclosure order barring Times executives from disclosing the request. After the disclosures drew public criticism, President Biden called the practice "simply wrong," and on July 19, 2021, Attorney General Merrick Garland issued a memorandum barring the department from using subpoenas, warrants, court orders or civil investigative demands to compel journalists' records or testimony in leak investigations while they are gathering news, subject to narrow exceptions such as an imminent threat to life. A department spokesman said prosecutors would no longer seek such compulsory process against journalists doing their jobs.
stated_justification: The Justice Department said the new policy reflected that "a free and independent press is vital to the functioning of our democracy," and committed the department to protecting First Amendment values and journalists' independence.
effect_on_reporting: The policy removed, for the time being, the threat that reporters covering national security and government leaks could have their phone or email records secretly seized by federal investigators, a practice that had already occurred at three major news organizations.
status: In effect from July 2021 until it was rescinded by Attorney General Pam Bondi in April 2025.
outcome_note: Attorney General Bondi rescinded these protections in April 2025, restoring the department's earlier discretionary balancing test.

title: Police raid Marion County Record newsroom and publisher's home in Kansas
summary: Police in Marion, Kansas, led by Chief Gideon Cody, raided the Marion County Record's newsroom and publisher Eric Meyer's home, seizing computers, phones and files, on a warrant tied to an identity-theft investigation. The paper's 98-year-old co-owner, Joan Meyer, died the next day; a special prosecutor later found no evidence the paper had committed a crime.
issue_of_the_day: The Record had been investigating the driving record of local restaurant owner Kari Newell, who had accused the paper of accessing her personal information without authorization, the claim the search warrant cited as its basis.
what_happened: On August 11, 2023, Marion, Kansas police chief Gideon Cody led officers in searches of the Marion County Record's newsroom and the home of its publisher, Eric Meyer, seizing computers, servers, backup drives, cellphones and reporting files. The warrant cited an investigation into identity theft and unauthorized computer use tied to restaurant owner Kari Newell, whose driving record the paper had examined while verifying a tip. Eric Meyer's 98-year-old mother and Record co-owner, Joan Meyer, collapsed and died the day after the raid; the newspaper's staff attributed her death to the stress it caused. Local prosecutors withdrew the search warrants five days later, saying the evidence did not establish a sufficient link between the alleged crime and the newsroom. A special prosecutor's investigation released in August 2024 found no evidence Record reporters had committed a crime and said Cody would face a charge of obstructing the judicial process.
stated_justification: The warrant cited a criminal investigation into identity theft and unlawful use of a computer connected to how the Record had obtained information about Kari Newell's driving record.
effect_on_reporting: The newspaper lost its computers, servers and reporting files for the length of the investigation, and the raid drew national attention to the use of search warrants against a working newsroom over a routine reporting inquiry.
status: The warrants were withdrawn in August 2023; former chief Gideon Cody faced a criminal charge following the August 2024 special-prosecutor findings.
outcome_note: Special prosecutors found no evidence Record reporters had committed a crime and moved to charge former police chief Gideon Cody.

title: Federal court strikes down Arizona's law banning recording police within 8 feet
summary: Arizona's 2022 law making it a crime to record police within eight feet after a warning was struck down by a federal judge in July 2023, who found it chilled a substantial amount of activity protected by the First Amendment and was not necessary given other laws already protecting officers.
issue_of_the_day: The bill's sponsor said it responded to concerns that groups he described as antagonistic toward police followed officers around filming encounters and came dangerously close during potentially violent incidents.
what_happened: In 2022, Arizona Governor Doug Ducey signed House Bill 2319, making it a class 3 misdemeanor, punishable by up to thirty days in jail, to knowingly video record police activity from within eight feet after an officer warned the person to stop. News organizations and the American Civil Liberties Union sued, arguing the law would prevent journalists and bystanders from documenting police conduct, including alleged misconduct, from a normal filming distance. On July 21, 2023, U.S. District Judge John Tuchi permanently enjoined enforcement of the law, ruling it restricted a substantial amount of activity protected by the First Amendment without being necessary, since Arizona already had laws against physically interfering with police. Arizona's attorney general did not appeal, and the parties later entered a stipulated permanent injunction confirming the law could not be enforced.
stated_justification: The bill's Republican sponsor, State Representative John Kavanagh, said the law responded to groups he considered opposed to police that followed officers to film encounters and came dangerously close to potentially violent incidents.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists and bystanders in Arizona had faced criminal liability for filming police from a normal reporting distance for more than a year before the law was enjoined.
status: Permanently enjoined; the law cannot be enforced in Arizona.
outcome_note: A federal judge permanently enjoined enforcement of the law, and Arizona's attorney general did not appeal.

title: FCC chair reopens 'news distortion' complaints against CBS and NBC
summary: Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr reopened complaints alleging CBS and NBC distorted the news, demanding CBS turn over the full tape and transcript of a 60 Minutes interview and later accusing NBC's parent Comcast of misleading coverage of an immigration case.
issue_of_the_day: The CBS complaint concerned 60 Minutes' October 2024 interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris; the NBC complaint, filed in April 2025, concerned coverage of the wrongful deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia.
what_happened: On January 29, 2025, newly installed FCC Chair Brendan Carr revived a 'news distortion' complaint against CBS over how 60 Minutes edited an October 2024 interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris, complaints his predecessor had earlier rejected as being at odds with the First Amendment. The FCC demanded CBS turn over the interview's full, unedited transcript and camera feeds; CBS complied on February 3 and 5, 2025, saying the broadcast was not doctored. On April 16, 2025, Carr said Comcast's NBC and MSNBC had spent days misleading the public about Abrego Garcia's case, and on April 21 the advocacy group Center for American Rights filed a complaint against NBC, ABC and CBS alleging misleading coverage, adding to investigations Carr had already reopened against the three networks in February.

title: Congress cuts $1.1 billion in federal funding for public broadcasting
summary: At President Trump's request, Congress passed a rescissions package clawing back roughly $1.1 billion already appropriated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, eliminating federal funding for NPR, PBS and their member stations.
issue_of_the_day: The rescission followed years of conservative criticism that NPR and PBS produced one-sided coverage, and came weeks after President Trump's May 2025 executive order directing agencies to stop funding the two networks.
what_happened: In July 2025, at the White House's request, Congress passed a rescissions package clawing back about $1.1 billion in funding Congress had already appropriated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting for the following two fiscal years. The House passed the package 216 to 213, with all but two Republicans in favor, after a Senate 'vote-a-rama' in which nearly every amendment failed along party lines; the measure became law on July 18, 2025. NPR chief executive Katherine Maher said public funding had supported a distinctive system of cultural and educational programming, while PBS chief executive Paula Kerger said the cuts would fall hardest on smaller and rural stations. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the package an affront to the normal appropriations process, while at least one Republican member said stations, rather than network editorial staff, would bear the consequences.
stated_justification: Supporters of the rescission cited long-standing conservative complaints that NPR and PBS produce one-sided news coverage that should not receive taxpayer funding.
effect_on_reporting: CPB's federal appropriation was eliminated, threatening the operating budgets of public radio and television stations, especially smaller rural and tribal stations that depend most heavily on CPB grants for local news coverage.
status: The rescission became law on July 18, 2025; CPB's federal funding was not restored.
what_we_dont_know: The precise station-by-station effect of the cuts on local news coverage was not fully detailed in the source reviewed.

title: Trump sues Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over Epstein birthday letter story
summary: President Trump sued The Wall Street Journal, its owner Rupert Murdoch and two reporters for at least $10 billion, disputing the newspaper's report describing a bawdy letter he was said to have sent Jeffrey Epstein for a 2003 birthday album.
issue_of_the_day: The Journal had reported on a letter, bearing Trump's name and an outline of a naked woman, compiled into a birthday album for Jeffrey Epstein in 2003; the story renewed scrutiny of Trump's past relationship with Epstein.

President Trump filed a defamation suit in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida against the Journal, its parent News Corp, chief executive Robert Thomson, owner Rupert Murdoch and two reporters, seeking at least $10 billion in damages and calling the story "false, malicious, and defamatory." Trump said he looked forward to questioning Murdoch under oath. In September 2025, Dow Jones, the Journal's publisher, moved to dismiss the case, arguing the suit sought to penalize true reporting and that Trump could not show the actual-malice required of a public figure.

effect_on_reporting: The lawsuit sought $10 billion in damages from a major news organization and its owner over a single investigative story, and Dow Jones said it was defending reporting it maintained was accurate and later corroborated by documents Congress released.

title: Trump sues Des Moines Register and pollster Ann Selzer over final Iowa poll
summary: President-elect Trump sued the Des Moines Register and longtime pollster Ann Selzer under Iowa's consumer fraud law over her final pre-election poll, which showed Kamala Harris ahead in Iowa days before Trump won the state; a judge later questioned whether the case could proceed without discouraging election reporting.
issue_of_the_day: Selzer's final Iowa poll, published days before the November 2024 election, showed Harris leading in a state Trump went on to win by more than ten points, prompting Trump to call the poll itself a form of election interference.
what_happened: On December 16, 2024, Trump sued the Des Moines Register, its parent Gannett, and pollster J. Ann Selzer in federal court in Iowa, invoking the state's consumer fraud act and alleging Selzer's final pre-election poll, which showed Kamala Harris ahead in Iowa, amounted to what he called "brazen election interference" rather than a simple polling error. Trump said Selzer "knew exactly what she was doing." The defendants denied the claims. In June 2025, Trump's lawyers withdrew the case from federal court and refiled it in Polk County District Court, a move that let two Iowa-resident co-plaintiffs remain in the suit after jurisdictional problems in federal court. At a July 2026 hearing on the defendants' motion to dismiss, Judge Scott Beattie said allowing the case to proceed could carry broad consequences for anyone who publishes polling or predictions before an election.
stated_justification: Trump's complaint said Selzer's poll was not a mere misfire but "brazen election interference," and Trump said publicly that Selzer "knew exactly what she was doing."
effect_on_reporting: A sitting president used a state consumer-protection statute, usually applied to commercial transactions, against a newspaper's published opinion poll, raising the question of whether pollsters and outlets could face liability for predictions that do not match an election result.
status: The case remained at the motion-to-dismiss stage in Iowa state court as of the hearing in July 2026.

outcome_note: The judge said allowing the suit to proceed could broadly discourage election polling and reporting; a ruling on dismissal was pending.

title: Trump files, then refiles, $15 billion defamation suit against the New York Times
summary: President Trump sued The New York Times and four of its journalists for $15 billion over articles and a book published before the 2024 election; a judge dismissed the sprawling original complaint for violating basic pleading rules, and Trump refiled a shorter version a month later.

title: Officer shoots Australian journalist with rubber bullet during Los Angeles immigration protests
summary: A law enforcement officer shot Nine News Australia correspondent Lauren Tomasi with a rubber bullet while she was reporting live from a Los Angeles protest against federal immigration raids, prompting Australia's prime minister to call the incident unacceptable and raise it with the U.S. government.
issue_of_the_day: The protests followed a series of federal immigration enforcement raids in the Los Angeles area in early June 2025, which drew large crowds and a heavy police and, later, National Guard presence downtown.
what_happened: On June 9, 2025, Nine News Australia correspondent Lauren Tomasi was reporting live from downtown Los Angeles on protests against federal immigration raids when an officer behind her raised a firearm and fired at close range, striking her leg with a rubber bullet on live television. Tomasi said she and her cameraman were safe and called the incident one of the unfortunate realities of covering events like the protests. title: 60 Minutes executive producer resigns, citing lost editorial independence

title: White House ends wire services' guaranteed seat in the press pool
summary: The White House ended the decades-old practice of guaranteeing wire services Associated Press, Reuters and Bloomberg a daily seat in the small press pool that covers the president, making them compete instead for a single rotating print slot alongside other outlets.

title: FCC approves Paramount-Skydance merger after CBS ombudsman and anti-DEI pledges
summary: The Federal Communications Commission approved Paramount's sale to Skydance Media after Skydance agreed to install an ombudsman to review complaints of bias at CBS News for two years and pledged to end diversity, equity and inclusion programs, over the objection of the commission's sole Democratic member.
issue_of_the_day: The approval came weeks after Paramount paid $16 million to settle President Trump's lawsuit over 60 Minutes' editing of a Harris interview, a settlement critics said was made to smooth the path for the FCC's review of the Skydance sale.
what_happened: On July 24, 2025, the Federal Communications Commission approved Paramount's sale to Skydance Media, a deal Chair Brendan Carr said came with written commitments to ensure a diversity of viewpoints across the company's news and entertainment programming. As part of the approval, Skydance agreed to hire a CBS News ombudsman to review complaints of editorial bias for at least two years and confirmed the company would not maintain diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Carr said Americans no longer trusted legacy news organizations to report fully, accurately and fairly. Commissioner Anna Gomez, the panel's sole Democrat, dissented, saying Paramount had made concessions she called excessive to settle a lawsuit she said lacked merit, as part of clearing the way for the merger.
stated_justification: Carr said the commitments were needed because "Americans no longer trust the legacy national news media to report fully, accurately, and fairly."
effect_on_reporting: As a condition of a federal merger approval, CBS News agreed to an outside ombudsman reviewing complaints about its editorial content and to end its diversity programs, conditions a dissenting commissioner said were extracted through regulatory leverage over the sale.
status: The merger closed on the FCC's approved terms, including the ombudsman requirement.
outcome_note: The FCC approved the merger with the ombudsman and anti-DEI conditions in place; Commissioner Gomez's dissent did not change the outcome.

title: White House closes 'Upper Press' section of West Wing to reporters
summary: The White House began requiring reporters to make appointments before entering the 'Upper Press' area of the West Wing, home to the press secretary's and senior press aides' offices, citing a need to protect sensitive material after accusing reporters of secretly recording conversations there.
issue_of_the_day: The White House said it acted after concluding that reporters had secretly recorded video and audio inside West Wing press offices and entered restricted areas, though it did not identify the reporters or recordings involved.
what_happened: On October 31, 2025, the White House announced that the 'Upper Press' section of the West Wing, which houses the offices of the press secretary and senior press aides, would require reporters to have a prior appointment before entering, while the 'Lower Press' office next to the briefing room remained open. A White House memorandum said the change would ensure adherence to best practices for access to sensitive material. Communications Director Steven Cheung said reporters had surreptitiously recorded video and audio in West Wing offices, entered restricted areas and listened in on private meetings. White House Correspondents' Association president Weijia Jiang said the new restrictions would hinder the press corps' ability to question officials and hold the government accountable.
stated_justification: The White House said the policy would "ensure adherence to best practices pertaining to access to sensitive material," and Communications Director Steven Cheung said reporters had recorded video and audio without permission and entered restricted areas.
effect_on_reporting: Reporters lost the informal, walk-in access to senior press aides' offices that had allowed them to ask quick follow-up questions and observe the press operation at close range, a practice long used to gather information outside formal briefings.
status: The restriction remained in effect as of the source reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The White House did not publicly identify which reporters it said had recorded conversations without permission or when the recordings occurred.
outcome_note: The restricted access to Upper Press remained in effect; the WHCA's objection did not lead to a reversal in the source reviewed.

title: Appeals court orders FCC to respond to challenge over 'news distortion' policy
summary: A bipartisan group of former Federal Communications Commission chairs, commissioners and the Radio Television Digital News Association petitioned a federal appeals court to force the FCC to act on a long-pending request to rescind its decades-old 'news distortion' policy after Chair Brendan Carr repeatedly invoked it against broadcasters; the court gave the FCC thirty days to respond.
issue_of_the_day: Under Chair Brendan Carr, the FCC had used its news distortion policy to open or reopen inquiries into CBS, NBC and ABC's election-season coverage, prompting the petitioners to argue the unresolved policy itself had become a tool of pressure on broadcasters.
what_happened: In November 2025, a bipartisan coalition of former FCC chairs and commissioners, senior former staff and the Radio Television Digital News Association filed a petition asking the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to order the FCC to rule on a long-pending request to rescind the agency's news distortion policy, which the petitioners argued Chair Brendan Carr had used to pressure broadcasters over their election coverage without the FCC ever taking a formal vote on the underlying rule. On April 28, 2026, the three-judge panel ordered the FCC to respond to the mandamus petition within thirty days. Former FCC Chairman Mark Fowler said press freedom would remain at risk until the policy was repealed, and Protect Democracy's Conor Gaffney said Carr's refusal to bring the petition to a commission vote was itself a threat to the First Amendment. Carr responded to the news of the court order on social media with, "How about no."
stated_justification: The FCC did not offer a substantive defense of retaining the news distortion policy in the source reviewed; Chair Carr's public response was dismissive rather than explanatory.
effect_on_reporting: A policy that broadcasters said the FCC's own chair had used as leverage over election coverage remained unresolved for months even as a federal court intervened to compel the agency to act on whether to keep or rescind it.
status: The court ordered the FCC to respond within thirty days; the underlying policy remained in place as of the order.
what_we_dont_know: Whether the FCC met the court's thirty-day deadline, and how it responded, was not established in the source reviewed.
outcome_note: A federal appeals court ordered the FCC to respond to the mandamus petition within thirty days; the underlying policy remained unresolved.

title: Minneapolis police projectile permanently blinds photojournalist Linda Tirado
summary: Freelance photojournalist Linda Tirado was struck in the face by a less-lethal round fired by Minneapolis police while covering protests over George Floyd's killing, permanently blinding her in one eye; the city settled her lawsuit for $600,000 in 2022 while continuing to deny an officer had fired the shot.
issue_of_the_day: Tirado was documenting the police response to protests over George Floyd's killing in Minneapolis when she was struck; a federal judge later found her case was one of numerous similar reports of journalists being hit by less-lethal munitions during the same unrest.
what_happened: On May 29, 2020, freelance photojournalist Linda Tirado was covering protests in Minneapolis over George Floyd's killing when she was struck by a tracking round and foam bullets fired by police; one projectile shattered her protective goggles and permanently blinded her in her left eye. Tirado sued the city, police officials and others on June 10, 2020. The Minneapolis Police Department did not respond to requests for comment on the incident. A federal judge, ruling on Tirado's case, found the allegations plausibly suggested a broader pattern, contrary to the First Amendment, of police intentionally using less-lethal munitions against identified journalists, since numerous other reporters described similar experiences during the same unrest. The city reached a $600,000 settlement with Tirado in May 2022, while continuing to deny wrongdoing and never acknowledging that an officer had fired the projectile that blinded her.
stated_justification: The city did not offer a public justification for the specific shot that struck Tirado and denied that any identified officer had fired it.
effect_on_reporting: Tirado said the injury effectively ended a part of her career as a print photojournalist, though she continued working with adapted equipment; the case became a widely cited example of the physical risk journalists faced covering the 2020 protests.
status: Settled in May 2022 for $600,000; the city denied wrongdoing.
what_we_dont_know: The identity of the officer who fired the projectile that struck Tirado was never confirmed by the city.
outcome_note: The city paid $600,000 in a 2022 settlement while continuing to deny that an identified officer fired the projectile.

title: FBI raids Project Veritas founder's home over Ashley Biden diary investigation
summary: FBI agents raided Project Veritas founder James O'Keefe's New York home and seized his phones as part of an investigation into the alleged theft of a diary belonging to Ashley Biden, President Biden's daughter, which the group had reported on; O'Keefe was never charged.
issue_of_the_day: Project Veritas had obtained and reported on a diary purportedly belonging to Ashley Biden during the 2020 campaign; federal prosecutors were investigating how the diary had been obtained and transported across state lines.
what_happened: On November 6, 2021, FBI agents searched the Mamaroneck, New York home of Project Veritas founder James O'Keefe and seized two of his iPhones as part of a Justice Department investigation into the alleged theft of a diary belonging to Ashley Biden, daughter of President Biden, which O'Keefe's organization had reported on during the 2020 campaign. O'Keefe said the phones contained reporters' notes, confidential sources unrelated to the diary story and other newsroom material, and said it appeared prosecutors now had journalists "in their sights" for doing their jobs. His attorney said the underlying warrant cited potential charges including misprision of a felony and transporting stolen property across state lines. Two people involved in obtaining the diary pleaded guilty in August 2022; a court later allowed prosecutors to review the seized phones, but no charges were ever filed against O'Keefe himself, and he left Project Veritas in 2023 for unrelated reasons.
stated_justification: The search warrant cited a criminal investigation into the theft and interstate transport of Ashley Biden's diary; prosecutors did not separately justify seizing O'Keefe's phones rather than pursuing other investigative steps.
effect_on_reporting: A journalist's personal phones, containing what he said were confidential sources and reporting materials unrelated to the underlying investigation, were seized and later reviewed by federal prosecutors despite no charges ever being filed against him.
status: No charges were filed against O'Keefe; the phones were reviewed by prosecutors under a later court order.
what_we_dont_know: The full contents of what prosecutors reviewed on O'Keefe's phones, and whether any of it was used in other investigations, was not established in the source reviewed.
outcome_note: No charges were ever filed against O'Keefe; a court later allowed prosecutors to review the seized phones.

title: Customs officers seize Grayzone editor's phones at Virginia airport over Iran reporting
summary: U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers stopped Grayzone editor Max Blumenthal at Washington Dulles Airport, questioned him about his reporting trips to Iran, and seized both of his phones without his consent; the phones were returned a week later after he sued.
issue_of_the_day: Blumenthal had traveled to and reported from Iran, a country CBP's own cited policy treats as grounds for additional scrutiny of travelers who have worked in or visited it.
what_happened: On July 10, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers stopped Grayzone editor Max Blumenthal at Washington Dulles International Airport, questioned him about his reporting trips to Iran, searched his luggage and seized both of his cellphones without his consent; one officer told him they would "hook them up to machines" to extract the phones' data. CBP said its actions followed standard policy allowing additional scrutiny for travelers who had worked in or visited countries the government designates as state sponsors of terrorism, including Iran. Blumenthal said the stop was obviously connected to his reporting rather than routine screening. He sued on July 16, 2026, and the agency returned his phones the following day; his attorney said the case would proceed to discovery over whether agents had copied data from the devices before returning them.
stated_justification: CBP said "additional scrutiny and increased inspection may be conducted, including if an individual has worked in or traveled to a high-risk country such as a State Sponsor of Terrorism, including Iran."
effect_on_reporting: A journalist's phones, containing reporting materials and source contacts, were held by federal border agents for a week, and his attorney said the episode had already discouraged sources from communicating with him and made him wary of further travel.
