title: Hungary criminalizes false coronavirus information and grants Orban decree powers
summary: Hungary's parliament passed an emergency coronavirus law allowing prison terms of up to five years for spreading information the government deemed false or distorted about the pandemic, and let Prime Minister Viktor Orban rule by decree for an unlimited period.
issue_of_the_day: The law was passed as Hungary, like much of Europe, entered its first coronavirus lockdown in March 2020; the government said it needed emergency powers to respond quickly to the pandemic.
what_happened: On March 30, 2020, Hungary's parliament passed a coronavirus emergency law criminalizing the publication of information the government deemed false or distorted about the pandemic, with penalties of up to five years in prison, and gave Prime Minister Viktor Orban the power to rule by decree for as long as the state of danger lasted, without a fixed end date. Reporters Without Borders said the law could let the government arbitrarily decide which reports were false and use that power against independent newsrooms. The International Press Institute said the law criminalized spreading information deemed to undermine the authorities' pandemic response, with fines and up to five years in prison. Under European pressure, Hungary's government said in late May 2020 it would ask parliament to end the decree powers by June 20, 2020, while the underlying criminal provision on false pandemic information remained on the books in a narrower form.
stated_justification: The government said the emergency powers and the criminal penalty for false pandemic information were necessary to respond quickly and combat what it called disinformation about the coronavirus.
effect_on_reporting: Hungarian outlets faced the prospect of prison sentences for coronavirus reporting the government might later deem false or distorted, at the same time the government could rule by decree without a parliamentary check.
status: Hungary's government said in May 2020 it would ask parliament to end the decree powers by June 20, 2020; the sources reviewed did not establish the criminal provision's later fate in detail.
what_we_dont_know: Whether the criminal penalty for false pandemic information was narrowed or repealed after the state of danger ended was not established in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: Hungary's government said it would end Orban's decree powers by June 20, 2020; the false-information provision's later fate was not established.

title: Myanmar junta revokes five outlets' licenses and raids newsrooms after coup
summary: Weeks after seizing power, Myanmar's military junta revoked the operating licenses of five independent media outlets covering protests against the coup and raided two of their newsrooms, seizing computers and files; journalists from the outlets were later arrested and charged under a broadened penal-code provision on spreading 'false news.'
issue_of_the_day: The outlets had been covering nationwide protests against the military's February 1, 2021 seizure of power from Myanmar's elected government, coverage the junta sought to stop by removing the outlets' legal authorization to operate.
what_happened: On March 8 and 9, 2021, Myanmar's military junta revoked the licenses of five independent outlets, Mizzima, Myanmar Now, 7Day News, Democratic Voice of Burma and Khit Thit Media, which had been covering protests against the February 1 coup. Soldiers and police raided Myanmar Now's Yangon office, seizing computers, documents and server equipment, and raided Mizzima's head office the following day. Two weeks after the coup, the junta had broadened Article 505(a) of the penal code to criminalize spreading what it called false news, raising the maximum penalty from two to three years in prison; journalists from the affected outlets were later arrested and charged under the provision while covering the protests. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the junta must immediately reverse the license suspensions and let the outlets resume normal operations.
stated_justification: Myanmar's Ministry of Information did not respond to CPJ's request for comment explaining the license revocations; the junta separately said in public statements that it respected media freedom while warning outlets against using words like "coup" and "junta."
effect_on_reporting: Five of Myanmar's most prominent independent outlets lost their legal authority to operate inside the country, and reporting on the coup and its aftermath increasingly had to be produced from exile or underground.
status: The licenses were not restored; CPJ documented dozens of journalists still imprisoned under the amended penal-code provision months later.
outcome_note: The five outlets' licenses were not restored; CPJ counted at least 32 journalists still imprisoned as of July 2021.

title: Belarus blocks Tut.by and arrests its editors as 'extremist'
summary: Belarusian authorities blocked access to Tut.by, the country's most-read independent news site, searched its offices in three cities and arrested at least eleven staff, including its editor-in-chief, citing alleged media-law violations after the site had already lost its official media status.
issue_of_the_day: Tut.by had continued reporting on the government's response to protests following the disputed August 2020 presidential election that kept Alexander Lukashenko in power; authorities revoked the outlet's official media registration in January 2021.
what_happened: On May 19, 2021, Belarusian authorities blocked online access to Tut.by, the country's most-visited independent news site, and searched its headquarters in Minsk and regional offices in Brest and Hrodna, arresting at least eleven employees, including editor-in-chief Marina Zolotova and publisher Volha Loyka, and opening criminal proceedings against the outlet's leadership. The information ministry said the site had committed "multiple media law violations, including the publication of banned information." Reporters Without Borders said the accusations were invented as a pretext to shut down one of the country's most popular outlets, which had already lost its official media status in January 2021 and whose staff separately faced tax-fraud charges RSF called fabricated. The outlet later continued reporting from exile under the name Zerkalo.
stated_justification: Belarus's information ministry said it was acting against "multiple media law violations, including the publication of banned information," and Deputy Information Minister Andrey Kuncevic said the government would continue "protecting the country's information space."
effect_on_reporting: Belarus's largest independent news site was blocked inside the country and its editorial leadership arrested, forcing its journalists to continue reporting from exile under a new name.
status: Tut.by remained blocked inside Belarus; its former staff continued reporting from abroad as Zerkalo.

title: Russia criminalizes 'fake' reporting on the military, up to 15 years in prison
summary: Russia's parliament passed a law criminalizing the publication of information about the military that contradicts official statements, with penalties up to 15 years in prison, prompting Novaya Gazeta to pull its Ukraine war coverage and the BBC, CNN and other outlets to suspend operations inside Russia.
issue_of_the_day: The law followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, and was aimed at reporting on the war that differed from the Russian defense ministry's official statements about casualties and military conduct.
what_happened: On March 4, 2022, Russia's parliament passed a law criminalizing the publication of what officials called deliberately false information about the military, including reporting on the invasion of Ukraine that contradicted official statements, with penalties of up to three years for a basic offense and up to 15 years in cases deemed to have caused severe consequences. Parliament speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said the law was meant to protect Russian soldiers and the truth. Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia's few remaining independent outlets, removed its Ukraine war coverage from its site, warning that restrictions on reporting had moved from threats of blocking outlets to threats of criminal prosecution of journalists and ordinary citizens. The BBC suspended its Russian news operations, with director-general Tim Davie saying the safety of staff came first, and other foreign broadcasters and independent Russian outlets closed or left the country in the days that followed.
stated_justification: Parliament speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said the law was needed "to protect our soldiers and officers, and to protect the truth."
effect_on_reporting: Independent and foreign reporting on the war from inside Russia largely ended within days, as outlets weighed the risk of years-long prison sentences for staff against continuing to report on the invasion.
status: The law remained in force; independent Russian outlets that had not closed continued operating from outside the country.
outcome_note: The law remained in force; independent outlets that avoided closure continued operating from outside Russia.

title: Indian tax authorities search BBC offices weeks after Modi documentary ban
summary: India's Income Tax Department searched BBC offices in Delhi and Mumbai for alleged tax evasion, three weeks after the government used emergency powers to block a BBC documentary examining Prime Minister Narendra Modi's response to 2002 communal violence.
issue_of_the_day: The searches followed the government's ban, weeks earlier, of the BBC documentary 'India: The Modi Question,' which examined Modi's record as Gujarat's chief minister during 2002 riots that killed mostly Muslims.
what_happened: On February 14, 2023, India's Income Tax Department conducted what officials called surveys, sealing off and searching BBC offices in Delhi and Mumbai and confiscating documents and journalists' phones, in what the government said was an investigation into tax evasion. The searches came about three weeks after the government invoked emergency powers under India's Information Technology Rules to block domestic access to the BBC's two-part documentary 'India: The Modi Question,' which examined Modi's response to 2002 communal violence in Gujarat, where he was then chief minister. A spokesperson for the governing party called the BBC "the most corrupt organization in the world," while Human Rights Watch said the raid and the documentary ban were part of an escalating pattern of using government agencies to pressure civil-society groups and media outlets. India's Editors Guild called the searches a continuation of a trend of using government agencies to pressure press organizations.
stated_justification: Officials said the tax searches were routine "surveys, not searches," aimed at investigating alleged tax evasion by the BBC.
effect_on_reporting: The BBC's Indian bureaus lost access to documents and staff phones for the length of the search, coming so soon after the documentary ban that press-freedom groups treated the two actions as connected pressure on the same outlet.
status: No subsequent tax penalty or further government action against the BBC was reported in the source reviewed; the broadcaster's India operations continued.
what_we_dont_know: The outcome of the tax investigation itself was not established in the source reviewed.

title: Bombay High Court strikes down India's government 'fact check unit' rule
summary: India's 2023 amendment to its Information Technology Rules empowered a government-run Fact Check Unit to label online content about the central government 'fake' or 'false' and require its removal; comedian Kunal Kamra and media groups challenged it, and the Bombay High Court struck the rule down as unconstitutionally vague.
issue_of_the_day: The government said the Fact Check Unit was needed to combat misinformation about its own policies and announcements online, at a time when it separately faced criticism over content restrictions ahead of India's 2024 general election.
what_happened: In 2023, India's government amended its Information Technology Rules to create a Fact Check Unit empowered to identify online content about the central government's own affairs as "fake, false or misleading" and require platforms to remove it or lose their legal protection from liability for user content. Comedian Kunal Kamra, the Editors Guild of India and the Association of Indian Magazines challenged the rule, arguing there was no constitutional "right to the truth" that could justify a government body policing facts about itself. India's Supreme Court stayed the unit's operation while the case proceeded. After a split verdict, a tie-breaking judge on the Bombay High Court struck down the rule in September 2024, finding its key terms "vague and overbroad" and the government's own definition of misinformation legally unsound.
stated_justification: The government said the Fact Check Unit was needed to address "misinformation concerning the Central Government's affairs" and to identify content that was "fake" or "false."
effect_on_reporting: Had it taken effect, the rule would have let a government body decide which online statements about its own policies counted as false and require platforms to remove them, a power that never came into force because of the legal challenge.
status: The rule was struck down; the Fact Check Unit never operated after the Supreme Court's stay.
outcome_note: The Bombay High Court struck down the rule, finding its key terms 'vague and overbroad,' after the Supreme Court had already stayed its operation.

title: Guatemala convicts investigative journalist Jose Ruben Zamora on money-laundering charge
summary: A Guatemalan court convicted El Periodico founder Jose Ruben Zamora of money laundering and sentenced him to six years in prison, months after his newspaper, known for investigating government corruption, was forced to close; press-freedom groups said the case was connected to his investigative reporting rather than the financial charge alone.
issue_of_the_day: El Periodico had published more than 120 investigations into government corruption since January 2020 before its forced closure in May 2023, shortly before Zamora's conviction.
what_happened: On June 14, 2023, a Guatemalan court convicted journalist Jose Ruben Zamora, founder of the investigative newspaper El Periodico, of laundering approximately $40,000, sentencing him to six years in prison and a fine of more than $38,000. Zamora had been arrested the previous July, and El Periodico, which had published more than 120 investigations into government corruption since January 2020, was forced to close in May 2023, with its leadership citing pressure on its advertisers and on its operations. Zamora said prosecutors had "treated us like criminals" and destroyed evidence; his son said the state had effectively kidnapped an innocent man. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the case sent a message that reporting on corruption could itself be treated as a crime, and the court separately found that Zamora's reporting had harmed the Guatemalan economy.
stated_justification: The court convicted Zamora of money laundering and found that his conduct had harmed the Guatemalan economy; President Giammattei's government said Guatemala had a free press and denied any political motivation.
effect_on_reporting: One of Guatemala's most prominent investigative outlets closed and its founder was imprisoned within the same year, a sequence press-freedom groups said sent a message to other Guatemalan journalists covering official corruption.
status: Zamora's case continued through appeals and shifting custody arrangements in the years that followed, including a return to prison in March 2025 after a period of house arrest.
outcome_note: Zamora's case continued through appeals and changing custody arrangements; he remained in the criminal justice system.

title: Nicaragua strips 94 political opponents, including journalists, of citizenship
summary: A Nicaraguan appeals court stripped 94 government opponents, including exiled journalists Carlos Fernando Chamorro and Alvaro Navarro, of their citizenship, days after President Daniel Ortega released 222 political prisoners to the United States and immediately declared them stateless too.
issue_of_the_day: The rulings followed years of pressure on Nicaragua's independent press, including the earlier forced closure of the country's oldest newspaper, La Prensa, and came days after Ortega's government released 222 jailed dissidents to the United States and stripped their citizenship as well.
what_happened: On February 16, 2023, a Nicaraguan appeals court stripped 94 government opponents, described in the ruling as human rights defenders, politicians, journalists and students, of their Nicaraguan citizenship, on top of 222 political prisoners flown to the United States days earlier who had already been declared stateless. Journalists Carlos Fernando Chamorro and Alvaro Navarro were among those named. Appeals Court Justice Ernesto Rodriguez Mejia said those affected were guilty of "spreading false news" and conspiring to undermine national integrity. Navarro responded that he remained Nicaraguan regardless of the ruling. Civil Rights Defenders said Ortega was clearly trying to eliminate anyone who stood up against his government and called for international bodies to raise Nicaragua's deteriorating human rights record.
stated_justification: The court found those whose citizenship had been revoked guilty of "spreading false news" and "conspiracy to undermine national integrity."
effect_on_reporting: Exiled Nicaraguan journalists, already unable to work safely inside the country, lost their legal nationality entirely, cutting off their ability to hold a Nicaraguan passport or return under any legal status.
status: Citizenship was not restored to those named; Ortega's government continued similar measures against critics in the years that followed.
outcome_note: Citizenship was not restored to those named; Ortega's government continued comparable actions against critics afterward.

title: Slovakia's parliament dissolves public broadcaster RTVS, replaces it with STVR
summary: Slovakia's parliament, controlled by Prime Minister Robert Fico's coalition, dissolved public broadcaster RTVS and replaced it with a new entity, STVR, whose director is now chosen through a process giving parliament and the culture ministry more direct control, prompting protests and criticism from the European Union.
issue_of_the_day: Fico's government accused RTVS of one-sided, activist coverage against it, a complaint it made after RTVS reporting the government considered unfavorable during Fico's return to power in late 2023.
what_happened: Slovakia's parliament passed a law dissolving the public broadcaster RTVS and creating a successor, Slovak Television and Radio (STVR), which took effect on July 4, 2024. Under the new structure, parliament and the culture ministry nominate nine council members who select STVR's director-general, replacing RTVS's previous, more independent selection process; the displaced RTVS director, Lubos Machaj, kept only his separate parliamentary mandate through 2027. The parliamentary culture committee's chairman defended the change, describing RTVS as an "activist TV" whose editors lacked political neutrality. Opposition lawmaker Zora Jaurova said private media owners were being pressured to accept a different approach to political coverage, and Slovak journalist Ivan Brada said the country appeared to be following Hungary's path toward government-controlled media. Thousands protested in Bratislava, and European institutions criticized the law.
stated_justification: The parliamentary committee chairman overseeing the bill said RTVS operated as an "activist TV" whose editorial staff lacked political neutrality.
effect_on_reporting: Slovakia's public broadcaster was dissolved and re-formed under a leadership-selection process giving the governing coalition direct influence over who runs it, a structural change press-freedom monitors said increased the government's leverage over public-service journalism.
status: STVR replaced RTVS as planned in July 2024; the government did not reverse the change.
outcome_note: STVR replaced RTVS as planned; the ousted director-general kept only his separate parliamentary mandate.

title: Georgia enacts 'foreign influence' law requiring media to register as foreign-backed
summary: Georgia's parliament passed a law requiring media and civil-society groups that receive 20 percent or more of their funding from abroad to register as organizations "serving the interests of a foreign power," over mass street protests and international criticism that the label would be used to marginalize independent outlets.
issue_of_the_day: The governing Georgian Dream party framed the law as protecting Georgian sovereignty against foreign-funded groups it accused of trying to organize unrest, at a time when the party also faced growing opposition ahead of Georgia's 2024 parliamentary election.
what_happened: Georgia's parliament passed the "law on transparency of foreign influence" in May 2024, requiring media outlets and non-governmental organizations that receive twenty percent or more of their annual revenue from foreign sources to register with the justice ministry as "organizations serving the interests of a foreign power," subjecting them to additional reporting requirements, inspections and fines of roughly $9,300 for noncompliance. Human Rights Watch's Europe director, Hugh Williamson, said labeling independent groups and media as serving foreign interests was intended to marginalize and stifle critical voices, and called on Georgian authorities to drop the bill. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze defended the law as directed at groups he said were trying to "organize a revolution," promote what he called "LGBT propaganda," and "discredit the police, judiciary, and the Georgian Orthodox Church." Mass protests in Tbilisi and statements from United Nations experts condemning the law did not stop its passage.
stated_justification: Prime Minister Kobakhidze said the law addressed groups attempting to "organize a revolution" and to "discredit the police, judiciary, and the Georgian Orthodox Church."
effect_on_reporting: Independent Georgian outlets that rely on foreign grants faced a stigmatizing official label, new inspections and fines, pressure press-freedom groups said was designed to make continued foreign-funded reporting more difficult.
status: The law took effect over the protests and international criticism documented; Georgian Dream did not withdraw it.
outcome_note: The law took effect despite mass protests and international criticism; the governing party did not withdraw it.

title: Hong Kong court convicts Stand News editors of sedition
summary: A Hong Kong court convicted former Stand News editors Chung Pui-kuen and Patrick Lam of conspiring to publish seditious material, under a colonial-era law, over articles the outlet had run before police raided its newsroom and it closed at the end of 2021.
issue_of_the_day: The prosecution centered on opinion pieces and interviews Stand News had published examining Hong Kong's 2019 protests and the 2020 National Security Law, coverage prosecutors said smeared the security law and law enforcement.
what_happened: On August 29, 2024, Hong Kong District Court Judge Kwok Wai-kin convicted former Stand News editor-in-chief Chung Pui-kuen and acting editor-in-chief Patrick Lam of conspiring to publish and reproduce seditious material, finding that 11 of 17 articles the prosecution presented had been seditious under a sedition law dating to the colonial era. Stand News had already ceased operating in December 2021 after a police raid on its offices. Chung argued in response that free speech should not be limited to eliminating dangerous ideas but should instead be used to counter them. A U.S. State Department spokesperson said the verdict directly harmed media freedom. Both editors were sentenced on September 26, 2024, facing up to two years in prison.
stated_justification: The court found that the articles were seditious because they were capable of undermining public confidence in the Hong Kong or Chinese central government, and prosecutors argued certain pieces promoted ideologies the law prohibited or smeared the security law and police.
effect_on_reporting: A once-prominent Hong Kong outlet had already closed under police pressure, and the criminal conviction of its editors for material it had published established that ordinary opinion journalism about the security law could carry a prison sentence.
status: Both editors were sentenced in September 2024; the convictions were not overturned in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: Both editors were sentenced in September 2024; no reversal of the convictions was reported.

title: Milei's government shuts down Argentina's state news agency Telam
summary: President Javier Milei's government fenced off and shut down Telam, Argentina's state-owned news agency, calling it a public-relations operation for the prior Kirchnerist governments; unions and journalist groups called the closure one of the most serious blows to press freedom in decades of Argentine democracy.
issue_of_the_day: Milei had campaigned against what he called wasteful and politically one-sided state spending, and Telam, founded in 1945, had long been associated with the governments of the Kirchner political movement he defeated in the 2023 election.
what_happened: On the night of March 3 into March 4, 2024, Milei's government fenced off Telam's Buenos Aires offices and blocked staff from entering, taking the agency's website offline and placing its roughly seven hundred employees on seven days of paid leave while the closure proceeded. Milei said it was wrong for a poor country's government to spend public money buying journalists' favor, calling Telam "a covert propaganda ministry" and "a Kirchnerist propaganda agency for the last decades." The Buenos Aires Press Union, SiPreBA, called the closure one of the worst actions against freedom of expression in forty years of Argentine democracy, and the Argentine Journalism Forum, Fopea, said the decision would deepen intolerance toward journalism. Workers and press-freedom advocates organized protests, including a symbolic gathering around the building, but the closure proceeded.
stated_justification: Milei said it was "immoral that in a poor country like ours, the government spends the people's money to buy the will of journalists," describing Telam as "a covert propaganda ministry."
effect_on_reporting: Argentina's national wire service, which many regional and local outlets relied on for national and international news feeds, stopped operating, and roughly seven hundred journalists and staff lost their positions.
status: Telam's newsroom remained closed; the agency was later reorganized as a smaller state communications operation.
outcome_note: Telam's original newsroom remained closed; the agency was later reorganized as a smaller state communications operation.

title: Serbian police strike, detain and disarm journalists covering anti-government protests
summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists documented at least 28 Serbian journalists reporting being struck, detained, sprayed with chemical irritants or having their equipment destroyed by police between June and September 2025 while covering nationwide anti-government protests; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.
issue_of_the_day: The protests, which grew through the summer of 2025, followed months of demonstrations against President Aleksandar Vucic's government that began after a deadly railway-station canopy collapse in Novi Sad in late 2024.
what_happened: Between June and September 2025, Serbian police repeatedly used force against journalists covering nationwide anti-government protests, according to a Committee to Protect Journalists report published September 25, 2025 documenting at least 28 affected journalists. On September 5 in Novi Sad, police kicked reporter Emir Kahrimanovic despite his visible press vest, forced Vreme reporter Katarina Stevanovic to lie on the ground for about fifteen minutes, and grabbed and smashed KTV reporter Nemanja Sarovic's microphone while he was reporting live. On September 1, an officer seized Beta news agency reporter Bozidar Milovac's phone and forced him to delete footage despite his identifying himself as a journalist. In earlier incidents in Belgrade and other cities in July and August, reporters described being struck with batons and shields, sprayed with an unknown chemical substance, and having memory cards destroyed. CPJ's Europe representative called for swift, transparent investigations and accountability for the officers involved; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.
stated_justification: No Serbian official offered a public justification for the specific incidents documented; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists covering the protests described routinely facing physical force, confiscation or destruction of equipment, and orders to stop filming, even when visibly identified as press, narrowing on-the-ground coverage of the demonstrations.
status: No officer was reported disciplined for any of the documented incidents as of CPJ's report.
what_we_dont_know: Whether any internal investigation into individual officers' conduct was opened was not established in the source reviewed.
outcome_note: The interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment, and no officer was reported disciplined for the incidents documented.

title: Ethiopia arrests at least six journalists including Sheger FM staff over election-year coverage
summary: Ethiopian authorities arrested at least six journalists between August and September 2025, including three from Sheger FM after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered the station to delete a broadcast it accused of bias and inciting violence, ahead of national elections scheduled for 2026.
issue_of_the_day: The arrests came ahead of Ethiopia's national elections scheduled for 2026, after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered Sheger FM to remove an August 29, 2025 broadcast it said was one-sided and incited violence.
what_happened: Between August and September 2025, Ethiopian authorities arrested at least six journalists and media workers, including radio host Khadar Mohamed Ismail on August 5, radio host Abdulsemed Mohammed on August 11, and journalist Yonas Amare, who was abducted on August 13 and released on August 22 along with Mohammed. On September 3, Sheger FM journalists Tigist Zerihun, Mintamir Tsegaw and Eshete Assefa were arrested after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered the station to delete an August 29 broadcast it accused of bias and inciting violence. Human Rights Watch said the authorities' renewed efforts to limit independent reporting were aimed at preventing public scrutiny of the government ahead of elections scheduled for 2026, adding that a free press mattered more, not less, in the run-up to a vote. Some of the Sheger FM journalists were granted bail in mid-September while an appeal proceeded.
stated_justification: The Ethiopian Media Authority accused the Sheger FM broadcast of "bias and inciting violence" when it ordered the station to remove it.
effect_on_reporting: Independent Ethiopian broadcasters described feeling pressure to delete their own content and hold back coverage under threat of arrest, narrowing reporting on politically sensitive events ahead of the 2026 election.
status: Some journalists were granted bail while an appeal proceeded; the media authority's order against Sheger FM remained in force.
what_we_dont_know: The final legal outcome for each of the six journalists named was not established in the source reviewed.
outcome_note: Some journalists were granted bail while an appeal proceeded; the media authority's order against Sheger FM remained in force.

title: Pakistan amends cybercrime law to create new agency policing 'fake' online content
summary: Pakistan's parliament amended the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act to create a new Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority with power to block online content and a Social Media Protection Tribunal, and made spreading information deemed 'fake or false' punishable by up to three years in prison, prompting nationwide journalist protests.
issue_of_the_day: The government said the amendment was needed to curb online disinformation, but journalists said the new offense's vague wording, covering content merely believed likely to cause "fear, panic, disorder or unrest," gave authorities broad discretion over ordinary reporting.
what_happened: On January 29, 2025, Pakistan's parliament passed amendments to the 2016 Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act creating a government-appointed Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority, empowered to order the removal or blocking of online content, and a separate Social Media Protection Tribunal to hear related cases. A new provision, Section 26A, made it a crime punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine of about $7,000 to knowingly disseminate information believed to be false or fake and likely to cause "fear, panic, disorder or unrest." The Pakistan Press Foundation said the lack of clarity around the amendments raised questions about the government's real intent, and Human Rights Watch called for the law's repeal, saying it lacked any exemption protecting journalistic work. The Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists organized nationwide protests, calling the law an infringement on people's rights.
stated_justification: The law's Section 26A targets the "intentional dissemination, exhibition or transmission of information...that the sender knows or believes to be false or fake and likely to cause or create a sense of public fear, panic, disorder or unrest."
effect_on_reporting: Journalists faced a vaguely worded criminal offense, enforced by a government-appointed authority and tribunal rather than the courts, for publishing information officials could later deem false, with no exemption for journalistic work.
status: The amendment remained law despite the nationwide protests and Human Rights Watch's call for repeal.
outcome_note: The amendment remained law despite nationwide journalist protests and a Human Rights Watch call for its repeal.

title: Journalists beaten in Bangladesh in separate incidents as interim government drafts new cyber laws
summary: On a single day in February 2025, groups of men beat at least eight journalists in two separate incidents in rural Bangladesh while they investigated a medical-negligence tip and a land dispute; the incidents came as the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus drafted new cyber ordinances rights groups said could add legal risk on top of the physical one.
issue_of_the_day: The incidents occurred six months into the interim government that took power after Sheikh Hasina's government fell in August 2024, a period in which press-freedom groups said journalists faced both continued street violence and new draft cyber-security legislation.
what_happened: On February 3, 2025, ten to twelve men beat Samakal correspondent Shohag Khan Sujon with a hammer and knife while he investigated allegations of medical negligence in Shariatpur district, and four other journalists who intervened were also beaten. The same day, in Laxmipur district, four correspondents covering a land dispute were beaten with bamboo sticks by a separate group that also fired guns, wounding one journalist with shrapnel. Days earlier, British freelance journalist Shafiur Rahman received threatening emails after publishing an article about a government security meeting, warning him to "stop or suffer the consequences." The Committee to Protect Journalists said the interim government's draft Cyber Protection Ordinance and Personal Data Protection Ordinance, introduced in January 2025, risked giving authorities broad new power over online content and user data on top of the continuing physical violence journalists faced covering local disputes.
stated_justification: No government official offered a public justification for the beatings, which were carried out by private individuals; the interim government described its draft cyber ordinances as necessary data-protection and security measures.
effect_on_reporting: Reporters covering local corruption and land disputes in rural Bangladesh faced serious physical violence in a single day, while a freelance journalist covering national-security matters received written threats, illustrating the range of pressure facing the press during the political transition.
status: No arrests in the beatings were reported in the source reviewed, and the proposed cyber ordinances remained under review.
outcome_note: No arrests were reported in the incidents described, and the proposed cyber ordinances remained under review.

title: Venezuela detains, expels and restricts journalists after disputed 2024 election
summary: In the two weeks after Venezuela's disputed July 28, 2024 presidential election, Reporters Without Borders documented 70 press-freedom violations, including nine detentions, nine expulsions of foreign correspondents and the suspension of the social media platform X, as President Nicolas Maduro's government moved to control coverage of the disputed result.
issue_of_the_day: Venezuela's July 28, 2024 election, in which the National Electoral Council declared Maduro the winner without releasing detailed vote tallies opposition figures disputed, triggered protests and a surge of restrictions on the journalists covering them.
what_happened: In the fifteen days after Venezuela's July 28, 2024 election, Reporters Without Borders documented 70 press-freedom violations, including 18 access restrictions, 30 cases of threats or coercion, nine detentions, nine expulsions of foreign journalists and four instances of physical violence. Colombian journalists Carolina Trinidad and Vanessa de la Torre were expelled from the Caracas airport without explanation on election day, Chilean journalists Ivan Nunez and Jose Luis Tapia were held incommunicado at a military post until their embassy intervened, and Spanish journalist Alvaro Nieto was deported after a two-hour interrogation. Venezuelan photojournalists and broadcasters, including Yousnel Alvarado and Deisy Pena, were detained and, in some cases, held on terrorism-related charges. The government also opened a criminal investigation into the opposition-aligned results website ResultadosConVzla, suspended X for ten days and blocked Signal and Reddit. RSF's Latin America director said the pattern of violations showed the government's determination to limit public debate.
stated_justification: No specific public justification for the individual detentions and expulsions was documented; the government separately described the platform suspensions as necessary to prevent the spread of what it called disinformation about the election.
effect_on_reporting: Foreign correspondents were expelled or detained within days of the vote, Venezuelan journalists were jailed on serious charges including terrorism, and major communication platforms were blocked or suspended, sharply narrowing independent coverage of the disputed result.
status: Detained journalists faced continuing prosecution, and social-platform restrictions remained in place after the fifteen-day period RSF documented.
outcome_note: Detained journalists faced continuing prosecution, and social-platform restrictions remained in place after the documented period.

title: Turkish authorities detain three journalists under 'disinformation' law
summary: Turkish authorities detained three journalists, jailing columnist Tolga Sardan pending trial, under a 2022 law criminalizing the spread of disinformation, after the government's own disinformation-fighting body disputed their reporting on a leaked intelligence document and a story about released prisoners.
issue_of_the_day: Sardan had written about an alleged Turkish intelligence report on judicial corruption, which the government's Center for Combating Disinformation denied existed; Halk TV's Dincer Gokce had reported on people released from prison who were later linked to further crimes.
what_happened: On November 1 and 2, 2023, Turkish authorities detained T24 columnist Tolga Sardan, Halk TV news editor Dincer Gokce and Kisa Dalga reporter Cengiz Erdinc under Turkiye's 2022 law criminalizing the spread of what officials call disinformation. Sardan was jailed pending trial after writing about an intelligence report on judicial corruption that the government's Center for Combating Disinformation said did not exist. Gokce was released after a court ordered him to read books about journalism, over an article about people released from prison who authorities said had been wrongly described. Erdinc was released the following day. The Committee to Protect Journalists called on Turkish authorities to release Sardan and Erdinc without delay and said the vague law would continue to stifle reporting in the country.
stated_justification: Turkey's Center for Combating Disinformation denied the existence of the intelligence report Sardan had written about, and authorities said Gokce's article about released prisoners had proven inaccurate.
effect_on_reporting: A columnist was jailed pending trial and another journalist was ordered by a court to read books about journalism, over stories the government's own disinformation body disputed rather than a court finding of falsity through an ordinary defamation process.
status: Two of the three detained journalists were released within a day or two; Sardan remained jailed pending trial.
outcome_note: Two of the three journalists were released within a day; Tolga Sardan remained jailed pending trial.

title: Tunisia's cybercrime decree pushes jailed-journalist count to highest since 1992
summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists found at least four journalists imprisoned under Tunisia's 2022 Decree-Law 54 on cybercrime as of January 2025, including radio hosts Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies, pushing the country's jailed-journalist count to its highest since 1992 under President Kais Saied.
issue_of_the_day: Decree-Law 54, issued by President Kais Saied in 2022 without a sitting parliament, criminalized spreading what authorities deem "false news" online, and by January 2025 had become the basis for jailing a record number of Tunisian journalists.
what_happened: The Committee to Protect Journalists reported on January 16, 2025 that at least four of five imprisoned Tunisian journalists were convicted under Decree-Law 54, a 2022 cybercrime decree President Kais Saied issued while ruling by decree without a sitting parliament. Radio hosts Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies of IFM each received one-year sentences, commentator Sonia Dahmani's one-year sentence was reduced to eight months on appeal before she received an additional two-year sentence, and journalist Mohamed Boughaleb received six months on a separate defamation charge. The head of Tunisia's journalists' union, Ziad Debbar, said the decree had turned every journalist into a suspect. The International Commission of Jurists said Tunisian authorities were using the decree to arbitrarily restrict dissenting voices, in violation of the country's human rights obligations, subjecting journalists, politicians and rights defenders to prosecution, investigation and imprisonment.
stated_justification: Decree-Law 54 targets content that "produces, spreads, disseminates, sends or writes false news" seen as threatening "rights of others, public safety or national defense or sowing terror."
effect_on_reporting: Tunisia, once cited as a rare post-Arab Spring press-freedom success, reached its highest count of imprisoned journalists since 1992, with radio hosts and commentators serving sentences of six months to more than two years for broadcast commentary and online statements.
status: Decree-Law 54 remained in force and continued to produce new prosecutions as of CPJ's report.
outcome_note: Decree-Law 54 remained in force and continued to produce new prosecutions, which CPJ said brought jailed-journalist numbers to a record.

claims.evidence_quote: The Tunisian authorities are using Decree 54 to arbitrarily silence dissenting and independent voices, in clear violation of the country's obligations under international human rights law

title: Tanzania shuts down internet access on election day amid unrest
summary: Tanzania's government restricted internet and social-media access on October 29, 2025, as citizens voted in a general election marked by protests, cutting national internet traffic by nearly 90 percent and leaving both local and foreign journalists unable to report on the vote and its aftermath in real time.
issue_of_the_day: The shutdown coincided with a disputed general election and protests against President Samia Suluhu Hassan's government, which Human Rights Watch later said was followed by killings and broader restrictions once the results were announced.
what_happened: On October 29, 2025, as Tanzanians voted in a general election, national internet traffic began falling sharply around 12:30 p.m. local time, dropping to nearly 90 percent below the previous week's levels, according to monitoring cited by TechCabal; three journalists in Dar es Salaam and Arusha said social media platforms were unreachable without a virtual private network. Neither the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority nor telecom operators responded publicly to questions about the outage, and Tanzanian authorities did not issue a statement explaining it. Human Rights Watch reported on November 4, 2025 that the shutdown prevented media from reporting on the election and the protests that followed, and said authorities appeared to have also blocked foreign journalists from covering the vote by not responding to their accreditation applications.
stated_justification: Tanzanian authorities did not issue a public statement explaining the internet restrictions.
effect_on_reporting: Local and international journalists lost the ability to report in real time on the election and the protests that followed, while some foreign correspondents said their accreditation requests to cover the vote went unanswered.
status: Disruptions to social platforms continued for at least several days after the vote; authorities did not explain or formally end the restrictions.
what_we_dont_know: The precise date full connectivity was restored was not established in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: Authorities did not explain the shutdown, and disruptions to social platforms continued for several days after the vote.

claims.evidence_quote: The authorities appear to have blocked foreign journalists from covering the elections by failing in some instances to respond to accreditation applications.

title: Court orders RCMP to stop restricting press access at Fairy Creek logging blockades
summary: A British Columbia court found the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had failed to justify wide exclusion zones that kept journalists away from its enforcement of a logging injunction at the Fairy Creek old-growth blockades, and ordered police to keep the media's role in a free society in mind when deciding whether to remove or arrest reporters.
issue_of_the_day: The RCMP was enforcing a court injunction won by logging company Teal-Jones against protesters blocking old-growth logging roads near Fairy Creek on Vancouver Island, and had required journalists to check in and stay escorted rather than observe enforcement directly.
what_happened: Through the summer of 2021, journalists covering the RCMP's enforcement of a court injunction against old-growth logging protesters at Fairy Creek, on Vancouver Island in British Columbia, said police required them to check in at set times and remain escorted rather than observe arrests directly, restricting their ability to independently document the operation. A coalition of Canadian news organizations went to court, and on July 20, 2021, Justice Douglas Thompson found the RCMP had not justified the extensive exclusion zones it had imposed on media access. The judge ordered that future enforcement decisions be made with an explicit reminder of the media's role in a free and democratic society and the need to avoid unnecessary interference with journalism. The RCMP had defended the restrictions as reasonably necessary given hazardous terrain, limited space for enforcement and poor cell coverage.
stated_justification: The RCMP said the restrictions were "reasonably necessary" because of hazardous terrain, limited space to safely conduct enforcement, and poor cell phone coverage at the blockade sites.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists had been kept at a distance from arrests and enforcement actions for weeks under an escort system that limited independent verification of how the operation was being conducted, before the court intervened.
status: The court granted the media coalition's request; the RCMP was required to factor press access into future enforcement decisions.
outcome_note: The court granted the media coalition's request, requiring the RCMP to account for press access in future enforcement decisions.

claims.evidence_quote: It's sort of a strong affirmation [of] what we've been saying all along amongst this [media] group that the public's right to know is worth fighting for and that democracy demands freedom of the press.

title: Australia's High Court invalidates warrant for raid on journalist Annika Smethurst
summary: Australia's High Court ruled that the warrant the Australian Federal Police used to raid News Corp journalist Annika Smethurst's home over a national-security leak was invalid, and weeks later the AFP said it would not lay charges against her, citing insufficient evidence.
issue_of_the_day: The 2019 raid stemmed from Smethurst's reporting on leaked, classified plans to expand the Australian Signals Directorate's domestic surveillance powers, which the government treated as a national-security leak investigation.
what_happened: The Australian Federal Police had searched journalist Annika Smethurst's Canberra home in 2019 over her reporting on leaked documents describing plans to expand the Australian Signals Directorate's powers to monitor Australians domestically. Smethurst challenged the warrant, and on April 15, 2020, Australia's High Court unanimously ruled it invalid because it failed to properly specify the offense being investigated, though the court allowed police to keep the seized material for any future prosecution. On May 27, 2020, AFP Deputy Commissioner Ian McCartney announced the agency would not charge Smethurst, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the path the leaked document had taken or who had provided it. The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance said the case showed how national-security laws could be misused against legitimate public-interest journalism, and the Law Council of Australia's president said the law still left journalists exposed to investigation and prosecution.
stated_justification: The AFP said its investigation could not establish, with sufficient evidence, how the leaked document had moved or who had provided it to Smethurst.
effect_on_reporting: A journalist's home was searched and her devices seized over a story about government surveillance powers, and although the warrant was ultimately found invalid and no charges followed, press-freedom groups said the case showed reporters remained exposed to similar national-security investigations.
status: The AFP closed its investigation without charges after the High Court found the original warrant invalid.
outcome_note: The High Court found the 2019 warrant invalid, and the AFP announced weeks later it would not charge Smethurst.

claims.evidence_quote: The law continues to leave journalists and media organisations exposed to possible police investigation and prosecution.

title: China expels American journalists from three major U.S. newspapers
summary: China ordered American correspondents for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to leave the country, in a reciprocal response to the Trump administration capping the number of Chinese state-media employees allowed in the United States, which itself followed China's earlier expulsion of three Journal reporters over an opinion headline.
issue_of_the_day: The expulsions followed a rapid exchange of measures: a Wall Street Journal opinion piece China objected to, the U.S. capping Chinese state-media staff, and China's decision to expel American reporters from three outlets in response, all unfolding as the coronavirus pandemic was spreading globally.
what_happened: In February 2020, after The Wall Street Journal published an opinion column China's government objected to, Beijing revoked the press credentials of three Journal reporters based in China. On March 2, 2020, the Trump administration capped the number of Chinese state-media employees allowed to work in the United States at 100, down from about 160. On March 17, 2020, China's foreign ministry announced it would require American journalists working for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post whose press cards were due to expire that year to leave the country, and said they would not be allowed to work as journalists in mainland China, Hong Kong or Macau. China's foreign ministry called the move "entirely necessary and reciprocal countermeasures" against what it described as American measures aimed exclusively at Chinese media organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said he regretted China's decision to further limit free press operations worldwide.
stated_justification: China's foreign ministry described the expulsions as "entirely necessary and reciprocal countermeasures," saying "what the US has done is exclusively targeting Chinese media organizations, and hence driven by a Cold War mentality."
effect_on_reporting: American correspondents for three of the country's largest newspapers lost their accreditation to report from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau at the outset of the global coronavirus pandemic, cutting into independent Western reporting from China during a major global story.
status: The expelled journalists' credentials were not restored in the source reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The precise number of journalists affected across the three outlets was not specified in the source reviewed.
outcome_note: The expelled journalists' press credentials were not restored; reciprocal media restrictions between the two countries continued for years afterward.

claims.evidence_quote: They will not be allowed to continue working as journalists in the People's Republic of China, including its Hong Kong and Macao Special Administrative Regions.

claims.evidence_quote: entirely necessary and reciprocal countermeasures

claims.evidence_quote: I regret China's decision to further foreclose the world's ability to conduct free press operations.

title: Zimbabwe's Patriotic Act criminalizes journalists' contact with foreign governments
summary: President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed the Patriotic Act, which criminalizes meeting foreign governments or officials with intent to harm Zimbabwe's sovereignty, with penalties up to death for advocating armed intervention and up to ten years for supporting sanctions, weeks before the country's 2023 general election.
issue_of_the_day: The bill passed weeks before Zimbabwe's August 2023 general election, at a time when the government accused foreign-linked civil-society and media figures of working to undermine it ahead of the vote.
what_happened: Zimbabwe's parliament passed the Criminal Law Amendment (Patriotic Act) in June 2023, and President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed it into law on July 14, 2023. The law criminalizes meetings with foreign governments or their agents intended to subvert, overthrow or damage Zimbabwe's sovereignty, with penalties as severe as life imprisonment or death for advocating armed intervention, and up to ten years in prison or a fine for advocating sanctions or trade boycotts against the country. The Committee to Protect Journalists' Angela Quintal said journalists must be free to report and meet whomever they choose, including foreign diplomats, without risking imprisonment, and called on Mnangagwa to reject the bill. Information Minister Monica Mutsvangwa said the law did not criminalize journalists' ordinary work but only meetings intended to injure the country's sovereignty. Zimbabwean journalist Dumisani Muleya asked whether an interview eliciting an unfavorable answer could itself be treated as a crime under the law.
stated_justification: Information Minister Monica Mutsvangwa said the bill "did not criminalize journalists' work in Zimbabwe but barred meetings with foreign governments...that have 'the intention to injure the sovereignty.'"
effect_on_reporting: Zimbabwean journalists who interview foreign diplomats or officials, a routine part of covering international affairs, faced the risk that authorities could later characterize such contact as intended to damage the country's sovereignty, carrying penalties as severe as life imprisonment.
status: President Mnangagwa signed the bill into law in July 2023 despite CPJ's call for a veto; a journalists' court challenge did not block it.
outcome_note: President Mnangagwa signed the bill into law despite CPJ's call for a veto; a court challenge by journalists did not block it.

title: Hungary: a ruling-party mayor forcibly removes Telex reporters from a campaign event
summary: A mayor from Hungary's ruling Fidesz party physically removed two Telex journalists from a campaign forum in a community center, covering their camera lens and pushing them out after they declined to leave what he called a closed event.
issue_of_the_day: Telex, an independent Hungarian outlet, was covering a campaign forum ahead of Hungary's April 2026 parliamentary election when the mayor hosting the event moved to stop the reporting.
what_happened: On March 10, 2026, Telex correspondent Judit Presinszky and camera operator Nora Siteri went to a campaign forum for the ruling Fidesz party in a community center in Csakbereny, central Hungary. Mayor Laszlo Vecsei, who was hosting the event, grabbed Siteri's camera to cover the lens and then pushed the journalists, grabbing one of them by the arm, before they were removed from the building. A member of a local civilian patrol group then prevented the pair from re-entering. Vecsei said he acted after the journalists refused to leave what he described as a closed, non-public campaign event, though Telex said it was covering a public function open to constituents. Telex said it had filed a criminal complaint over the removal. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the episode marked a new low for a Hungarian press corps that already faces years of exclusion from government events under Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
stated_justification: Mayor Vecsei said he removed the journalists "after they refused to leave what he described as a closed, non-public campaign event."
effect_on_reporting: Telex's reporters were prevented from covering the campaign forum in person and were physically blocked from returning to the building, and the outlet turned to a criminal complaint rather than continued on-site reporting.
status: Telex has filed a criminal complaint over the removal; no outcome of that complaint has been reported.
what_we_dont_know: It is not established in the sources reviewed whether the criminal complaint led to any charge against Mayor Vecsei.
outcome_note: Telex filed a criminal complaint the same period as the removal; the Committee to Protect Journalists reports no resolution of that complaint.
ladder_note: A government official used physical force to remove and bar named reporters from an event, rather than only denying a credential or building pass.

claims.evidence_quote: Telex's Judit Presinszky and Nora Siteri being forcibly removed while reporting on a public campaign event marks a new low

claims.evidence_quote: grabbed Siteri's camera to cover the lens

title: Russia: entry bans, visa restrictions and bureau closures for foreign correspondents
summary: Over several months in 2022, Russian authorities closed a Canadian broadcaster's Moscow bureau, barred dozens of named British and Australian journalists from entering the country, and suspended simplified visa rules for European journalists.
issue_of_the_day: Russia's actions followed Western governments' sanctions on Russian state broadcasters and officials after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
what_happened: Across the spring of 2022, Russian authorities took a series of steps to keep foreign journalists out of the country. On May 18, Russian authorities moved to close CBC/Radio-Canada's Moscow bureau and cancel the visa and accreditation of its journalists, matching Canada's decision to bar Russian state television. On June 14, Russia barred 49 British citizens, including 29 named journalists, from entering the country. Two days later, it barred 121 Australians, including journalists from ABC News, the Sydney Morning Herald, Nine News and Sky News. Separately, President Vladimir Putin signed a law suspending simplified visa procedures for several categories of visitors, including journalists, coming from most European countries. Russian officials framed each step as a response matching measures taken by the country concerned against Russian state media or officials, rather than as a general press policy.
stated_justification: Russian officials presented the entry bans on British and Australian journalists as a response matching measures the United Kingdom and Australia had taken against Russian journalists and officials; a specific legal justification beyond that framing was not detailed in the source reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: Named journalists from CBC, the BBC, the Sydney Morning Herald and other outlets lost the ability to report from inside Russia in person, and foreign outlets lost simplified visa access for future correspondents.
status: The entry bans and visa restrictions remained in force through 2022 with no indication of reversal in the source reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not give a complete published list of the 29 British or the Australian journalists named, or confirm whether any individual ban was later lifted.
outcome_note: The bans on named British and Australian journalists and the suspension of simplified visas for European journalists remained in effect through 2022 according to the source reviewed.
ladder_note: Dozens of named foreign correspondents were barred from entering the country by law and by sanction, not merely excluded from one building or briefing.

title: China: three Wall Street Journal correspondents expelled over an opinion headline
summary: China's foreign ministry expelled three Wall Street Journal correspondents and revoked their press credentials after an opinion column, unrelated to their own reporting, used a headline the ministry called offensive.
issue_of_the_day: The Wall Street Journal had published an opinion column on February 3, 2020, by an outside scholar, headlined "China Is the Real Sick Man of Asia," about the economic effects of the coronavirus outbreak.
what_happened: On February 19, 2020, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs ordered three Wall Street Journal correspondents in Beijing, deputy bureau chief Josh Chin and reporters Chao Deng and Philip Wen, to leave the country within five days and revoked their press credentials. The order came more than two weeks after the newspaper ran an opinion column by an outside academic, Hudson Institute scholar Walter Russell Mead, under the headline "China Is the Real Sick Man of Asia," discussing the coronavirus outbreak's economic effects. None of the three expelled journalists had written or edited the column. Foreign ministry spokesperson Geng Shuang called the headline "racist" and cited it as the basis for the expulsions. The Wall Street Journal's own reporters had separately criticized the headline as a poor editorial choice, but the paper declined to apologize on the newsroom's behalf for a piece written by an unrelated outside contributor.
stated_justification: Foreign ministry spokesperson Geng Shuang characterized the opinion headline as "racist" and cited it as the basis for revoking the journalists' press credentials.
effect_on_reporting: Three working Wall Street Journal correspondents lost their accreditation and were made to leave China within five days over content that none of them had written, reducing the paper's Beijing reporting capacity during the early coronavirus outbreak.
status: The expulsions were carried out as ordered; the source reviewed does not report any reversal.
what_we_dont_know: It is not stated in the source reviewed whether any of the three journalists were later permitted to return to China on assignment.
outcome_note: The three journalists' press credentials were revoked and the expulsion carried out; no reversal is reported in the source reviewed.
ladder_note: Working correspondents were expelled from the country over content written by someone outside their newsroom, not barred from one building or event.

title: Belarus: accreditation withdrawn from 17 journalists working for foreign outlets
summary: Belarus's government revoked the accreditation of at least 17 journalists working for foreign outlets, including the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press, Radio Liberty, AFP and Deutsche Welle, as they covered protests after a disputed presidential election.
issue_of_the_day: The journalists had been covering protests that followed Belarus's August 9, 2020, presidential election, which the opposition and Western governments said was falsified in favor of Alexander Lukashenko.
what_happened: On August 29, 2020, Belarusian authorities revoked the accreditation of at least 17 journalists who had been covering the post-election protests for foreign media outlets, among them the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Agence France-Presse and Deutsche Welle. Government spokesman Anatoly Glaz said the accreditation withdrawals followed a recommendation from Belarus's counter-terrorism unit. Some of the affected foreign journalists were deported to Russia the same day. The move came three weeks after Belarus's disputed presidential election, which had drawn large street protests and a heavy police response, and left foreign wire services and broadcasters largely unable to report from inside the country on the unrest as it continued into the autumn.
stated_justification: Government spokesman Anatoly Glaz said "the decision to revoke the media accreditations was made after a recommendation by Belarus's counter-terrorism unit."
effect_on_reporting: At least 17 journalists working for major international wire services and broadcasters lost their ability to report from inside Belarus, and some were deported the same day.
status: The accreditation withdrawals took effect immediately and some journalists were deported; the source reviewed does not report a reversal.
what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not name all 17 affected journalists or state whether any of them later regained accreditation.
outcome_note: The accreditation of at least 17 journalists was withdrawn and some were deported the same day, with no reversal reported in the source reviewed.
ladder_note: At least 17 journalists working for named international outlets lost accreditation nationwide and some were deported, not confined to one building or pool.

title: Philippines: a Rappler reporter is barred from the presidential palace
summary: President Rodrigo Duterte ordered Rappler reporter Pia Ranada and the outlet's CEO barred from Malacanang Palace, the seat of the Philippine presidency, after the government revoked Rappler's operating license.
issue_of_the_day: The ban followed the Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission's January 2018 revocation of Rappler's operating license over a foreign-ownership finding, a decision Rappler said was really aimed at its critical coverage of Duterte.
what_happened: On February 21, 2018, Jhopee Avancena, head of Malacanang Palace's internal house affairs office, told Rappler reporter Pia Ranada by text message that she and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa had been banned from the palace grounds on President Duterte's orders. Ranada was initially denied access by guards at the gate but was eventually allowed to join a televised news briefing that day. Presidential spokesperson Harry Roque said the government acted because Duterte had lost trust in Rappler over what he called "fake news" reporting, and said Rappler's reporters would have to cover the president's speeches and activities by television rather than in person from the palace. The ban followed weeks of government pressure on Rappler, including the Securities and Exchange Commission's revocation of its operating license the previous month, a decision widely read as retribution for the outlet's coverage of Duterte's campaign and his anti-drug enforcement policy.
stated_justification: Presidential spokesperson Harry Roque said the government banned Rappler's reporters because President Duterte had "lost trust" in the outlet's "fake news" reporting.
effect_on_reporting: Rappler's palace correspondent could no longer cover the president's activities in person and the outlet was told to rely on television broadcasts instead of first-hand access.
status: The ban remained in force for the remainder of Duterte's term; no reversal is reported in the source reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not state whether the ban was lifted after Duterte left office in mid-2022.
outcome_note: The source reviewed reports only the ban taking effect and does not state whether or when it ended.
ladder_note: The head of government personally ordered a named outlet's reporters excluded from the seat of government after revoking the outlet's corporate license.

title: Turkiye: the presidency's press card system is found restrictive by the country's top administrative court
summary: Turkiye's Council of State suspended 2018 rules under which the presidency's Communications Directorate could deny or cancel the yellow and turquoise press cards that let reporters work and enter official buildings, after finding the grounds for denial too broad.

title: Russia: a Moscow court suspends Novaya Gazeta's print license
summary: A Moscow court suspended the print license of Novaya Gazeta, whose editor Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, after the media regulator Roskomnadzor said the paper had not provided documents about a 2006 change of ownership.
issue_of_the_day: The suspension came about six months into Russia's invasion of Ukraine, during which several independent Russian outlets closed or moved abroad rather than operate under new wartime speech laws.
what_happened: On September 5, 2022, Moscow's Basmanny District Court suspended the print license of Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia's last major independent newspapers, at the request of Roskomnadzor, the state media regulator. Novaya Gazeta's editor, Dmitry Muratov, who had shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize for his work at the paper, called the suspension "a political hit job, without the slightest legal basis." The newspaper itself said on social media that the authorities had effectively ended the publication and taken thirty years of its staff's work. The suspension followed Novaya Gazeta's earlier decision, days after Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, to pause its print and online publishing rather than operate under new laws criminalizing what the government called false information about the military.

summary: Apple Daily, Hong Kong's largest pro-democracy newspaper, printed its final edition after the government froze its parent company's assets and arrested its editors under the national security law imposed on the territory in 2020.

Lai himself had already been detained and was, as of a December 2021 report, serving a separate 20-month prison term related to a conviction for his part in unauthorized demonstrations, while also awaiting trial on national security and fraud charges. On December 28, 2021, Hong Kong's Department of Justice filed further conspiracy charges accusing Lai and six former Apple Daily executives, including former chief executive Cheung Kim Hung and former editor-in-chief Ryan Law Wai-kwong, of printing seditious publications, a charge that could bring up to three years in prison on top of any national security sentence, which could reach life imprisonment.

title: Venezuela: the government declines to renew RCTV's broadcast concession
summary: Venezuela's government let Radio Caracas Television's twenty-year broadcast concession expire rather than renew it, replacing the country's most-watched channel with a new state broadcaster; a regional human rights court later found the decision violated free expression.
issue_of_the_day: President Hugo Chavez's government accused RCTV of supporting the failed April 2002 coup attempt against him, an accusation the government cited alongside the concession's scheduled expiration.
what_happened: Radio Caracas Television's twenty-year broadcast concession was due to expire at midnight on May 27, 2007, and Venezuela's government, led by President Hugo Chavez, chose not to renew it. Government officials accused RCTV's employees of having supported the failed 2002 coup against Chavez, and separately accused the channel of violating Venezuelan law and broadcasting indecent content; the administration described the non-renewal as the natural result of the concession's expiration rather than a deliberate act against the channel. title: Zimbabwe: police close the Daily News under the media registration law
summary: Zimbabwe's Supreme Court ruled the Daily News, the country's largest independent newspaper, was operating unregistered under a 2002 media law, and police shut its offices the next day; the paper stayed closed for nearly seven years.
issue_of_the_day: The closure came amid a wider campaign by President Robert Mugabe's government against independent media following the contested 2002 presidential election.
what_happened: On September 11, 2003, Zimbabwe's Supreme Court declared that the Daily News was violating the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA), a 2002 law requiring every media company to register with the government's Media and Information Commission (MIC). Because the paper's publisher had not registered, the court said it was operating outside the law and would consider constitutional arguments only after registration took place. The next day, police raided the newspaper's offices and ordered all journalists to leave the building, citing the Supreme Court's declaration. Administrative courts twice later ordered the Media and Information Commission to register the Daily News, but police closed the offices again each time journalists tried to resume work. Government officials said they were not interfering in the judicial process, while describing the independent press as serving foreign interests. The paper did not print again until the Media Commission granted it a new license in May 2010, nearly seven years later.

title: Hungary: Klubradio loses its terrestrial broadcast license over its tender application
summary: Hungary's Media Council ended Klubradio's decades-old terrestrial broadcast license, citing errors in its renewal application, after the station had built a following as one of the country's few remaining independent voices.
issue_of_the_day: The decision affected one of the last Hungarian broadcasters to carry news and talk programming independent of the government of Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
what_happened: Hungary's Media Council, the country's broadcast regulator known as the NMHH, denied Klubradio's license renewal in September 2020, and the station's terrestrial broadcasting ceased in February 2021 once its old license expired. The council said Klubradio's tender application contained incorrect, incomplete and contradictory submissions, pointing to specific issues such as an incompletely filled-out form and a program length recorded as 45 minutes rather than 50. The council also questioned the sustainability of a business model relying on listener donations. Klubradio's owner, Andras Arato, acknowledged one of the errors, saying the station had failed to complete a form correctly, but argued the underlying decision was aimed at the station's independent voice. effect_on_reporting: One of Hungary's few remaining independent broadcasters lost its terrestrial frequency, keeping its programming from radio listeners who did not seek it out online.

title: Israel: a court bars any mention of the 'Prisoner X' case
summary: An Israeli judge ordered Israeli media barred from any mention of a prisoner held under a false identity, or of the order itself, applying a system under which security-related stories must be reviewed and cleared by the military before publication.
issue_of_the_day: The order concerned the custody of a man later identified as Ben Zygier, an Australian-Israeli detained on suspicion of harming state security, whose case Israeli outlets could not report on for years under the order.
what_happened: In June 2010, Israeli district court judge Hila Gerstl issued a court order banning any mention of a prisoner who came to be known publicly only as "Prisoner X," or of the circumstances of his custody, and separately prohibited any mention that the order itself existed. The order operated alongside Israel's long-standing military review system, under which all news publications dealing with security issues must be approved in advance by a military reviewing authority before publication, a standard Israel's High Court has said requires proof that publication would cause imminent, certain and actual harm to state security. summary: Turkiye's broadcast regulator, RTUK, fined three television channels and suspended the next five episodes of two of their programs after they aired criticism of the government's response to the February 2023 earthquakes.
issue_of_the_day: Earthquakes in southern Turkiye in early February 2023 killed more than 50,000 people and drew widespread criticism of the government's building codes and disaster response.
