title: Egypt: a license requirement leaves an independent news site unable to operate legally for years
summary: Egypt's Supreme Council for Media Regulation required news websites to obtain a government license to operate, and independent outlet Al-Manassa's application, filed in 2018, went unanswered for more than two years.
issue_of_the_day: The licensing requirement operated alongside a 2018 cybercrime law that made it a crime to use certain software tools without the council's permission, according to Al-Manassa's editor.
what_happened: Egypt's Supreme Council for Media Regulation (SCMR), founded in 2018 to oversee print, broadcast and online media, required news websites operating in the country to obtain a license from it before they could publish legally. Younis also said Egypt's cybercrime law separately made it a criminal offense to use certain open-source software tools without the council's permission if doing so could be characterized as committing a crime, a provision she said gave authorities broad discretion over online publishers' technical operations as well as their editorial content.

effect_on_reporting: An independent news site operated for more than two years without a resolved license, unable to obtain the legal certainty the licensing system was meant to provide, under a regulator that could also treat unlicensed software use as a crime.

title: Russia: journalist Ivan Safronov is sentenced to 22 years for treason

title: Turkiye: journalist Sedef Kabas is arrested for a proverb about President Erdogan
summary: Turkish journalist Sedef Kabas was arrested and later convicted under Article 299 of the penal code, which criminalizes insulting the president, after quoting a proverb about a palace becoming a stable during a televised discussion of Erdogan.
issue_of_the_day: Kabas made the comment during a political talk show discussion of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, after also questioning his university diploma and alleging corruption in earlier social media posts.
what_happened: On January 22, 2022, Turkish police arrested journalist Sedef Kabas from her home after midnight, following comments she made during a televised political talk show in which she said, discussing President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, "When cattle enters a palace, it does not become king but the palace becomes a stable." Kabas was prosecuted under Article 299 of Turkiye's penal code, which criminalizes insulting the president and carries a sentence of up to four years in prison, with enhanced penalties where the insult is made publicly. She was found guilty and sentenced to two years and four months in prison, and was released pending appeal on March 11, 2022, after 49 days in detention. In June 2023, she faced a further trial on the same Article 299 charge over the same set of remarks, which had also included social media posts questioning Erdogan's university diploma and alleging corruption.

title: Thailand: magazine editor Somyot Prueksakasemsuk is sentenced to 11 years under the lese-majeste law
summary: A Thai court sentenced magazine editor Somyot Prueksakasemsuk to 11 years in prison under Article 112 of the penal code, the country's lese-majeste law barring insults to the royal family, over two articles he published under a pen name.
issue_of_the_day: The two articles that led to the charge, published in Voice of Taksin magazine in February and March 2010, were written under a pseudonym by a former government spokesman living in exile, whom Somyot identified only after his own prosecution began.
what_happened: On January 24, 2013, a Thai court sentenced magazine editor Somyot Prueksakasemsuk to 11 years in prison under Article 112 of Thailand's penal code, the country's lese-majeste law, which bars insults to the royal family and under which any Thai person may file a complaint even though royal family members themselves have never personally done so. The charge concerned two articles published in February and March 2010 in Voice of Taksin magazine under the pen name "Jit Polachan." Somyot later identified the true author as Jakrapob Penkair, a former government spokesman then living in exile in Cambodia. During his trial testimony, Somyot argued the articles referred to a broad aristocratic elite rather than the king specifically. CPJ's Asia program coordinator at the time, Bob Dietz, called the sentence the latest abuse of the lese-majeste law to suppress free expression in Thailand. Somyot completed his sentence in full and was released on April 30, 2018, telling reporters the country's military government had led Thailand backward and that he was disappointed democracy had not been restored.

title: Belarus: journalist Andrzej Poczobut is sentenced to eight years for inciting hatred

status: The Pegasus Project's findings on Panyi's phone were published in July 2021; the source reviewed does not report any Hungarian government accountability measure.
what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not state which specific stories Panyi was working on when the spyware was placed on his phone.
outcome_note: The finding prompted European Union scrutiny of Pegasus use against journalists, but the source reviewed does not report any Hungarian accountability measure.

title: Morocco: investigative journalist Omar Radi's phone is infected with Pegasus spyware and he is later detained
summary: Amnesty International confirmed Moroccan investigative journalist Omar Radi's phone had been infected with Pegasus spyware, and Moroccan police separately detained him overnight days later after private material from his devices circulated in pro-government media.
issue_of_the_day: Radi worked as an investigative journalist for the Moroccan outlet Le Desk and had faced a prior court conviction and government-aligned media allegations before the spyware finding.
what_happened: Amnesty International confirmed in 2020 that Pegasus spyware, made by Israel's NSO Group, had been used against Omar Radi, an investigative journalist for the Moroccan outlet Le Desk, one of at least two Moroccan journalists whose phones were identified as having been infected; the later Pegasus Project named Radi among seven Moroccan journalists identified as potential or confirmed recipients of the spyware. On July 5, 2020, Moroccan police detained Radi and fellow journalist Imad Stitou overnight following a dispute with a camera operator who had been following Radi since late June, and the pair were later summoned for investigation on additional allegations. Private communications belonging to Radi, including photographs, videos, texts and phone calls that a person close to him said had been obtained despite his taking every technical precaution against hacking, were later published in pro-government media outlets and used as evidence against him in separate court proceedings. Moroccan authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the spyware findings.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed; Moroccan authorities, including the National Brigade of Judicial Police and the Ministry of Justice, did not respond to requests for comment on the spyware findings or the detention.
effect_on_reporting: An investigative journalist's private communications, obtained despite his taking precautions against hacking, were later published by pro-government media and used against him in court, alongside a separate overnight detention.
status: Radi's phone was confirmed compromised in 2020, and he was separately convicted the following year on charges unrelated to the spyware finding itself.
what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed does not establish who placed the spyware on Radi's phone or link it directly to the later criminal charges against him.
outcome_note: Radi was released in July 2024 as part of a mass royal pardon, though he said his legal status left him unable to work as an accredited journalist afterward.
ladder_note: A journalist's private communications were covertly extracted despite his taking precautions against hacking, then published by pro-government media and used against him in court.

title: Saudi Arabia: spyware on an associate's phone precedes Jamal Khashoggi's killing by one day
summary: Citizen Lab found Pegasus spyware on the phone of Saudi dissident Omar Abdulaziz, a close associate and collaborator of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, one day before Saudi operatives killed Khashoggi inside the country's Istanbul consulate.
issue_of_the_day: Abdulaziz and Khashoggi had been collaborating on plans for a news and human rights website, and Khashoggi was, according to Abdulaziz, sharply critical of the Saudi crown prince in their private conversations.
what_happened: On October 1, 2018, the Canadian digital rights research group Citizen Lab published forensic analysis finding, with a high degree of confidence, that Saudi dissident Omar Abdulaziz's phone had been successfully infected with Pegasus spyware made by Israel's NSO Group, in an operation linked to Saudi government operators. Abdulaziz was a close associate of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and the two had been collaborating on plans for a news and human rights website; Abdulaziz said Khashoggi had been sharply critical of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in their private conversations, including through encrypted messages that the spyware would have exposed. The day after Citizen Lab published its findings, on October 2, 2018, Saudi operatives killed Khashoggi inside the country's consulate in Istanbul. Abdulaziz has said he cannot definitively link the spyware operation against his own phone to Khashoggi's killing, but the timing raised serious questions about how Saudi authorities may have learned of Khashoggi's private communications and views before his death.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed; no Saudi government justification for the spyware operation against Abdulaziz's phone is quoted in the source.
effect_on_reporting: Surveillance of a journalist's close collaborator exposed private communications and views the journalist believed were confidential, one day before he was killed inside his own country's consulate.
status: No public accountability measure for the spyware operation against Abdulaziz's phone is reported in the source reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The source reviewed states Abdulaziz cannot definitively link the spyware operation to Khashoggi's killing, and does not establish that link independently.
outcome_note: Citizen Lab's finding on the spyware operation itself was not followed, in the source reviewed, by any reported Saudi accountability measure.
ladder_note: A journalist's close collaborator was covertly surveilled one day before the journalist himself was killed inside his own country's consulate.

title: Mexico: journalist Carmen Aristegui receives Pegasus spyware through phishing texts
summary: Citizen Lab, R3D and Article 19 documented Pegasus spyware sent to Mexican investigative journalists Carmen Aristegui and Carlos Loret de Mola through phishing text messages, which the Mexican government denied having sent.
issue_of_the_day: Aristegui and Loret de Mola were among several Mexican investigative journalists, human rights defenders and anti-corruption figures sent the same spyware technique around the same period.
what_happened: On June 19 and 20, 2017, researchers at Citizen Lab, a University of Toronto research group, working with the Mexican digital rights organization R3D and the press freedom group Article 19, documented that investigative journalists Carmen Aristegui and Carlos Loret de Mola, along with several human rights defenders and anti-corruption figures, had received phishing text messages containing fabricated warnings about family members. Clicking the links in the messages installed Pegasus spyware, made by the Israeli firm NSO Group, on the recipients' phones. NSO Group has said it sells Pegasus exclusively to governments. President Enrique Pena Nieto's administration categorically denied that any of its members engaged in surveillance or communications operations against human rights defenders, journalists or anti-corruption activists without prior judicial authorization. Citizen Lab's report said the spyware itself could not be traced back to whoever had sent it, and that there was no conclusive evidence establishing who was responsible.
stated_justification: President Enrique Pena Nieto's administration "categorically denie[d] that any of its members engages in surveillance or communications operations against defenders of human rights, journalists, anti-corruption activists or any other person without prior judicial authorization."
effect_on_reporting: Prominent investigative journalists covering corruption and human rights in Mexico received spyware capable of reading their phones' communications, while the technical evidence could not conclusively identify who was responsible.
status: No individual or agency was conclusively identified as responsible in the source reviewed, and the government denied involvement.
what_we_dont_know: Citizen Lab's report states there was no conclusive evidence establishing who was responsible, and the source reviewed does not report that this was later resolved.
outcome_note: The government denied responsibility and Citizen Lab's report found no conclusive evidence establishing who sent the spyware, according to the source reviewed.
ladder_note: Investigative journalists' phones were secretly infected with spyware through fabricated personal warnings, with government responsibility denied and never conclusively established.

title: Hungary: formation of the KESMA pro-government media foundation
summary: Owners aligned with Hungary's governing party donated 476 outlets into one non-profit foundation, KESMA. The government exempted the merger from the antitrust review that would normally apply to a combination of that size.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On November 29, 2018, the owners of 476 Hungarian outlets, including television channels, radio stations, news portals, newspapers and magazines, transferred them for no payment into a single non-profit body, the Central European Press and Media Foundation, known as KESMA. Most of these outlets had already been supportive of Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government; several had themselves been bought in earlier years by businesspeople close to the governing Fidesz party. Ordinarily a media combination of this scale would trigger a review by Hungary's competition authority to check its effect on media pluralism. The government instead declared the merger a matter of national interest and exempted it from that review by decree. KESMA's outlets now make up a large share of Hungary's total media market, alongside the country's state broadcaster.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: Hungary's press freedom organization Reporters Without Borders later said the government-aligned foundation and state broadcasting together dominate about eighty percent of the national media market, crowding out independent competitors for advertising and audience.
status: Sustained; KESMA continued to operate as of the sources reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the government's stated reason for exempting the merger from competition review.
outcome_note: The merger was completed and the exemption was not reported as reversed in the sources reviewed.

title: Hungary: editor fired and staff resign at Index.hu
summary: Index.hu, Hungary's most-read independent news site, fired editor-in-chief Szabolcs Dull weeks after he warned that a change in ownership threatened its independence. Most of the newsroom resigned within days.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: In March 2020, businessman Miklos Vaszily, who had previously run outlets aligned with Prime Minister Viktor Orban's government, gained an indirect stake in the company that sells advertising for Index.hu, Hungary's largest independent news site. On June 22, 2020, editor-in-chief Szabolcs Dull published a public letter, co-signed by most of the newsroom, saying the site's independence was in danger. Index.hu added a public indicator it called a barometer to track the threat. On July 22, 2020, company leadership fired Dull. Two days later, more than seventy of the outlet's roughly ninety journalists resigned, saying they could no longer guarantee independent coverage. Many of the departing staff went on to found a new outlet, Telex.hu, later that year. Index.hu continued operating under new ownership and editorial leadership.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: The mass resignation removed most of the reporting staff Index.hu had built over two decades and shifted its ownership toward people described in the sources reviewed as close to the government.
status: Sustained; Dull's dismissal was not reversed and Index.hu continued under its new ownership.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the company's stated reason for dismissing Dull.
outcome_note: Dull's dismissal stood and the outlet continued under its changed ownership; the sources reviewed do not report a reversal.

title: Poland: state oil company Orlen buys the Polska Press newspaper group
summary: Poland's state-controlled oil company PKN Orlen completed the purchase of Polska Press, a group of 20 regional newspapers reaching millions of readers, from its German owner, over objections from Poland's human rights commissioner.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: PKN Orlen, an oil and gas company majority owned by the Polish state, announced on December 7, 2020, that it would buy Polska Press, a group of 20 regional daily newspapers and about 120 local weeklies and websites reaching an estimated 17.4 million readers, from Germany's Verlagsgruppe Passau. Poland's national human rights commissioner, Adam Bodnar, warned in March 2021 that state control over the group could let officials influence editorial boards. Orlen completed the acquisition in April 2021 and installed a new management team. Some journalists at member papers, including Polska Times, said their day-to-day assignments had not changed immediately but that they feared future interference. On February 10, 2021, dozens of independent Polish outlets, including national broadcasters, staged a one-day protest against a separate proposed advertising tax, running the message "Media without choice" instead of normal programming, a protest that took place against the backdrop of the Orlen deal.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.

status: Sustained as of the sources reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report whether Orlen changed the editorial line of specific Polska Press titles after the sale closed.

title: Turkiye: court installs trustees at Zaman newspaper
summary: An Istanbul court put Turkiye's best-selling newspaper, Zaman, and its parent company under trustees after ruling it supported a group the government called a terrorist organization. Police used tear gas on a crowd that gathered in support.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On March 4, 2016, an Istanbul court ruled that Feza Media Group, publisher of the newspapers Zaman and Today's Zaman and the Cihan news agency, supported a movement led by the exiled cleric Fethullah Gulen that Turkiye's government had labeled a terrorist organization. The court ordered the company placed under court-appointed trustees, who took control of its board, servers and archives and blocked existing journalists' access to their own systems. Police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse a crowd that had gathered outside Zaman's Istanbul office in support of the paper. Within days, the new management removed critical stories from the paper's history and installed an editorial line supportive of the government; the paper's foreign editor and other senior staff were dismissed. Today's Zaman continued for several more months before all Feza-linked outlets were permanently closed by a state-of-emergency decree following the failed coup attempt of July 2016.
stated_justification: "the new administration does not want any stories that were 'critical of Turkey'"
effect_on_reporting: Journalists said the paper reversed its editorial line within days and that the takeover was part of a broader effort described by one ousted editor as aimed at every independent voice, not only Zaman.
status: Sustained until the outlets were later closed entirely by decree in July 2016.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not include the trustees' own account of why specific staff were dismissed.
outcome_note: Editorial control was not restored to the original owners; the outlets were later shut down entirely under a separate July 2016 decree.

title: Turkiye: Dogan Holding sells its media outlets to Demiroren
summary: Turkiye's largest independent media group, including the newspaper Hurriyet and the broadcaster CNN Turk, was sold to the Demiroren conglomerate, a buyer with ties to the governing party, for a reported 1.1 billion dollars.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: Dogan Holding, one of Turkiye's largest conglomerates, announced on March 21, 2018, that it would sell its media assets, including the newspapers Hurriyet and Posta and the television channels Kanal D and CNN Turk, to Demiroren Holding for a reported 1.1 billion dollars. Dogan's outlets had been among the few remaining large media companies not aligned with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government, though the group had already softened its coverage under years of tax disputes and legal pressure. Demiroren had a record of changing coverage after previous purchases: when it bought the newspapers Milliyet and Vatan from Dogan in 2011, both switched to a government-supportive editorial line. Journalists said the sale would place Turkiye's mass media even more directly under pro-government ownership, since Demiroren's chairman had personal and business ties to Erdogan.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: Journalists covering the sale said it would extend pro-government ownership over the last major independent broadcaster and newspaper group, following the same pattern seen at Demiroren's earlier acquisitions.
status: Sustained; the sale closed as announced.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the sale's final confirmed price beyond the reported figure.

title: Russia: CBC/Radio-Canada bureau closed and journalists' visas cancelled
summary: Russian authorities ordered the Canadian broadcaster CBC/Radio-Canada's Moscow bureau closed and cancelled its journalists' visas and accreditation, part of a wave of expulsions and non-renewals of foreign correspondents after the invasion of Ukraine.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On May 18, 2022, Russian authorities moved to close the Moscow bureau of CBC/Radio-Canada, Canada's public broadcaster, and cancelled the visas and accreditation of its correspondents there, ending the outlet's ability to report from inside the country. The action came three months into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, during a period in which Russia also blocked the websites of the BBC's Russian service, Germany's Deutsche Welle and other outlets, and later denied visa renewals to correspondents from the Netherlands and Finland and expelled two German journalists. Canada had imposed sanctions on Russian officials and state media figures over the invasion, and Russian officials described several of these press-related measures as reciprocal steps against countries that had sanctioned Russia or its state broadcasters.

title: Ethiopia: Economist correspondent Tom Gardner expelled

title: Nicaragua: freelance correspondent detained and deported after online campaign
summary: A coordinated online campaign accused freelance correspondent Carl David Goette-Luciak of being a foreign agent and circulated his home address, after which he was detained and deported from Nicaragua in September 2018.

The posts accused him of working for the Central Intelligence Agency and of trying to destabilize the country, and some included his home address; other users called for him to be captured and handed to police, or expelled. Some of the accounts sharing the material were linked to government-affiliated organizations. Goette-Luciak was later detained and deported from Nicaragua that September.

title: Turkiye: Dutch freelance journalist Ans Boersma deported
summary: Turkish authorities detained Dutch freelance journalist Ans Boersma while she tried to renew her residence permit in Istanbul and deported her the next day, citing an alleged link to a Syrian armed group that the Netherlands said it had never been asked about.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On January 16, 2019, Turkish authorities took Ans Boersma, a Dutch freelance journalist based in Istanbul, into custody while she attempted to renew her residence permit at the city's Foreigners' Office. She was held overnight at a police station and deported the next day, January 17, without being allowed to return to her home to collect belongings. Turkish officials linked the deportation to an allegation that Boersma had ties to Jabhat al-Nusra, a Syrian armed group. The Dutch government said Turkey had made no request for her detention, expulsion or extradition and that it had not been consulted about the allegation before she was removed. Boersma had reported on Turkiye and Syria for several years before the deportation.
stated_justification: "The Netherlands told Turkey that the reporter, who was deported today, had links to Jabhat al-Nusra."

title: India: journalist Aatish Taseer's overseas citizenship revoked
summary: India's government cancelled writer and journalist Aatish Taseer's Overseas Citizen of India status months after he wrote a Time magazine cover story critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, citing his father's Pakistani nationality.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: In May 2019, Time magazine published a cover story by writer and journalist Aatish Taseer that was critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi ahead of that year's general election. On August 13, 2019, India's Home Ministry sent Taseer a notice threatening to revoke his Overseas Citizen of India status, a form of long-term immigration status that lets people of Indian origin live and work in the country without a visa. The ministry said Taseer was ineligible for the status because his father, the Pakistani politician Salmaan Taseer, was a Pakistani national, and Pakistani nationals cannot hold it. On November 7, 2019, the government made the cancellation official. Taseer disputed the notice, said he did not hold Pakistani citizenship, and said he believed the action was linked to his criticism of the Modi government.

title: Myanmar: military cuts mobile internet after seizing power
summary: After seizing power on February 1, 2021, Myanmar's military cut mobile data service nationwide, leaving reporters in rural townships and Rakhine State unable to send news and blocking large areas from outside communication for months.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On February 1, 2021, Myanmar's military, led by Commander-in-Chief Min Aung Hlaing, seized power from the elected government and detained its leaders. In the weeks that followed, the military ordered mobile internet providers to cut data service, first intermittently and then for extended stretches, across large parts of the country. Reporters for local outlets said the blackout made it difficult or impossible to send news out of affected areas; one editor said reporters in different townships found it very hard to file their stories once mobile data was blocked. In Rakhine State, in the country's west, journalists described a total blockage of mobile data across northern cities and rural areas for months. The shutdown compounded restrictions the military had already placed on domestic media licenses and on journalists' movement.

title: Ethiopia: internet and phone service cut across Tigray

title: Russia: regulator blocks BBC Russian, Deutsche Welle and other outlets
summary: Russia's media regulator Roskomnadzor blocked access nationwide to the websites of BBC Russian, Deutsche Welle, Meduza, Voice of America's Russian service and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty within days of invading Ukraine, alongside new prison terms for reporting the regulator called false.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On March 4, 2022, Russia's state media regulator, Roskomnadzor, blocked access within Russia to the websites of the BBC's Russian-language service, Germany's public broadcaster Deutsche Welle, the independent news site Meduza, the Russian-language service of the United States Congress-funded broadcaster Voice of America, and several services of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, another United States Congress-funded broadcaster. Roskomnadzor separately confirmed that Facebook and Twitter were blocked in the country. The same day, Russia's legislature adopted amendments to the criminal code creating prison terms of up to fifteen years for people convicted of spreading what the amendments called "fakes" about the military, a category that came to include most independent reporting on the invasion, which Russian law required media to call a "special military operation."

title: Iran: near-total internet shutdown during fuel-price protests

Human rights monitors said the blackout appeared aimed at stopping the flow of news about the protests and about the security forces' violent response to them. During the shutdown and the days that followed, at least eleven journalists, including photographers and camera operators, were arrested in connection with the protests. One journalist, Mohammad Mosaed, was arrested specifically for posting on social media about the internet shutdown itself and was released on bail the following month.

title: India: Gaon Savera's Facebook and X accounts blocked

title: China: citizen journalist Zhang Zhan imprisoned for Wuhan reporting
summary: China detained citizen journalist Zhang Zhan for posting independent video reports from Wuhan during the early COVID-19 outbreak, later convicting her of "picking quarrels and provoking trouble" and, after her release, detaining her again years later.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: Zhang Zhan, a former lawyer, traveled to Wuhan in February 2020 and began posting independent video reports on Twitter and YouTube about the early coronavirus outbreak there, including interviews with affected residents and business owners. She went missing on May 14, 2020, and was confirmed arrested and detained the next day. Chinese authorities held her on the charge of "picking quarrels and provoking trouble," a broadly worded offense that press freedom groups say Chinese courts use against government critics generally. A court sentenced her to four years in prison in December 2020. Zhang staged repeated hunger strikes in detention and was released in May 2024 after completing her sentence, only for CPJ to report that Chinese authorities brought a second case against her the following year, keeping her under continued restriction.
stated_justification: "picking quarrels and provoking trouble"
effect_on_reporting: Zhang's imprisonment and later re-detention removed one of the few independent voices who had reported directly from Wuhan during the outbreak's earliest weeks, before China's official narrative was established.
status: Ongoing; CPJ reported a second case against her in 2025 after her initial release.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the specific evidence used to support the 'picking quarrels' charge.

title: Belarus: journalist Andrzej Poczobut sentenced to eight years
summary: Belarus sentenced Polish-Belarusian correspondent Andrzej Poczobut to eight years in prison on charges of inciting hatred and calling for sanctions, after holding him since March 2021. He was freed five years later in a multi-country prisoner exchange.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: Andrzej Poczobut, a correspondent for Poland's Gazeta Wyborcza and a political commentator based in the Hrodna region of Belarus, had already faced repeated prosecution for his reporting on the country's Polish minority, including a suspended sentence for defamation and insulting the president in 2011. Belarusian security forces detained him again in March 2021. On February 8, 2023, a Belarusian court convicted him of inciting hatred and calling for sanctions against Belarus and sentenced him to eight years in prison. The same court proceedings led to the detention of another journalist, Anastasia Sharkevich, who appeared in a video circulated by a pro-government Telegram channel saying she had been arrested by security forces. Poczobut remained imprisoned for a total of 1,860 days before being freed on April 28, 2026, as part of a prisoner exchange involving Belarus, Poland and several other countries.

title: Russia: Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich sentenced to 16 years
summary: Russia arrested Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in March 2023 on an espionage charge his employer called fabricated, held him for about 15 months before a closed trial, and sentenced him to 16 years before releasing him in a prisoner exchange.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: Russian security services arrested Evan Gershkovich, a correspondent for The Wall Street Journal, in Yekaterinburg on March 29, 2023, accusing him of collecting secret information for the United States Central Intelligence Agency about a Russian tank factory. He was held for nearly 15 months before a closed-door trial opened on June 26, 2024. On July 19, 2024, a Russian judge sentenced him to 16 years in a penal colony. The Wall Street Journal's leadership called the conviction a sham and said Russian authorities had failed to present evidence of a crime. The United States Embassy in Russia said he had done nothing wrong. On August 1, 2024, Gershkovich was released along with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty editor Alsu Kurmasheva and other prisoners in a multi-country exchange.

title: Azerbaijan: investigative journalist Khadija Ismayilova sentenced to 7.5 years

title: Philippines: Rappler's Maria Ressa arrested over cyber libel case

title: Eritrea: independent press closed and journalists jailed without trial
summary: Eritrea's government closed every private newspaper and jailed at least nineteen journalists, including Dawit Isaac of the paper Setit, without charge or trial in September 2001, after suspending the constitution. Several have never been publicly accounted for since.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On September 18, 2001, as international attention was focused on the aftermath of the September 11, 2001 hijackings in the United States, Eritrea's government under President Isaias Afwerki closed the country's private newspapers and arrested their editors and reporters, including Dawit Isaac, a Swedish-Eritrean journalist and co-owner of the newspaper Setit. At least nineteen journalists were detained in the restrictions that followed, along with a group of senior political dissidents. None of them has ever been publicly charged with a crime or given a trial. Authorities have refused to disclose the detainees' locations or confirm whether they remain alive, a practice that international law treats as enforced disappearance. Isaac was reported to have been held for 3,127 days as of a 2010 accounting, with no public update on his status since.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: The closures ended Eritrea's independent press entirely, and the indefinite, uncharged detention of its journalists has kept the country at the bottom of international press freedom rankings for more than two decades.
status: Unresolved; the detainees' fates remain unconfirmed as of the source reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not confirm whether Dawit Isaac or the other detained journalists are alive.
outcome_note: As of the 2010 source reviewed, none of the journalists detained in 2001 had been charged, tried or publicly accounted for.

title: Philippines: Maria Ressa convicted of cyber libel
summary: A Manila court convicted Rappler's Maria Ressa and researcher Reynaldo Santos Jr. of criminal cyber libel and sentenced them to up to six years in prison, over a 2012 story republished after the cybercrime law used to charge them took effect.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: A Manila trial court issued its verdict on June 15, 2020, convicting Rappler executive editor Maria Ressa and former researcher Reynaldo Santos Jr. of cyber libel over a 2012 article that linked a businessman to a Philippine chief justice. The government's case relied on Rappler's 2014 correction of a single word in the story, arguing that the correction restarted the clock for a libel charge under the Cybercrime Prevention Act, a law that took effect only after the article was first published. The court sentenced both to a prison term of up to six years, though they remained free pending appeal. CPJ said the conviction and sentencing amounted to, in its words, "an outrageous crime against press freedom," and urged Philippine authorities not to pursue the case further. The case became one of several legal proceedings Rappler faced during President Rodrigo Duterte's administration.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: A criminal conviction carrying a possible prison term became a central legal threat hanging over Rappler's leadership for years afterward, even as the outlet continued publishing.
status: Ongoing on appeal as of the source reviewed.

outcome_note: Ressa and Santos were convicted and sentenced but remained free pending appeal, according to the source reviewed.

title: Turkiye: journalist Sedef Kabas tried for insulting the president
summary: Turkish authorities tried journalist Sedef Kabas repeatedly for insulting President Erdogan over her on-air comments and tweets questioning his college diploma and alleging corruption, an offense carrying up to four years in prison.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: Turkish journalist Sedef Kabas was arrested on January 14, 2022, over on-air comments prosecutors said insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdogan under Article 299 of Turkiye's penal code, an offense that can carry up to four years in prison, with an added penalty if the insult was made publicly. She was convicted and sentenced to two years and four months in prison but was released pending appeal on March 11, 2022. Turkish prosecutors then pursued a separate case over a series of her tweets, in which she questioned the validity of Erdogan's college diploma, made allegations of corruption, and criticized several of his policies and statements. On June 22, 2023, an Istanbul court denied a motion to dismiss that second insult charge, keeping Kabas on trial for statements made from outside any official capacity, as an independent journalist and commentator.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.

title: Russia: outlet fined $338,000 under the foreign agents law
summary: A Moscow court fined the magazine The New Times 22.3 million rubles, about $338,000, for a paperwork lapse under Russia's foreign agents law, a sum its editor said was designed to force the outlet to close.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On October 26, 2018, a Moscow court ordered the magazine The New Times to pay 22.3 million rubles, about $338,000, for failing to provide financial information required under Russia's foreign agents law, which requires organizations that receive funding from abroad to register and report on their finances or face penalties. The New Times had already been financially strained, having stopped producing a print edition in June 2017 for lack of money. Its editor said she had in fact reported the required information correctly to the proper authorities and said she would appeal the fine. CPJ said the fine was clearly intended to cripple the outlet and amounted to a serious threat to what remained of press freedom in Russia, since a sum of that size threatened the magazine's ability to keep operating at all.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: A fine of that size, imposed on an outlet already unable to afford printing, threatened to end The New Times' operations entirely rather than simply penalize a specific story.

title: Malta: minister orders reporter's bank account frozen
summary: A month after journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia published reporting on members of Malta's government, the economy minister had her bank account frozen, one of dozens of legal actions she faced before she was killed in a car bombing in October 2017.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta's best-known investigative journalist, published reporting in January 2017 that included compromising information about members of Prime Minister Joseph Muscat's government. The following month, February 2017, Malta's economy minister had her bank account frozen, an administrative order that cut off her access to her own funds while she continued reporting. The freeze came during a period in which Caruana Galizia faced dozens of civil defamation suits from government officials and businesspeople she had reported on, filed in Malta and abroad, which press freedom groups later described as an attempt to exhaust her financially and legally rather than to win any single case. Caruana Galizia was killed in a car bombing outside her home on October 16, 2017, while several of the suits against her remained pending.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: The frozen account was one of many financial and legal pressures Caruana Galizia faced in the months before her killing, alongside dozens of separate lawsuits from officials and businesspeople named in her reporting.
status: Unresolved as of her killing in October 2017; legal actions against her family continued afterward.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not state when or whether the freeze on her account was lifted before her death.
outcome_note: The source reviewed does not report the freeze being lifted before her 2017 killing; five people were later sentenced over the killing itself between 2022 and 2026, while defamation suits continued against her family.

title: Kazakhstan: fabricated copyright complaints used against journalists
summary: An investigation found paid services in Kazakhstan filing fabricated copyright complaints, impersonating global brands, to get social media platforms to remove journalists' accounts and posts, alongside criminal prosecutions of the press.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: CPJ reported on August 20, 2026, that journalists in Kazakhstan faced a pattern of legal and platform-based pressure that included prosecutions, professional bans and what it called spurious copyright claims. One case involved journalist Azamat Omarov, whose YouTube and Instagram accounts were repeatedly removed or blocked based on copyright complaints CPJ said appeared fabricated. An investigation by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, cited in the CPJ report, found an underground market of agencies charging up to $5,000 to file false copyright complaints against journalists, sometimes using email addresses that impersonated global brands including L'Oreal and Giorgio Armani. Diana Okremova of the Legal Media Center said platforms needed to account for Kazakhstan's political context before acting on a single complaint against a journalist or public figure.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.

title: Russia: new laws penalize online "fake news" and "disrespecting authorities"
summary: Russia's parliament passed laws letting courts jail and fine people, including journalists, for posting information the government alone judges to be false, or for statements found to disrespect officials or state symbols online.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On March 7, 2019, Russia's State Duma passed legislation permitting courts to jail and fine people who use the internet to spread what the law calls "fake news" or to disrespect government officials and state symbols, including President Vladimir Putin. Under the fake-news provisions, individuals, including journalists, could be fined up to 100,000 rubles, and companies up to 500,000 rubles, for posting unverified information that authorities determine threatens someone's life, health or property, or threatens mass public disorder. Separately, people found guilty of posting what courts call indecent statements about the government could face up to 15 days in administrative detention, with fines rising to 200,000 rubles and repeat violations carrying additional jail time. CPJ said the legislation was clearly aimed at tightening state control over independent media and pressuring journalists into restraining their own reporting.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: The law gave authorities a standing legal tool to fine or briefly jail journalists and ordinary internet users over reporting or commentary the government alone determined to be false or disrespectful, without a specific factual dispute needing to be argued in court beforehand.
status: Sustained; the laws remained in force and were later expanded during the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report how many people were fined or jailed under the law in its first year.
outcome_note: The laws were enacted and were later expanded in March 2022 to include prison terms of up to 15 years for wartime 'fakes.'

title: Russia: independent outlet Meduza designated a 'foreign agent'
summary: Russia's Justice Ministry labeled the independent news site Meduza and outlet PASMI "foreign agents," a status requiring constant public disclosure, quarterly reports and audits, and carrying up to two years in prison for noncompliance, which Meduza said would destroy its advertising business.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On April 23, 2021, Russia's Justice Ministry added the independent news site Meduza, which is based in Latvia and widely read inside Russia, and the outlet PASMI to its register of "foreign agents." The designation, created under a law expanded over several years to cover media organizations and individuals, requires labeled outlets to mark every piece of content with a foreign agent notice, provide a legal representative inside Russia, file quarterly financial reports and semi-annual activity reports, and undergo annual audits. People working for a foreign agent outlet who fail to comply can face up to two years in prison. Meduza's editor said the label would deprive the outlet of the ability to fully practice journalism inside Russia and would destroy its business, since advertisers would avoid being associated with a designated outlet. CPJ called on Russia to stop labeling independent outlets as foreign agents.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: Meduza's editor said the label would cut off the outlet's advertising revenue and constrain its ability to operate as a normal news organization inside Russia, years before Russia banned it outright in 2023.
status: Sustained; the designation remained in place and Russia later outlawed Meduza entirely.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not give the Justice Ministry's specific stated reason for designating Meduza on that date.
outcome_note: The designation was not reversed; Russia later declared Meduza an 'undesirable organization' and outlawed it entirely.

title: Egypt: media law used to fine and block news site al-Mashhad

what_happened: Egypt's Law No. 180 of 2018 applies to every online and offline media outlet and, separately, to any social media account with more than 5,000 followers, treating such accounts as media outlets subject to regulation by the state's Supreme Council for Media Regulation. The law bans content the council judges to be false news, defamatory, obscene, or a threat to national security, with violators facing fines of up to 250,000 Egyptian pounds and having their websites blocked. On March 22, 2019, the council fined the news site al-Mashhad 50,000 Egyptian pounds and ordered Egyptian internet providers to block the site for six months. Al-Mashhad appealed, and on April 7 the council reduced the block to one month starting from the appeal date, but the site remained inaccessible inside Egypt as of May 7, 2019, according to the source reviewed.

title: Vietnam: Decree 72 restricts blogs to personal information
summary: Vietnam's Decree 72 took effect in September 2013, barring bloggers and social media users from linking to or reposting news from press organizations or foreign government websites, restricting them to sharing personal information only.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: Vietnam's government issued Decree 72 in 2013, and it took effect on September 1, 2013, broadly prohibiting Vietnamese bloggers and internet users from linking to or reposting news from press organizations or information from foreign government websites, restricting personal blogs and social media accounts to sharing personal information only. The decree did not specify how global internet companies would be penalized if they refused to cooperate with government orders to identify bloggers who violated it or restrict their posts. A coalition of internet companies, the Asia Internet Coalition, said the decree would negatively affect Vietnam's internet economy and discourage businesses from operating in the country. A Vietnamese Ministry of Information official denied the decree amounted to a ban, saying the government had never stopped people from sharing information or linking to news from other websites.
stated_justification: "We never ban people from sharing information or linking news from websites."

status: Sustained as of the source reviewed.

title: Belarus: Deutsche Welle and other outlets labeled 'extremist'
summary: A Minsk court declared all output from German broadcaster Deutsche Welle "extremist," alongside a local newspaper and a Russian blogger's videos, making it a crime to produce, store or share the labeled material, as a former correspondent was jailed the same week.
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
what_happened: On March 3, 2022, a Minsk district court sentenced Aleh Hruzdzilovich, a former correspondent for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, to a year and a half in prison over his participation in three protests in 2020. Days later, on March 9, 2022, Minsk's Central District Court declared all information products of Deutsche Welle, Germany's public broadcaster, to be extremist material, effectively banning the outlet inside Belarus. The same order labeled the independent newspaper Regionalnaya Gazeta and videos by Russian blogger Yuriy Dud extremist as well, bringing the total number of outlets Belarus had designated extremist to 20. Under Belarusian law, anyone convicted of producing, storing or sharing material labeled extremist can be fined up to 960 rubles or detained for up to 15 days; Belarus's information ministry separately warned that even subscribing to a labeled outlet's Telegram channel could lead to prosecution.
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
effect_on_reporting: The designation made it a punishable offense inside Belarus to read, store or share Deutsche Welle's reporting, cutting off a foreign broadcaster's audience by criminalizing the audience's own conduct rather than the broadcaster's.
status: Sustained as of the source reviewed.
what_we_dont_know: The sources reviewed do not report whether the designation was later narrowed or lifted.
outcome_note: The designation brought the total number of outlets labeled extremist in Belarus to 20 and was not reported as reversed.
